roles.title: Veterinary Technologists and Technicians
aliases: Internal Medicine Veterinary Technician (Internal Medicine Vet Tech)
roles.description: Perform medical tests in a laboratory environment for use in the treatment and diagnosis of diseases in animals. Prepare vaccines and serums for prevention of diseases. Prepare tissue samples, take blood samples, and execute laboratory tests, such as urinalysis and blood counts. Clean and sterilize instruments and materials and maintain equipment and machines. May assist a veterinarian during surgery.

tasks.label: Administer anesthesia to animals, under the direction of a veterinarian, and monitor animals' responses to anesthetics so that dosages can be adjusted.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Small-animal general practice, surgery suite: dog or cat for elective surgery or dental. Tech calculates and draws drugs, gives IM premed to a conscious, sometimes squirming animal, clips and places an IV catheter, induces with IV propofol/alfaxalone to effect, intubates and cuffs the ET tube, connects to the isoflurane circuit, attaches ECG/SpO2/BP/capnograph leads, assesses depth (jaw tone, palpebral reflex, eye position) and titrates the vaporizer, then extubates and monitors recovery.

Small-animal clinic, sedation without intubation for short procedures (radiographs, laceration repair, ear flush, mass aspirate, fractious cat). Tech restrains a resistant, awake animal, gives IM/IV sedation, watches respiration, mucous membranes, and response to stimulation, tops up or reverses the dose, and monitors until the animal is sternal.

Emergency/specialty or teaching hospital: high-risk patient (geriatric, brachycephalic, cardiac, trauma, C-section, MRI). Tech places catheters, inducts and intubates, runs CRIs and multiple monitors, responds to hypotension, apnea, arrhythmias or light plane by adjusting vaporizer, boluses, and vasopressor rates, often on a mechanical ventilator, under a veterinarian's direction.

High-volume spay/neuter or shelter clinic (including mobile units): batches of dogs and cats on injectable protocols, weight-based dosing, IM injection in kennel, mask or IV induction, intubation for larger dogs, rapid-turnover monitoring of several patients in a row and staged recoveries in cages.

Equine or other large-animal work: standing sedation on a farm or at a hospital stocks for dentistry/laceration repair, or field/hospital induction and recumbency for castration or colic surgery. Uneven footing, an animal that can injure handlers, dose titrated by head position, ataxia, and response to stimulation.

Laboratory animal facility (research institution, AAALAC-standard vivarium/procedure room): protocol-driven anesthesia of rodents, e.g., weigh the mouse, place it in an isoflurane induction chamber or give IP ketamine/xylazine, confirm depth by toe pinch, transfer to a nose cone on a warming pad, apply eye lube, monitor respiration and adjust vaporizer through the procedure, then observe recovery.

sources.title: Closed-loop control of anesthetic state in nonhuman primates | PNAS Nexus
sources.claim: A closed-loop anesthesia delivery (CLAD) system autonomously titrated propofol infusion in rhesus macaques from an LFP-derived marker of unconsciousness, controlling depth for the maintenance period only; the IV catheter, electrode implants, induction, and airway care were done by humans in a research lab.
sources.transferJustification: Directly relevant to the 'monitor responses so dosages can be adjusted' element, but it is a sub-step: the machine only titrates an already-established IV infusion in an instrumented, restrained animal; it does not restrain, catheterize, induce, intubate, or recover the animal.

sources.title: A new way to monitor induced comas | MIT News
sources.claim: A closed-loop anesthetic delivery system controlled propofol dosing in rats in real time from EEG burst-suppression, i.e. automated dose adjustment during maintenance in a laboratory rodent, with catheterization, induction and instrumentation performed by researchers.
sources.transferJustification: Related task (medically induced coma in rats) shares the dose-titration-from-physiologic-feedback element of this task, but covers only maintenance titration through a pre-placed IV line, not the handling, induction, airway, or recovery steps.

sources.system: Computer-controlled closed-loop norepinephrine infusion system (Sasaki et al.)
sources.developer: National Cerebral and Cardiovascular Center / collaborators (Japan)
sources.title: Computer-controlled closed-loop norepinephrine infusion system for automated control of mean arterial pressure in dogs under isoflurane-induced hypotension: a feasibility study
sources.claim: A computer-controlled closed-loop infusion system automatically titrated norepinephrine to a mean-arterial-pressure target in isoflurane-anesthetized dogs; the anesthesia itself, catheter placement, and airway management were performed by veterinary staff.
sources.transferJustification: Related task (automated intra-operative blood-pressure support in dogs) shows automated drug titration is feasible in canine anesthesia, but it manages a vasopressor in an already anesthetized, instrumented dog rather than delivering or adjusting the anesthetic itself.

sources.system: SomnoSuite Low-Flow Anesthesia System with Integrated Digital Vaporizer
sources.title: Kent Scientific SomnoSuite Low-Flow Anesthesia System with Integrated Digital Vaporizer Mouse, Rat
sources.claim: A commercial low-flow rodent anesthesia system automatically computes and delivers isoflurane dose from the animal's body weight through a chamber or nose cone; the technician still places and positions the animal, checks depth, and decides on changes.

sources.title: First robotic tracheal intubations in humans using the Kepler intubation system - British Journal of Anaesthesia
sources.claim: The best-documented robotic tracheal intubation system was demonstrated in human patients but was driven by an anesthesiologist through a remote joystick interface, i.e. operator-controlled rather than autonomous, and has no animal-airway equivalent.
sources.transferJustification: Related task (endotracheal intubation) is a required step of inhalant anesthesia in dogs and cats; the evidence is negative for autonomy — the device was operator-driven, in humans, with a cooperative, positioned, paralyzed patient.

sources.title: Vitestro gains CE mark for autonomous blood drawing robot - Medical Device Network
sources.claim: The most mature autonomous vascular-access robot performs venipuncture on human patients whose arm is immobilized in the device using ultrasound/near-infrared vein imaging; nothing comparable exists for placing IV catheters in awake, furred, non-cooperative animals.
sources.transferJustification: Related task (peripheral venous access) is a core step of anesthetic induction; transfer fails because the device relies on a cooperative human placing a bare, still arm into a fixture, unlike a fractious, furred veterinary patient.

sources.developer: UC San Diego Advanced Robotics and Controls Lab
sources.title: Humanoid robots complete laparoscopic gallbladder surgery for first time | Fox News
sources.claim: The state of the art for general-purpose robots performing procedures on live animals as of mid-2026 is full teleoperation: surgeons remotely drove humanoid robots through gallbladder removals in anesthetized pigs.
sources.transferJustification: Related task (robotic procedures on live animal patients) bounds the field: even in a purpose-built operating setting, robots working on animals are continuously human-driven, which does not satisfy the limited-intervention requirement.

tasks.label: Care for and monitor the condition of animals recovering from surgery.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Small-animal general practice: a dog or cat recovering from a routine spay/neuter, dental, or mass removal. The tech extubates at the right reflex point, monitors temperature/pulse/respiration and mucous membranes every 5-15 minutes, provides active warming, repositions the sternally recumbent patient, checks the incision and IV catheter, gives pain medication, moves the patient to a recovery kennel, records observations and readies it for discharge.

Emergency/specialty hospital ICU: a post-op critical patient (orthopedic repair, GDV, exploratory laparotomy) monitored over hours to days. Continuous ECG/BP/SpO2 hookup, pain scoring, IV line and CRI management, bandage and drain checks, bladder expression or urinary catheter care, hand-walking outside, syringe feeding, and cleaning soiled bedding and patients.

High-volume spay/neuter or shelter clinic: a dozen or more cats and dogs recovering simultaneously on recovery tables and in stacked kennels. Rapid serial checks for hypothermia, hemorrhage, rough recovery or dysphoria; lifting and transferring animals; warming; watching feral or fractious cats through squeeze-cage handling until they are safe to release or discharge.

Research animal facility: rodents recovering from survival surgery. Placing the mouse or rat on a warming pad, watching for return of righting reflex, returning it to a clean cage, timed analgesic injections, daily wound/suture checks, body weight and body-condition/grimace scoring, and welfare records under an IACUC protocol.

Equine/large-animal hospital: a horse recovering from general anesthesia in a padded recovery stall. Monitoring respiration, pulse, and depth of recovery in a darkened stall, managing head and tail ropes or a sling, controlling attempts to stand, checking the jugular catheter and nasotracheal tube, and monitoring for colic or myopathy after the horse is standing.

sources.title: Robotic Cage Handling System for Tunnel Washers - Getinge
sources.claim: Commercial robotic cage-handling systems automate laboratory animal cage handling within the cage-wash process — empty/dirty cages in a fenced industrial cell, with no live animals handled.
sources.transferJustification: Closest deployed robotics in an animal facility, but it manipulates cages and racks on the wash line, not live post-surgical animals; no monitoring of an animal's physiologic condition, no restraint, medication, or wound assessment, so it does not transfer to post-operative animal care.

sources.system: Laboratory animal management robot (Nikkyo Technos / Yaskawa Electric)

sources.claim: A prototype six-axis robot for laboratory animal colony management performs husbandry tasks — changing cage bedding, topping up food, and changing water — in an enclosed, purpose-built animal room, paired with camera monitoring.
sources.transferJustification: Related task is routine rodent husbandry (bedding/food/water) on caged, healthy animals in a machine-built room. It does not assess recovery from anesthesia, handle or restrain an individual animal for examination, administer analgesia, or check surgical sites, so it does not substantiate post-surgical care.

tasks.label: Maintain controlled drug inventory and related log books.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Small-animal clinic: tech unlocks the controlled-drug safe/cabinet, removes a vial of hydromorphone or counts out 30 tramadol tablets for a client prescription, and records drug, strength, quantity, patient, date, user and the new running balance in the controlled substance log.

Clinic treatment area: tech draws a patient-specific dose from a multi-dose controlled vial, administers it, wastes the residual with a second staff member witnessing, and documents amount administered, amount wasted, witness signature and remaining vial volume in the log.

Periodic (weekly/monthly) reconciliation in the clinic pharmacy: open the safe, physically count every controlled item (tablets in opened bottles, full and partial vials), compare with running log balances, investigate and document any discrepancy, and sign off.

Receiving a controlled-substance order: unpack the shipment, verify contents against the invoice/DEA 222 or CSOS order, record date and quantity received, open a log page with the new balance, and place the stock in the locked safe/cabinet, updating the perpetual inventory.

Compliance cycle for the whole registered location: biennial DEA inventory (physical count of all controlled substances on hand, including anesthesia/crash cart and exam-room stock), maintaining two years of log books and receipts, generating usage/discrepancy reports, and preparing records for a DEA or state board inspection.

Ambulatory/large-animal or mobile-unit practice: maintaining the portable controlled drug box in the practice vehicle, securing it, and making log entries and counts at barns, farms, shelters or roadside stops away from the clinic.

tasks.label: Perform laboratory tests on blood, urine, or feces, such as urinalyses or blood counts, to assist in the diagnosis and treatment of animal health problems.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Companion-animal clinic in-house lab: run a CBC on a canine/feline EDTA tube (invert/mix, drop tube into point-of-care hematology analyzer, run), then wedge-prepare, stain and microscopically review a blood smear when the analyzer flags morphology, platelet clumps or a differential is needed; report to the DVM within minutes.

Clinic lab: serum/plasma chemistry panel or electrolytes - spin the clot tube in a bench centrifuge, separate serum, pipette onto slides/rotor or into a sample cup, load the in-house chemistry analyzer, run the QC-checked panel and enter results in the record.

Clinic lab: complete urinalysis on a cystocentesis or free-catch sample - dipstick chemistry read, specific gravity by refractometer, centrifuge an aliquot, decant, resuspend sediment onto a slide and examine microscopically for cells, crystals, casts and bacteria (or run an automated sediment analyzer cartridge).

Clinic lab: fecal parasite examination - measure a feces aliquot, mix with flotation solution, strain, centrifugal or passive flotation, coverslip, and microscopic read for ova, oocysts and larvae; sometimes a fecal antigen immunoassay or direct saline smear instead.

Veterinary reference, university teaching-hospital or corporate specialty-hospital laboratory: batch processing of many accessioned blood/urine/fecal specimens on higher-throughput racked analyzers with LIS integration, including reflex slide review and result release.

Ambulatory large-animal/equine or shelter work: fecal egg count (McMaster), PCV/total protein by microhematocrit and refractometer, or urine dipstick performed on a truck tailgate, barn tack room or shelter treatment area with portable equipment and variable conditions.

sources.developer: research group publishing in Diagnostics (MDPI); implementation in a centralized medical laboratory
sources.title: Collaborative Robotic Systems for Pre-Analytical Processing of Biological Specimens in a Medical Laboratory
sources.claim: A cobot-based pre-analytical system implemented in a centralized medical laboratory autonomously performs decapping, barcode orientation, analyzer loading, aliquoting and specimen ... LIS integration, cutting labor input 87%.
sources.transferJustification: Human clinical-laboratory specimen handling: identical objects (capped blood/urine tubes in racks) and identical sub-steps (centrifugation, decapping, aliquoting, loading analyzers) to the veterinary technician's blood and urine test workflow.

tasks.label: Prepare and administer medications, vaccines, serums, or treatments, as prescribed by veterinarians.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Companion-animal wellness or shelter/high-volume vaccination: tech reconstitutes or draws up the correct vaccine per the veterinarian's order, confirms patient identity and weight, restrains a dog or cat on an exam table or lap, gives SQ/IM injection at the correct site, watches for reactions, and records lot number and site in the medical record.

Hospitalized/ICU or surgical patient: tech calculates a weight-based dose, draws up injectable drugs (opioids, antibiotics, induction agents), places or uses an IV catheter, gives IV push or sets an infusion/CRI on a pump in the treatment room, and monitors and charts the response.

Oral and topical medications to caged patients in the ward: pilling a fractious cat, syringing liquid antibiotic, applying eye/ear drops or transdermal gel, ensuring the animal swallows, per the treatment sheet.

Dairy or feedlot herd work: routine vaccination and reproductive-hormone shots to cows restrained in a parlor exit lane, headlocks, or a squeeze chute, identified by ear tag/RFID, with treatments recorded in herd software.

Equine or mixed farm call: IM/IV injection, oral paste dewormer or antibiotic, or wound treatment given to a horse, goat, or calf in a private barn aisle, stall, or paddock with variable handling facilities and footing.

Laboratory animal facility: protocol dosing of rodents (IP/SQ injections, oral gavage, analgesics post-procedure), individually identified, dosed by body weight, with records kept for the IACUC protocol.

tasks.label: Restrain animals during exams or procedures.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Companion-animal clinic exam room: technician holds an awake, mostly cooperative dog or cat on the exam table or floor for a physical exam, vaccination, nail trim, ear flush, or cephalic/jugular venipuncture — continuously reading body language, adjusting grip and position on the veterinarian's cue, and preventing injury to patient and staff.

Clinic treatment area / imaging suite: sedated or anesthetized dog or cat positioned and held for radiographs, dental work, ultrasound, or IV catheter placement — manipulating a limp body and limbs into precise views, holding still through exposure, protecting the airway and lines.

Fractious, fearful, painful or emergency patient: aggressive dog or feral/head-shy cat restrained with towel wrap, muzzle, cat bag or squeeze cage, or held for emergency treatment — unpredictable, fast-changing behavior with high bite/scratch and escape risk.

Large-animal or ambulatory work on farms and stables: cattle, small ruminants, pigs or horses haltered, run into a race/chute/stanchion, or twitched and held for vaccination, blood draw, pregnancy check, foot work or wound care; premises and equipment vary site to site.

Research, teaching or diagnostic animal facility: rodents (and fish/other small species) restrained in a vivarium for dosing, blood collection, physiologic recording or imaging, under standardized protocols and repeated many times per session.
