tasks.label: Dress and suture wounds and apply splints or other protective devices.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Small-animal clinic treatment room: tech cleans/flushes a wound or post-op incision on a dog or cat (often awake or lightly sedated, restrained by a colleague), applies a primary contact dressing, cast padding, conforming gauze and a cohesive outer wrap at correct tension over a limb, tail or torso; also routine bandage changes on hospitalized patients.

Surgery suite: tech closes routine surgical incisions (e.g., spay/neuter, mass removal) or sutures a repaired skin laceration on an anesthetized patient under veterinarian supervision — appositional skin sutures/staples, subcutaneous layer, knot tying and cutting.

Splint/immobilization device: modified Robert Jones bandage, spoon or lateral splint over a fractured or sprained limb, Ehmer or Velpeau sling, on a sedated dog or cat in the clinic treatment area; requires correct limb positioning, padding thickness and pressure to avoid bandage-related injury.

Protective devices on an awake, sometimes uncooperative patient in clinic or at discharge: fitting an Elizabethan collar or recovery suit, taping/wrapping an IV catheter, applying a bandage cover or bootie, and checking fit before sending the animal home.

Large-animal/ambulatory call at a client farm or barn: dressing a leg or hoof wound and applying a standing/support wrap or hoof bandage on a horse (or treating a cow in a chute) in a stall or aisle with dirt bedding, dust, variable footing and a large animal that shifts and may kick.

Emergency/ICU: rapid pressure or stabilizing bandage on an actively bleeding or trauma patient (hit-by-car, degloving, bite wound), painful/fractious animal, time-critical, work interleaved with monitoring and other staff crowding the table.

sources.title: Robot performs first laparoscopic surgery without human help | ScienceDaily

sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic suturing of soft tissue in a live animal. It bears on veterinary suturing because the needle-and-thread manipulation and tissue handling are comparable, but STAR works only on manually marked, laparoscopically presented bowel in a purpose-built research rig, not on an arbitrary skin wound.

sources.transferJustification: Same related task (autonomous soft-tissue suturing); quantifies the residual human intervention that prevents whole-instance completion of a wound closure.

tasks.label: Provide assistance with animal euthanasia and the disposal of remains.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Companion-animal euthanasia in a small-animal clinic exam room with the owner present: the tech carries/positions the dog or cat, places and secures an IV catheter or holds off a vein, restrains and comforts the animal through sedation and the pentobarbital injection, monitors and confirms death by auscultation, then makes a paw print/fur clipping and cleans up.

Post-euthanasia handling of remains at the clinic: wrapping the limp body in a shroud/bag, attaching ID tags matching the owner's private-vs-communal cremation choice, logging the disposition, lifting the 5-70 lb body into a chest freezer or cooler, and later transferring bagged bodies to the crematory service driver at the back door.

High-volume euthanasia at an animal shelter or humane society: scanning microchips and confirming identity/paperwork, restraining fractious or feral cats and dogs, giving pre-euthanasia sedation IM, holding off the vein or assisting IP/IC injection, verifying death on each animal, and moving carcasses to the shelter's freezer or rendering barrel.

Laboratory rodent euthanasia in a research vivarium: retrieving home cages from ventilated racks, docking or loading them into a CO2 chamber/station, running the cycle, applying a required secondary confirmatory method (cervical dislocation, thoracotomy, decapitation) to each animal, then bagging and labeling carcasses and placing them in the carcass/morgue freezer.

In-home (mobile/hospice) euthanasia visit: setting up in a family's living room or yard on a bed, couch or blanket, restraining and catheterizing a pet in an unpredictable layout with family members and other pets present, confirming death, then wrapping the body and carrying it out to the vehicle.

Large-animal euthanasia in the field: assisting the veterinarian with a horse, cow or small-ruminant on a farm or pasture — haltering and controlling the animal, administering sedation, standing clear of the fall, confirming death, and then arranging/assisting carcass removal by loader, winch or rendering truck in mud, weather and uneven footing.

tasks.label: Monitor medical supplies and place orders when inventory is low.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Small companion-animal private practice: the technician walks the treatment area and stock room on a weekly schedule, eyeballs par levels for syringes, needles, IV fluids, bandaging material, vaccines and common injectables, notes shortfalls on a running list or whiteboard, and then submits the order through a distributor's web portal (e.g., Covetrus, Patterson, MWI) or by phone with the rep.

Multi-doctor referral, specialty or 24-hour emergency hospital with a practice-management/inventory module: the technician reviews automated low-stock and usage reports, performs cycle counts with a barcode scanner to reconcile on-hand quantities against the system, adjusts reorder points, and generates purchase requisitions routed to the practice manager for approval.

Controlled-substance and high-value drug monitoring: the technician reconciles counts of ketamine, hydromorphone, butorphanol, etc. against the controlled-drug log, identifies discrepancies and near-depleted items, and initiates reorder through the DEA-compliant ordering process (CSOS/222 form or licensed distributor account).

Diagnostic laboratory / university teaching hospital setting: the technologist tracks reagents, test cartridges, stains, culture media and lab consumables, checks lot numbers and expiration dates, rotates stock, and orders through institutional procurement or e-procurement systems with cost-center coding.

Mobile or large-animal ambulatory practice: the technician checks the inventory carried in the practice vehicle before and after farm calls (vaccines, anthelmintics, sedatives, obstetric and surgical supplies, cold-chain items), reconciles what was used against records, and places restock orders with the clinic or distributor.

instances.label: Senior vet tech at a small-animal general practice orients and coaches a newly hired veterinary assistant: explains clinic protocols for patient intake, watches the new hire perform restraint and blood draws, gives verbal corrections and feedback, and signs off when the skill is judged competent.

Credentialed technician at a teaching hospital or clinic hosting a vet-tech program supervises externship students on a rotation: assigns cases, observes and critiques technique on anesthesia monitoring, radiographic positioning and lab work, answers questions, and completes the school's competency evaluation forms.

Lead/head technician at a multi-doctor practice or emergency hospital supervises a shift of technicians and assistants: sets task assignments and priorities, oversees workflow and treatment sheets, monitors adherence to protocols and safety rules, intervenes when errors or capacity problems occur, and documents performance issues.

Technician in a research, diagnostic-lab, or shelter setting trains staff on new equipment, SOPs, biosafety and controlled-substance handling: delivers in-service instruction, demonstrates and explains procedures, checks understanding, and records completed training for compliance.
Technician mentors a junior colleague informally over time — coaching on client communication, case discussion, career development, and periodic performance conversations with the practice manager.

tasks.label: Bathe animals, clip nails or claws, and brush or cut animals' hair.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine nail trim on a dog in a veterinary clinic treatment area: tech (often with a second person) restrains the patient on a table or floor, lifts each paw, judges the quick on light and dark nails, clips or grinds 16-20 nails, applies styptic if a nail bleeds; the patient may pull away, vocalize or struggle.

Claw trim on a cat, rabbit, ferret or bird in a clinic exam/treatment room: towel or scruff restraint of a fractious or fearful animal, extending each digit, trimming very small nails close to but not into the quick, sometimes with a second tech restraining or under sedation.

Clipping hair for a medical purpose: shaving a surgical site, IV catheter or ultrasound window, clipping fur around a wound, abscess or bandage, or shaving out badly matted fur, using electric clippers close to skin on an anesthetized or restrained live animal without nicking skin.
Routine full bath and dry of a reasonably cooperative dog in a clinic or boarding tub: wet down, shampoo, scrub, rinse, towel and force- or cage-dry before discharge or after a dirty stay.

Difficult bathing: medicated/dermatologic bath with prescribed contact time, bathing a cat, or cleaning a soiled, painful, post-operative or recumbent hospitalized patient whose catheters and bandages must stay dry.
Brushing, combing, de-shedding or de-matting a hospitalized or boarding patient in the ward, including grooming long-haired or debilitated animals in the cage or on a table between treatments.

Grooming on a farm call, mobile practice or in a client's home/barn: brushing a horse or livestock animal before a procedure, hosing/washing a large animal, or bathing a pet at the owner's house on a house-call visit.

tasks.label: Conduct specialized procedures, such as animal branding or tattooing or hoof trimming.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: High-volume spay/neuter or general small-animal clinic: applying the permanent identification (sterilization) tattoo — a short green ink line/mark — to the shaved, prepped abdominal skin of an anesthetized dog or cat on the surgery table, then confirming the mark is legible and recording it.

Permanent ID marking on conscious, manually restrained animals: ear tattoo with tattoo pliers/ink in a shelter cat or rabbit, lab rodent ear/tail tattoo, calfhood brucellosis ("bangs") ear tattoo, greyhound/horse lip tattoo, plus microchip implantation and verification — animal squirming, thin pinna held against a backing, ink rubbed in.

Dairy or beef herd on-farm hoof (claw) trimming: cows run into a hydraulic tilt/stand chute, feet lifted and secured, functional trim of both claws with an angle grinder and hoof knife, paring out sole ulcers/white-line lesions, gluing a block on the healthy claw and wrapping, in a manure-splashed barn alley.

Equine practice at a boarding barn, farm call, or hospital: holding up and cleaning a horse's foot, paring the sole/hoof wall with knife and nippers, rasping an overgrown hoof, pulling a shoe, opening and packing an abscess, applying a hoof wrap or treatment plate on a standing, shifting horse.

Small ruminant, camelid, or swine foot care on a farm or hobby holding: goats/sheep held on a stand or tipped onto the rump, alpacas restrained in a chute, overgrown hooves trimmed with shears and hoof knife, footrot lesions pared and treated; pens and footing vary site to site.

Ranch/feedlot branding and identification day: hot-iron or freeze branding calves and horses in a squeeze chute or roped on the ground in a pasture, plus ear tagging and tattooing, in dust, wind, and crowding, with animals struggling.

sources.system: Blackdot tattoo device / AERO (Artist Enabled Robotic Operator)
sources.title: Blackdot's AI Tattoo Machine is Essentially a Robot That Inks Your Skin - TechEBlog
sources.claim: Blackdot's robotic tattoo device uses a robotic arm with camera/laser skin-surface mapping and AI-set needle depth to deposit ink autonomously into living skin after an operator uploads and sizes the design; it is in commercial operation in tattoo studios.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: tattooing human skin in a studio. It transfers to the veterinary identification tattoo on an anesthetized patient because the object is the same class (soft, deformable living skin prepared and presented flat at a fixed station), the precision demanded of a legible ID mark is far below the sub-millimeter grayscale work the device already delivers, and the patient under anesthesia is as motionless as a seated client. It does not transfer to ear-pinna plier tattoos on conscious animals or to hoof work.

sources.claim: The Blackdot machine is deployed and doing paid tattoo work in a commercial studio, with the human artist supplying only the design.
sources.transferJustification: Same transfer as above: it establishes that the device performs the marking itself, at worker-acceptable quality, in routine paid use rather than as a one-off demo.

roles.title: Ophthalmic Medical Technicians
aliases: Certified Ophthalmic Medical Technician (Certified Ophthalmic Medical Tech)
roles.description: Assist ophthalmologists by performing ophthalmic clinical functions. May administer eye exams, administer eye medications, and instruct the patient in care and use of corrective lenses.

tasks.label: Take and document patients' medical histories.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Conduct tonometry or tonography tests to measure intraocular pressure.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Goldmann applanation tonometry (GAT) at the slit lamp in an ophthalmology exam lane for a glaucoma, ocular-hypertension or post-op patient: tech instills anesthetic/fluorescein drops, seats and aligns the patient at the slit lamp, swings in the prism, advances it into corneal contact, turns the dial until the mires just touch, reads mmHg, disinfects the tip and records the value for the physician's target-IOP decision.

Automated non-contact (air-puff) tonometry at a pre-test station during a routine comprehensive exam: cooperative adult is seated, chin/forehead placed on the instrument rest, tech instructs the patient to keep both eyes open and fixate, triggers measurement of both eyes, checks reliability indicators, repeats if flagged, records IOP.

Handheld contact tonometry in the exam lane on a cooperative adult — iCare rebound tonometer or Tono-Pen — used because the practice's standard is handheld, or because the cornea is irregular/edematous/post-surgical or the patient cannot be positioned at the slit lamp; tech holds the probe 4-8 mm from and perpendicular to the corneal apex, takes multiple readings, checks the reliability indicator, records IOP.

Tonometry on a difficult or non-standard patient: young child, patient with dementia or blepharospasm, wheelchair user, supine patient at the bedside or in the OR/procedure room; requires coaxing or lid-holding, an approach angle chosen on the fly, handheld rebound or Tono-Pen measurement, and judgment about which readings to trust.

Extended IOP testing: electronic tonography (weighted tonometer held on the anesthetized cornea of a supine patient for ~4 minutes with continuous tracing), diurnal IOP curves with repeated timed measurements, or water-drinking provocative testing, with tracing/series prepared for the ophthalmologist.

sources.title: TX-20 Full Auto Tonometer | Canon Medical Systems USA
sources.claim: Canon's TX-20 'Full Auto' non-contact tonometer uses three-dimensional pupil tracking and, after a single button press, automatically aligns to and measures IOP in both eyes of a patient resting at the instrument; a commercially sold clinical device.

sources.title: CT-800/CT-800A - Topcon Healthcare - APAC
sources.claim: Topcon's CT-800A non-contact tonometer performs 3D auto-alignment and automatic measurement once the operator completes an initial coarse alignment of the seated patient; standard equipment in ophthalmology and optometry clinics.

sources.title: Reichert 7CR | Auto Tonometer | Corneal Response Technology
sources.claim: The Reichert 7CR auto tonometer measures IOP with fully automated alignment and measurement while the patient simply leans against a forehead rest, without a chinrest; widely deployed commercial clinic instrument.

sources.system: Topcon TRK-3 OMNIA automated non-contact tonometer
sources.developer: Topcon Healthcare (study at Illinois College of Optometry and UC San Diego)
sources.title: Clinical Assessment of Automated Non-Contact Tonometer: Interchangeability with Goldmann Applanation Tonometry and Repeatability
sources.claim: A prospective multicenter clinical study of 120 subjects found the automated non-contact tonometer TRK-3 OMNIA statistically equivalent to Goldmann applanation tonometry within a predefined +/-5 mmHg margin, with excellent repeatability (ICC 0.94), supporting routine clinical use of automated air-puff IOP readings.

sources.title: Contactless optical coherence tomography of the eyes of freestanding individuals with a robotic scanner
sources.claim: A robot-mounted OCT scanner autonomously locates and tracks the eye of a freestanding human subject and acquires retinal volumes of tabletop quality with no operator intervention and no chinrest or headrest; a research demonstration (later piloted on emergency-department patients).
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous robotic alignment of an ophthalmic instrument to a patient's eye without head fixation. It shows the alignment sub-step of tonometry is achievable robotically outside a fixtured presentation, but it is imaging only - no air puff, no corneal contact, and no validated IOP output - so it does not substantiate completion of a tonometry instance.

sources.date: 2022 start; status verified 2025-06, TERMINATED ("device updates needed")
sources.title: Automated Applanation Tonometry | Clinical Research Trial Listing (NCT05235321)
sources.claim: Efforts to automate Goldmann applanation tonometry remain at the prototype stage: a Duke University clinical study to develop an automated, objective applanation method using standard slit-lamp equipment and two portable prototypes was terminated because the device needed updates.

tasks.label: Operate ophthalmic equipment, such as autorefractors, phoropters, tomographs, or retinoscopes.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine pre-test workup in an ophthalmology/optometry clinic pretest room: a cooperative adult is seated at a table-mounted autorefractor/keratometer, chin and forehead positioned, instrument aligned to each eye, objective refraction and Ks captured and transferred to the chart/EHR.

Subjective refraction in the exam lane: technician sets up the (manual or digital) phoropter at the patient's PD, loads the objective starting point, runs sphere/cylinder/axis refinement, JCC, binocular balance and acuity, and records the final refraction and best-corrected acuity for a cooperative adult.

Diagnostic imaging on an adult clinic patient with eye disease: macular/optic-nerve OCT or corneal tomography — select scan protocol, seat and position patient at the instrument, align, focus, capture both eyes, check signal/image quality, repeat scans as needed, save and print report.

Testing patients who cannot self-direct: young children (retinoscopy with a handheld retinoscope and loose lenses or handheld autorefractor, often cycloplegic), nonverbal or demented adults, wheelchair-bound, tremulous, low-vision or post-op patients — technician physically supports/repositions the patient, chases fixation, and interprets a reflex or partial data.

Off-site vision screening of ambulatory adults: health fair, worksite, retail/optical venue or mobile unit, where a station is set up and a stream of adults is measured with refraction/acuity equipment and results handed off for doctor review.

Off-site testing with portable equipment where the patient cannot come to a station: preschool/school screening lines, nursing-home rooms, or hospital bedside/OR with handheld autorefractor, portable topographer or handheld OCT carried to the patient.

sources.title: This AI Bot Has A Rapid View on Vision Testing - Techstrong.ai
sources.claim: Eyebot S1 is a self-service, fully autonomous vision-testing kiosk that performs a complete vision test (acuity plus wavefront aberrometry-based refraction) on a walk-up patient in about 90 seconds with no technician present, yielding a doctor-verified spectacle prescription.

sources.title: Eyebot Vision Kiosks Pilot at Walmart, Sam's Club in PA - Review of Optometric Business

sources.system: Topcon CV-5000 phoropter with SightPilot NAVi

sources.title: Comparison of a Novel Binocular Refraction System with Standard Digital Phoropter Refraction - PMC
sources.claim: Peer-reviewed comparison in 70 adults found the Chronos automated binocular refraction system agrees with standard digital phoropter subjective refraction with no clinically significant bias, supporting worker-quality output from the automated refraction sequence.

sources.title: Contactless, autonomous robotic alignment of optical coherence tomography for in vivo evaluation of diseased retinas - PMC
sources.claim: Duke's robotically aligned OCT (RAOCT) autonomously finds and tracks the eye of a seated/standing patient without a chinrest and captures retinal OCT volumes; in a powered clinical study of healthy and diseased retinas its measurements matched technician-operated clinical OCT.

sources.system: Robotic OCT scanner (robot arm-mounted scan head)
sources.title: Contactless optical coherence tomography of the eyes of freestanding individuals with a robotic scanner | Nature Biomedical Engineering
sources.claim: A robot-mounted OCT scanner acquired volumetric retinal images of freestanding human subjects by robotically positioning itself to the eye and actively compensating pupil location and eye motion, removing the head-stabilization and manual alignment a technician normally provides.

sources.system: Maestro2 (3D OCT-1) robotic OCT fundus camera

sources.claim: Topcon's Maestro2, marketed as a robotic OCT/fundus camera and widely installed in eye clinics, executes alignment, focus, optimization and capture of the OCT and colour fundus image automatically after a single touch.

sources.claim: Notal Vision's SCANLY Home OCT, granted FDA De Novo authorization in May 2024, performs technician-free OCT scanning: in the pivotal study 97% of patients obtained usable OCT images themselves, the device handling fixation, alignment and capture.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: OCT image capture performed without a trained operator. Same modality, same alignment/fixation precision and same acceptance criterion (gradable retinal volume) as the technician's clinic OCT capture, so the automated capture chain transfers.

tasks.label: Take anatomical or functional ocular measurements of the eye or surrounding tissue, such as axial length measurements.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Pre-operative cataract/refractive biometry in an ophthalmology clinic testing lane: cooperative adult seated at a table-mounted optical biometer (IOLMaster/ARGOS/Lenstar/OA-2000); tech adjusts table and chin/forehead rest, instructs fixation, acquires axial length, keratometry, ACD, lens thickness and white-to-white on both eyes, checks quality/SNR flags, repeats poor scans, exports to the IOL calculator.

Routine automated pretest battery in a clinic workup lane on cooperative adults: autorefraction/keratometry, non-contact tonometry, corneal topography/pachymetry and macular/RNFL OCT thickness measurements; patient moved between table-mounted instruments, positioned at the chin rest, results pushed to the EHR.

Functional testing requiring sustained patient cooperation and coaching: standard automated perimetry (Humphrey visual field) or similar - tech enters refractive correction, patches the fellow eye, positions the head, explains and re-instructs during the test, watches fixation losses/false positives, repeats unreliable tests.

Difficult patients and contact measurements: pediatric, demented, tremulous, deaf, wheelchair-bound or poorly fixating patients; dense cataracts or staphyloma where optical biometry fails and contact/immersion A-scan ultrasound or contact pachymetry is required after instilling topical anesthetic and touching the cornea with a probe.

Hand-held measurements of the eye and surrounding tissue in an exam room: Hertel exophthalmometry braced on the lateral orbital rims, eyelid measurements (MRD1/MRD2, palpebral fissure, levator function) with a millimeter ruler against the patient's face, corneal diameter and pupil size with a gauge.

Off-site screening: tech travels to a nursing home, school, mobile van or health fair and takes acuity, autorefraction, IOP and imaging measurements with portable devices in a room not designed for eye testing, with variable lighting, seating and participant cooperation.

sources.title: Topcon Maestro2 – The Robotic OCT Fundus Camera with OCTA
sources.claim: Commercial table-mounted OCT/fundus camera marketed as a 'robotic' instrument that performs eye alignment, focusing and capture automatically and outputs retinal, RNFL, ganglion-cell and macular thickness measurements; in routine use in optometry/ophthalmology clinics.
sources.transferJustification: Same task family: an anatomical ocular measurement (retinal/RNFL/GCL thickness) acquired by the instrument itself in a clinic lane - the measurement an ophthalmic technician would otherwise align and capture.

sources.title: ARGOS® Optical Biometer | Alcon Professional Global
sources.claim: Commercial swept-source optical biometer that automatically records axial length and associated biometric values when the patient's eye reaches optimal alignment, without operator steps.

sources.claim: Peer-reviewed clinical reproducibility study of an optical biometer whose auto-shot mode removes operator alignment error, measuring axial length on patients in a clinical setup.

sources.title: CT-1/CT-1P - Topcon Healthcare - APAC
sources.claim: Commercial non-contact tonometer with 3D auto-alignment that completes intraocular pressure measurement of both eyes automatically after a single screen touch.
sources.transferJustification: Intraocular pressure is a functional ocular measurement routinely taken by ophthalmic technicians; the instrument aligns to the eye and fires the measurement itself.

sources.title: This AI Bot Has A Rapid View on Vision Testing - Techstrong.ai
sources.claim: Self-service kiosk that performs objective refraction and vision measurement on a walk-up patient in about 90 seconds with no operator present.
sources.transferJustification: Refraction/autorefraction is a functional ocular measurement in the same pretest battery; it shows an unattended machine can align to and measure a walk-up patient's eyes to a clinically usable standard.

sources.title: Automated vision-testing kiosks face concerns amid national expansion
sources.claim: Eyebot kiosks are in commercial operation inside optical retail settings, including pilots in Walmart Vision Centers and Sam's ..., and in malls, universities and grocery stores.

sources.title: The Ophthalmologist | OCT Closer to Home
sources.claim: FDA de novo-authorized home OCT device that patients operate themselves, capturing SD-OCT volumes of the macula that are automatically analyzed for retinal fluid.
sources.transferJustification: Retinal OCT imaging/fluid quantification is an anatomical ocular measurement of the kind technicians capture in clinic; here the device aligns and captures with no technician present.

sources.title: Contactless optical coherence tomography of the eyes of freestanding individuals with a robotic scanner
sources.claim: Research robotic scanner that autonomously positions itself and images the eyes of freestanding people without a chin rest, compensating for head and eye motion.
sources.transferJustification: Demonstrates autonomous robotic alignment to a human eye for an anatomical ocular measurement without headrest fixation - the alignment sub-task technicians perform.

sources.system: ZEISS Humphrey Field Analyzer 3 (HFA3) with Liquid Trial Lens / Head Tracker
sources.title: ZEISS HFA3 800 series Liquid Trial Lens white paper
sources.claim: Commercial perimeter with automated eye alignment and a motorized chin rest that re-centers the patient's eye behind the trial lens during the visual field test.
sources.transferJustification: Standard automated perimetry is the principal functional ocular measurement technicians perform; the machine handles refractive correction, alignment and stimulus presentation once the patient is set up.

tasks.label: Measure visual acuity, including near, distance, pinhole, or dynamic visual acuity, using appropriate tests.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine ophthalmology clinic visit: cooperative, verbal adult seated in the exam lane. Technician measures distance acuity each eye and both eyes, with and without habitual correction, using a projected/digital Snellen or ETDRS chart at the standard test distance, occluding one eye and recording OD/OS/OU in the chart.

Near acuity on a cooperative adult (usually presbyopic): technician hands or positions a near card / near chart at ~40 cm under adequate illumination, with reading correction in place, tests each eye and both eyes, and records the near acuity notation.

Pinhole acuity: distance acuity comes back reduced (worse than ~20/30), so the technician places a pinhole occluder in front of the eye, re-presents the chart, coaches the patient to find the hole, and records pinhole acuity for each affected eye.

Adult with poor vision or limited cooperation in the clinic or at the bedside/pre-op area: dense cataract, macular degeneration, post-op or trauma patient, hearing-impaired or cognitively impaired, wheelchair-bound or non-ambulatory. Requires coaching, moving the chart or the technician closer, and stepwise testing down to counting fingers, hand motion, and light perception with a transilluminator.

Pediatric or preverbal/nonverbal patient: technician selects an age-appropriate test (LEA symbols, HOTV with matching cards, tumbling E, Allen pictures, fixation-and-follow or fixation-preference), keeps the child engaged, prevents peeking around the patch/occluder, and records an acuity estimate.

sources.system: NIDEK/Marco TS-610 with Fully Assisted Refraction System (FARS)
sources.title: TS-610 with Fully Assisted Refraction System (FARS) » Marco
sources.claim: The NIDEK/Marco TS-610 tabletop refraction system with the Fully Assisted Refraction System (FARS) is a commercially sold, clinic-installed instrument whose motorized refractor head and integrated acuity chart run the acuity/refraction test itself: the patient is set up by staff, then completes the test alone with machine voice guidance and a response controller.

sources.title: Fully Assisted Refraction System for the TS-610 | NIDEK CO.,LTD.
sources.claim: Manufacturer documentation for FARS confirms the machine, not an operator, drives the test sequence: voice guidance issues the instructions, the patient answers with a joystick, the machine advances according to the responses, and a help button escalates to staff only if needed.

sources.title: Nidek Launches Fully Assisted Refraction System for TS-610 - Eyewire+
sources.claim: Trade coverage of the FARS launch confirms the patient can be left alone with the instrument during the test, with staff monitoring remotely - i.e. limited intervention rather than continuous operation.

sources.system: NIDEK TS-610 tabletop refraction system (RT-6100 head)
sources.title: Nidek Tabletop Refraction System TS-610 - Malaysia Ophthalmic Innovator
sources.claim: The TS-610 combines the motorized RT-6100 refractor head with a chart display that switches between distance (5 m) and near (40 cm) presentation, so the same instrument performs both distance and near visual acuity testing.
