sources.title: Chronos Automated Binocular Refraction System | Topcon Healthcare
sources.claim: Topcon's Chronos is an all-in-one automated ... instrument that includes visual acuity measurement; with SightPilot NAVi the patient completes the objective and subjective steps through machine-issued prompts rather than technician-by-technician control, and it is marketed and installed in ophthalmology (including cataract/refractive) practices.

sources.title: Chronos - Topcon Healthcare - APAC
sources.claim: Chronos physically actuates its measurement heads and lenses (theta movement mechanism, lens movement) to set convergence and test distance anywhere from 25 cm to 6 m, so both near-point and distance acuity targets are presented by machine-controlled optics.
sources.transferJustification: Hardware-specification item showing the mechanical actuation and near/distance target presentation of the machine whose autonomous guided operation is documented in item 4.

sources.title: The Ophthalmologist | Reinventing Patient Care
sources.claim: The subjective test battery run on Chronos includes visual acuity charts and near addition charts, i.e. near as well as distance acuity are part of the instrument's guided sequence.
sources.transferJustification: Capability item on the test battery of the instrument whose autonomous patient-guided operation is documented in item 4.

sources.title: Clinical validity of automated refraction with the Chronos binocular refraction system compared to standard refraction techniques - PubMed
sources.claim: A peer-reviewed single-centre clinical study compared guided automated refraction and acuity on Chronos against standard autorefraction plus manual subjective refraction and found good agreement, supporting that the machine's output is clinically acceptable in routine practice.
sources.transferJustification: Quality benchmark: establishes that measurements taken through the automated instrument agree with the technician/clinician-performed standard method for the same patients in the same clinic.

sources.system: Marco TRS-5100 digital refractor (NIDEK RT-5100 family)
sources.title: Marco TRS-5100 Digital Refractor - Ophthalmicmart
sources.claim: Motorized digital refractor heads of this class carry a machine-inserted pinhole aperture among their auxiliary lenses, but the pinhole is selected from an operator console rather than by an autonomous test program.
sources.transferJustification: Cited only to document that pinhole capability in these machines is operator-selected; it is used in a negative judgment, not to support completion.

tasks.label: Measure and record lens power, using lensometers.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine adult patient workup in an ophthalmology clinic pre-test room: technician takes the patient's single-vision spectacles, places them on the lens table of an auto-lensmeter, aligns the optical center, reads OD/OS sphere, cylinder and axis, and types the values into the EHR/chart before the exam.

Patient presents with progressive-addition or bifocal/trifocal spectacles: technician must locate the distance reference point and the near zone (or engraved PAL markings), measure distance power plus the add for each eye, and record both sets of values in the chart.

Clinic equipped with a manual lensometer (Bausch & Lomb / Topcon type): technician looks through the eyepiece, focuses the sphere and cylinder targets by turning the power drum and axis wheel, reads diopters and axis by eye, then hand-records the result.

Prism / centration work: verifying prescribed prism amount and base direction (e.g., strabismus or diplopia patients), checking for unwanted induced prism or decentration, and dotting/marking the optical centers on the lenses with the lensometer's inking device; results recorded in the chart.

Verifying a newly finished pair of spectacles in the practice's optical dispensary/finishing bench: neutralizing the edged, mounted lenses against the written Rx (sphere, cyl, axis, add, prism, PD/optical-center height) and signing off the job ticket before dispensing to the patient.

Non-standard items the routine flow cannot accept: rigid gas-permeable contact lens power checked on the lensometer with a contact-lens holder, warped or broken frames, very small pediatric frames, and aphakic high-plus lenses beyond typical instrument range; measured and recorded.

sources.system: Automation & Robotics AutoMapper V3 (with integrated Dual LensMapper)
sources.title: AutoMapper For Prescription Lenses — Automation & Robotics
sources.claim: A&R's AutoMapper V3 is a commercial, fully automatic lens-inspection unit integrated into prescription-lab lines that maps a spectacle lens and computes optical power at the distance and near reference points, plus prism and thickness, at 150 jobs/hour, exporting Go/NoGo results.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: in-line optical verification of prescription lenses in a lab rather than a clinic lensometer. Same measurand and precision (sphere, cylinder, axis, prism, near add, to ±0.02 D), same object class (finished spectacle lenses, uncut or cut), and the result is exported/recorded automatically, which is what the clinic task requires.

sources.system: Automation & Robotics MCEVS V2 Control and Packaging Unit for Stock Lenses
sources.title: Control and Packaging Unit for Stock Lenses MCEVS V2 — Automation & Robotics
sources.claim: The MCEVS V2 control-and-packaging unit automatically inspects the optical power (±0.02 D), prism and thickness of stock spectacle lenses and packs them at up to 900 lenses/hour on a fully automatic cycle; more than 100 units are installed worldwide.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated power/prism verification of spectacle lenses in a purpose-built production cell, including mechanical handling of each lens. It substantiates that machine-controlled equipment can measure lens power to clinical tolerance and act on the result without an operator handling each lens.

sources.system: Automation & Robotics Control & Inking Unit for Rx lenses (MCVP8 V2)
sources.title: AR - Control & Inking Unit for Rx lenses
sources.claim: A&R's Control & Inking Unit for Rx lenses is an automatic in-line machine that inspects all lens types to ISO/ANSI standards, maps freeform lenses, digitally inks reference/optical-center marks and laser engraves, and exports the measurement data for process control.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated lens verification plus marking in a lab line. It covers both halves of the clinic task—measuring power/prism and physically dotting optical-center or reference marks—and the exported measurement data is the recording step.

sources.title: AR - MEVP-V2 (AutoPacker) - Automation & Robotics
sources.claim: A&R's AutoPacker automatically unloads spectacle lenses from job trays, centers them, packages and labels them at 300 jobs/hour, with an operator needed only to refill consumables — evidence that machine handling of loose spectacle lenses in a lab line is routine.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: workpiece handling rather than measurement. It shows the presentation/loading step assumed by the E1 counterfactual (lens taken from a tray and centered at a station) is performed by machine at production rates in this exact object class.

sources.system: Visionix VX 40 Pro Auto Lensmeter / Lens Verifier
sources.title: Visionix VX 40 Pro Auto-lensmeter / Lens Verifier - Visionix
sources.claim: The Visionix VX 40 Pro auto-lensmeter measures mounted spectacles of any frame and lens type — single-vision, bifocal and progressive — checking sphere, cylinder, axis, prism and optical-center alignment; once the frame is placed the whole analysis, including switching between right and left lens, runs without operator input.
sources.transferJustification: Same task (lensometry of a patient's mounted spectacles), except that the frame is loaded by hand; under the E1 counterfactual the fixture presents the frame, after which the machine performs the alignment, measurement of sphere/cyl/axis/prism/add and output of the values.

sources.title: Dual LensMapper (type DLM) | Automation & Robotics
sources.claim: The A&R Dual LensMapper measures lens power automatically using combined reflection and transmission optics and is the only mapper that corrects for lens position and tilt, which is the failure mode for highly curved wrap frames.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: full-surface power mapping of spectacle lenses. Relevant because it addresses tilted/highly curved lens presentation, the main difficulty in neutralizing wrap and high-base-curve eyewear in the clinic instances.

sources.system: Daifuku/Wynright automated material handling arm in an optical lab
sources.title: Robots Enter the Optical Workforce — 20/20 Magazine
sources.claim: Robotic material handling is already used in optical laboratories: a robot arm supplied by Daifuku/Wynright picked lenses from inventory and paired them with frames in an optical lab installation reported by trade press.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: handling of lenses and frames in an ophthalmic lab. It supports the claim that the presentation/loading portion of lens verification is machine-performed in purpose-built optical facilities, not that the measurement itself is done by this system.

tasks.label: Administer topical ophthalmic or oral medications.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Pre-exam workup in an ophthalmology clinic exam/pretest room: tech verifies the order and allergies, washes hands, tilts a cooperative adult patient's head back, retracts the lower lid, instills one drop each of tropicamide and phenylephrine into the conjunctival sac of each eye without touching the bottle tip to lashes, blots, instructs the patient, and charts the drug/dose/time.

Diagnostic/anesthetic drops before tonometry or pachymetry: proparacaine plus fluorescein instilled in the exam lane, often with the patient seated at a slit lamp chin rest, immediately before an IOP measurement; drop must land on the ocular surface and take effect within seconds.

Difficult patients: young children, patients with tremor, blepharospasm, photophobia, dementia, or strong blink/squeeze reflex; requires coaxing, forcible but gentle lid separation or the closed-lid/inner-canthus technique, repeat attempts, and confirmation the drop reached the eye.

Peri-procedure regimen in a laser or ambulatory surgery suite: a timed sequence of dilating, antibiotic, NSAID and anesthetic drops repeated at set intervals, plus applying a ribbon of ophthalmic ointment into the lower fornix of a supine, sometimes sedated post-procedure patient.

Administering an oral medication per physician order in the clinic (e.g., acetazolamide tablet, antihistamine, or oral analgesic/anxiolytic): confirm order and allergies, retrieve the dose from clinic stock, identify the patient, hand the pill with water, observe it is taken, and document.

sources.developer: Duke University (Kuo, McNabb, Izatt, Draelos et al.)
sources.title: Contactless, autonomous robotic alignment of optical coherence tomography for in vivo evaluation of diseased retinas
sources.claim: Duke's robotically aligned OCT (RAOCT) autonomously tracks the face and pupil and images the retinas of awake human patients in a clinical study, but it is a contactless imaging system that delivers no medication and never touches the eye or eyelids.
sources.transferJustification: Closest autonomous robot acting on awake human eyes in an eye clinic. It substantiates autonomous eye/face tracking and precise positioning near the eye, but not the task in question: it delivers no drug, does not retract lids, does not verify that a drop landed, and has no liquid-delivery end effector, so it cannot substantiate completing topical medication administration.

sources.system: Autonomous retinal vein cannulation robot / ARISE-type autonomous intraocular system
sources.developer: Johns Hopkins University (Laboratory for Computational Sensing and Robotics / Wilmer Eye Institute)
sources.title: Autonomous robot takes a step towards high precision eye surgery
sources.claim: Johns Hopkins' autonomous intraocular robot performs targeted retinal vein cannulation, but the demonstrations were on pig eyes in a laboratory microscope setup, and researchers state clinical application is not imminent.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous drug delivery to the eye (intraocular injection). It does not transfer to instilling topical drops in an awake clinic patient — the work was on excised animal eyes under an operating microscope with the globe stabilized, with no awake-patient blink reflex, lid handling, patient identification, or clinic workflow.

sources.system: Eye drop aids (Autodrop, Nanodropper, DropEase and similar)
sources.title: Contemporary Eye Drop Aids - Glaucoma Research Foundation
sources.claim: The current state of practice for assisting eye-drop instillation consists of passive manual attachments and guides held by the patient or caregiver; no robotic instillation system is in clinical use.
sources.transferJustification: Cited to establish that the marketed devices for eye-drop administration are human-aimed mechanical aids, not machine-controlled systems; they cannot support a positive robotic judgment.

sources.title: MedaCube Medication Dispenser - Tech-enhanced Life
sources.claim: The MedaCube is a commercially sold automatic medication dispenser whose internal mechanism autonomously picks individual pills from bulk containers and dispenses the correct dose at the programmed time to the person it serves, alerting them and notifying a caregiver on failure.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: dispensing the correct oral dose to a patient at the correct time. Transfers to the oral-medication instance only under a purpose-built arrangement where the ordered drug is pre-loaded in a canister and the patient presents at the machine; it does not select from open clinic stock or verify patient identity in an ordinary exam room.

tasks.label: Conduct visual field tests to measure field of vision.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine threshold standard automated perimetry (Humphrey 24-2/30-2 SITA) in an ophthalmology or optometry clinic on a cooperative, experienced adult glaucoma or ocular-hypertension patient: tech enters demographics, patches the fellow eye, seats and positions the patient at the chin/forehead rest, sets refractive correction, instructs, starts the test, watches fixation and coaches, checks reliability indices, saves/prints the field.

Standard automated perimetry on a challenging patient in the same clinic: first-timer, frail or elderly, wheelchair transfer, kyphosis, ptosis requiring lid taping, drifting head, poor attention, hearing or cognitive impairment. Requires hands-on repositioning mid-test, pausing and restarting, repeated re-instruction, and often a repeat test to obtain a reliable field.

Confrontation visual field testing at the exam chair or hospital bedside: examiner faces the patient about a meter away, occludes one eye, presents fingers or hand motion in each quadrant, compares the patient's field with the examiner's own, and records the result in the chart.

Short suprathreshold/screening perimetry (FDT Matrix, HFA screening program, or a portable head-mounted screening perimeter) in a clinic lane, pre-op workup, or screening event on mostly healthy cooperative adults; setup, brief instruction, run, save result.

Specialized but machine-run programs on a cooperative adult: Esterman binocular driving/disability field, or semi-automated kinetic perimetry (Octopus 900 / HFA3 kinetic) for neuro-ophthalmic or peripheral field mapping, run with standard vectors or test patterns.

Specialized hands-on perimetry: pediatric or low-vision patients, or ptosis taped/untaped lid fields for oculoplastic documentation, requiring physical adaptation (taping lids, supporting the head, coaxing a child), examiner judgment about stimulus choice, and re-testing.

sources.system: ZEISS Humphrey Field Analyzer 3 (HFA3) with automated eye alignment and Liquid Trial Lens
sources.title: ZEISS HFA3 Humphrey Field Analyzer User Manual
sources.claim: The ZEISS Humphrey Field Analyzer 3, the standard commercial perimeter in US eye clinics, mechanically self-aligns the patient's eye to the ... maintains that alignment during the test, and its Liquid Trial Lens sets the refractive correction under machine control, so that once the patient is at the chin rest the instrument runs the threshold test and produces the field printout with reliability indices.
sources.transferJustification: Same task: this is the instrument that performs the visual field measurement; the cited features are the machine-actuated parts of the technician's setup (eye alignment, refractive correction) that occur after the patient is seated at the perimeter.

sources.system: NAO humanoid robot assistant + Octopus 900 perimeter (Open Perimetry Interface)
sources.developer: University of Melbourne (McKendrick et al.); robot by Aldebaran/SoftBank Robotics; perimeter by Haag-Streit
sources.title: Robot Assistants for Perimetry: A Study of Patient Experience and Performance (TVST)
sources.claim: A NAO humanoid robot delivered the instruction and ongoing feedback role of the perimetrist during Octopus 900 perimetry with no human operator in the room, and measured sensitivity, fixation losses and false positives were statistically indistinguishable from tests supervised in person by an optometrist, in both younger and older adults.
sources.transferJustification: Same task: visual field testing on a clinical perimeter; the robot supplied the coaching and monitoring the technician normally provides, and the study reports no significant effect of feedback ... field measures.

sources.system: Octopus 900 semi-automated kinetic perimetry / HFA3 kinetic
sources.developer: Haag-Streit Diagnostics; Carl Zeiss Meditec (study: KU Leuven, Bevers et al.)
sources.title: Semi-automated kinetic perimetry: Comparison of the Octopus 900 and Humphrey visual field analyzer 3 versus Goldmann perimetry
sources.claim: Semi-automated kinetic perimetry programs on the Octopus 900 and HFA3 move the stimulus along vectors and plot isopters under machine control, and in a prospective patient study were judged reproducible, clinically useful successors to manual Goldmann kinetic perimetry.
sources.transferJustification: Same task family (kinetic visual field measurement); the instrument performs the stimulus movement and isopter recording that a perimetrist performs by hand on a Goldmann bowl.

sources.title: Contactless, autonomous robotic alignment of optical coherence tomography for in vivo evaluation of diseased retinas
sources.claim: A robot-mounted OCT scanner autonomously located and tracked the eye of a seated patient and acquired retinal images without a chin rest or an operator, with retinal thickness and diagnostic readability equal to technician-operated clinical OCT in a powered clinical study at Duke.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous robotic alignment of an ophthalmic instrument to a live patient's eye in a clinic. It shows instrument-to-patient alignment can be robotized, but involves no eye occlusion, no head stabilization for a multi-minute interactive test and no patient coaching, so it does not substantiate completing a visual field test in an ordinary clinic lane.

tasks.label: Assist physicians in performing ophthalmic procedures, including surgery.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Assisting an ophthalmologist with in-office minor procedures in a clinic procedure room or at the slit lamp (corneal foreign-body/rust ring removal, chalazion incision and drainage, punctal plug insertion, lid lesion removal, suture/epilation): setting up and maintaining a sterile tray, instilling anesthetic drops, positioning and steadying the patient's head, handing and receiving fine instruments on the surgeon's call, blotting/irrigating, applying ointment and a patch, then breaking down and cleaning the setup.

Assisting with intravitreal anti-VEGF injections in a retina clinic (very high volume): verifying drug and eye, preparing the injection tray and syringe, instilling proparacaine and povidone-iodine, handing the lid speculum, calipers and loaded syringe to the physician, steadying/reassuring an awake patient, checking vision/light perception afterward, and giving post-injection instructions.

Assisting with in-office laser procedures (YAG capsulotomy, SLT, laser peripheral iridotomy, panretinal photocoagulation): dilating or constricting the eye with drops, seating and aligning the patient in the laser slit-lamp chin/forehead rest, applying coupling gel and handing/holding the contact lens, entering and adjusting laser parameters at the surgeon's direction, monitoring the patient, and cleaning the lens and checking post-laser IOP.

Assisting in the operating room of an ambulatory surgery center or hospital eye OR during cataract, pterygium, oculoplastic or vitreoretinal surgery (scrub or circulating tech role): pre-op dilation drops and skin prep, assisting with draping and microscope/patient positioning, opening sterile supplies, loading the IOL injector, passing microsurgical instruments and irrigation, adjusting the phaco console per the surgeon's calls, counting supplies and turning the room over.

Assisting during examinations and bedside/consult procedures on difficult or non-cooperative patients: holding lids open, applying scleral depression, immobilizing a child's or elderly patient's head, obtaining corneal cultures/scrapings for the physician, assisting with bandage contact lens placement, pressure patching, and helping during eye trauma workups in a hospital or urgent eye clinic.

sources.title: For the First Time, Newly Developed Robot Assists Doctors and Nurses in Operating Room | NYP
sources.claim: The Penelope Surgical Instrument Server, a voice-directed robotic arm, handed and retrieved instruments for a surgical team in a single human operation (benign lipoma excision) in June 2005; it covered only instrument handoff, was described as 'partly autonomous', and never reached commercial deployment.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: surgical instrument handoff, which is one sub-step of an ophthalmic tech's OR assist role. It is cited to show the state of the art in robotic surgical assistance, not to substantiate completion: it excludes patient prep, drops, positioning, retraction and room turnover, and was a one-off 2005 general-surgery case.

sources.title: Initial clinical experience with a partly autonomous robotic surgical instrument server | Surgical Endoscopy
sources.claim: The peer-reviewed clinical report of the same device characterizes it as a partly autonomous instrument server used in one operation, i.e., a first-of-kind trial rather than a worker-quality assistant.
sources.transferJustification: Related task (instrument handoff in surgery). Cited as evidence of the limits of the state of the art: a single case, partial autonomy, and no patient-contact steps of the ophthalmic assist task.

sources.developer: Kang et al., Advanced Intelligent Systems
sources.title: Vision-Based Handover and Organization of Robotic Scrub Nurse for Seamless Surgical Flow
sources.claim: The most recent robotic scrub-nurse work is a laboratory system: a KUKA LBR Med arm with a parallel gripper that estimates the surgeon's hand pose to hand over instruments; it is a bench prototype, not a clinically deployed assistant.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: instrument handover to a surgeon. Cited to show that even this narrow sub-step of the ophthalmic assist task exists only as a laboratory demonstration in 2026, with no patient-side capability.

sources.title: Robotic scrub nurse to anticipate surgical instruments based on real-time laparoscopic video analysis
sources.claim: A robotic scrub nurse that anticipates instruments from live laparoscopic video correctly predicts about 72% of instruments in advance — well below the reliability a surgical team would accept from a technician — and was evaluated on recorded/lab data.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: anticipating and supplying instruments during surgery. Cited to show reliability is far below worker quality even for the single easiest sub-step of the ophthalmic assist role.

sources.system: Teleoperated humanoid surgical robots (UC San Diego)
sources.developer: University of California San Diego (Yip, Liu et al.), published in Nature
sources.title: Surgeons Use Teleoperated Humanoid Robots to Perform Live Surgery–a World First | Newswise
sources.claim: The 2026 milestone for humanoid robots in the operating ... was fully teleoperated surgery on live animals in a preclinical trial; the developers state an autonomous surgical assistant remains a goal, not a capability.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: general surgical assisting/performing by a humanoid in an OR. Cited as a negative bound — the work is teleoperated and preclinical, so it cannot substitute for an ophthalmic technician's autonomous assist role.

sources.title: ForSight Robotics Performs World's First Fully Robot-Assisted Cataract Surgery in a Human Patient - Eyewire+
sources.claim: The leading ophthalmic surgical robot performed its first fully robot-assisted cataract surgery ... in April 2026, but the platform is surgeon-controlled (it replicates the surgeon's workflow) and is still moving toward clinical validation and regulatory submission; it does not perform the technician's assisting duties.
sources.transferJustification: Same clinical domain (ophthalmic surgery) but the surgeon's role, under surgeon control. Cited to show that even in eye surgery the robot occupies the operator seat and still requires human staff for prep, draping, docking and instrument support.

tasks.label: Measure corneal curvature with keratometers or ophthalmometers to aid in the diagnosis of conditions, such as astigmatism.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine pre-testing in an optometry/ophthalmology office: a cooperative adult is seated at a table-mounted auto ref/keratometer in the pretest room, chin on the rest and forehead against the bar; the tech obtains K1/K2 and axis for both eyes, checks the readings look plausible, and sends/prints them to the chart for the doctor's astigmatism assessment.

Pre-cataract-surgery keratometry/biometry in a surgical practice's diagnostic room: high-accuracy K readings on an optical biometer or keratometer for IOL power and toric axis planning, several captures per eye, repeat if values disagree or the tear film is poor, results exported to the IOL calculation/surgical planner.

Difficult patients in the clinic lane: elderly with head tremor or poor fixation, wheelchair users who must be transferred and propped, ptosis/deep-set eyes or heavy lashes needing the lid held up, anxious children; the tech coaxes fixation, holds lids, manually aligns the mires, repeats until a valid reading is obtained (sometimes with a handheld keratometer).

Irregular-cornea work in the clinic: keratoconus, post-graft, post-refractive or specialty contact lens fitting; keratometry plus corneal topography, multiple captures, quality/mire-regularity check and repeat, results filed for the fitter or surgeon.

Off-site screening with the same instrumentation: a portable/table auto ref-keratometer in a mobile vision van, a nursing-home exam room, or a school/community screening station; cooperative seated patients, high volume, results logged for referral.

Bedside/operating-room keratometry: handheld keratometer readings on a supine, anesthetized infant during an exam under anesthesia, or on an inpatient who cannot sit at a table instrument; the tech holds the device, opens the lids and captures readings.

sources.title: Auto Ref/Keratometer ARK-F, Auto Refractometer AR-F | NIDEK
sources.claim: The Nidek ARK-F auto ref/keratometer performs a complete fully-automated measurement: once the patient's chin is on the rest, its eye-detection camera finds the eyes, the motorized head aligns itself and measures refraction and corneal curvature for both eyes, with multilingual voice guidance to the patient. Commercial product sold worldwide for clinic pre-testing.

sources.title: RK-F3M Full Auto Ref-Keratometer | Canon Medical Systems USA
sources.claim: Canon's RK-F3m is a full auto ref-keratometer with 3D tracking and alignment that produces keratometry (K) readings for each eye sequentially from a single start command and exports or prints the result automatically.

sources.title: Chronos Automated Binocular Refraction System
sources.claim: Topcon's Chronos combines binocular autorefraction and keratometry with subjective testing in one clinic instrument; with SightPilot NAVi the patient is guided by voice prompts through the measurement while the doctor only supervises, explicitly reducing technician involvement. A 2025 peer-reviewed study found good agreement with standard refraction techniques.

sources.title: Optical Biometer AL-Scan | NIDEK
sources.claim: The Nidek AL-Scan optical biometer used for cataract/IOL planning performs 3D auto tracking of the eye in X-Y-Z and auto-shot capture, delivering double-mire-ring keratometry along with five other parameters in about ten seconds.

sources.title: Basic Software | Pentacam (OCULUS)
sources.claim: The Oculus Pentacam anterior-segment tomographer (a standard clinic device for corneal curvature/topography including irregular corneas) triggers its own measurement by auto-release once aligned and automatically runs a quality test on the scan, which the manufacturer says makes the exam examiner-independent and delegable.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: corneal tomography/keratometry capture on the same patients and instrument class; it establishes autonomous alignment, auto-trigger and automatic quality vetting of corneal curvature measurements, the same acceptance step the technician performs for keratometry.

sources.title: KR-1W Corneal Wavefront Analyzer | Topcon Healthcare
sources.claim: Topcon's KR-1W combines keratometry, corneal topography, aberrometry and autorefraction in one clinic pre-testing instrument with a fully automated measurement ....

sources.title: Contactless optical coherence tomography of the eyes of freestanding individuals with a robotic scanner | Nature Biomedical Engineering
sources.claim: A Duke University robot-mounted OCT scanner autonomously positions itself and images the eyes of freestanding people without any chinrest or head stabilization, locating the pupil and compensating for eye motion under machine control.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous optical measurement of the human eye. It shows a true robot arm solving the same alignment problem keratometry requires (finding and tracking a moving eye to sub-millimetre precision on a live person), supporting that automated eye-measurement alignment is not the limiting factor in a clinic.

tasks.label: Conduct ocular motility tests to measure function of eye muscles.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine comprehensive-exam workup in a general ophthalmology exam lane: cooperative adult seated in the exam chair; tech holds a fixation target/penlight and moves it through the cardinal gaze positions checking versions/ductions for limitation, overaction or diplopia, then does cover-uncover and alternate cover with a hand occluder at distance and near, and charts 'EOMs full, ortho' or the deviation found.

Quantitative alignment measurement on a cooperative teen/adult with strabismus or new diplopia (strabismus, neuro-ophthalmology or pre/post-op visit): prism bar or loose prisms plus alternate cover at distance and near, with correction on, repeated in secondary gazes as needed; result in prism diopters must be reliable enough for surgical planning.

Cooperative school-age child (about 6-12) in a pediatric or general clinic: accommodative fixation target, motility through the gaze positions, cover-uncover and alternate cover at distance and near, with coaxing and repeated attempts to hold attention.

Preverbal infant, toddler or developmentally disabled/uncooperative patient, often held on a parent's lap: tech uses toys, sounds and a light to attract fixation, judges the Hirschberg corneal light reflex, does Krimsky or thumb/hand occlusion cover testing in brief windows of cooperation, improvising as the child moves.

Complex or atypical adult: cranial-nerve palsy, thyroid eye disease, restrictive or paralytic strabismus, nystagmus, ptosis or poor fixation; testing includes ductions with the fellow eye covered, head-tilt (Bielschowsky) testing, red glass/Maddox rod diplopia charting, sometimes with the patient in a wheelchair, in a pre-op area or at a hospital bedside.

Supplementary binocular/motility measures in the lane on a cooperative patient: near point of convergence push-up with break and recovery, vergence amplitudes, Worth 4-dot, Maddox rod phoria measurement, recorded with the motility findings.

sources.developer: Pomeranian Medical University, Szczecin (2nd Dept. of Ophthalmology) with engineering partners
sources.title: Usefulness Assessment of Automated Strabismus Angle Measurements Using Innovative Strabiscan Device (J. Clin. Med. 13:1067)
sources.claim: Strabiscan, a bench-top automated strabismus instrument built at a university ophthalmology department, performs the cover test itself: LCD shutters alternately occlude each eye, a screen displaces the fixation point in place of prism bars, a drive system adjusts the optics to the patient's pupillary distance, and it outputs horizontal and vertical deviation at near and far fixation; in 30 strabismic and 30 healthy subjects results did not differ significantly from the manual prism cover-uncover test.

sources.system: Strabismus video goggles (infrared video goggles with laser target projection and LCD shutters)
sources.developer: University of Bern / Inselspital and collaborators
sources.title: Strabismus Measurements with Novel Video Goggles (Ophthalmology)
sources.claim: Binocular infrared video goggles with ... liquid-crystal shutters automatically occluded the eyes and measured horizontal and vertical ocular deviation of each eye at nine gaze positions in 41 adult and child patients aged 6 and over at a university hospital, with good agreement against the conventional Hess screen ocular-motility test (ICC 0.83 horizontal, 0.76 vertical).

sources.title: Comparison of the Surgical Treatment for Strabismus According to Its Type: Esotropia Versus Exotropia (J. Clin. Med.)
sources.claim: Gazelab, a commercial video-oculography instrument with two infrared cameras and a laser target projection system, measures ocular deviation in the nine diagnostic gaze positions and identifies the fixing eye; it is used in hospital eye clinics for pre- and post-operative strabismus measurement and has shown excellent agreement with the alternate prism cover test.

sources.system: Automated strabismus evaluation devices (class review: VR headsets, video-oculography, photographic Hirschberg systems)
sources.developer: multiple (review by University of Iowa / Iowa City VA authors)
sources.title: Automated strabismus evaluation: a critical review and meta-analysis (Frontiers in Neurology)
sources.claim: A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis of automated strabismus/ocular-motility evaluation devices (69 studies) reports pooled correlation 0.87 with expert clinical evaluation but concludes that devices still fail on children's fit, extreme deviation angles, paralytic strabismus and eyes with ptosis or small palpebral fissures, so they are not yet incorporated into routine clinical use.

sources.developer: DIVE Medical / Hospital Universitario Miguel Servet, Zaragoza
sources.title: Development and Clinical Validation of a Digital Eye-Tracking-Based Cover Test for Ocular Misalignment (Ophthalmology Science)
sources.claim: In the clinically validated DIVE Cover Test (eye-tracking device used at a pediatric ophthalmology unit, participants aged 3-74), the machine supplies the stimulus and computes the deviation, but the physical occlusion of each eye is still carried out by a human examiner following the device's prompts.

sources.system: Olleyes VisuALL Model S VR simulated alternate cover test
sources.developer: Olleyes, Inc. (Summit, NJ) with Lehigh Valley Health Network investigators
sources.title: A Virtual Reality Simulated Alternate Cover Test to Evaluate Adults with Strabismus (Ophthalmology Science)
sources.claim: A VR-headset simulated alternate cover test run against masked clinician alternate cover tests in adults showed only moderate agreement, with 95% limits of agreement of roughly plus/minus 18 to 26 prism diopters at distance and near, far outside the few-prism-diopter test-retest spread of clinician prism cover testing.

sources.system: Intelligent strabismus evaluation system with automated stimulus (cover) module
sources.developer: Wen et al. (Chinese Academy of Sciences / Xi'an), published in Applied Sciences
sources.title: Intelligent Evaluation of Strabismus in Videos Based on an Automated Cover Test (Applied Sciences 9:731)
sources.claim: A purpose-built automated cover-test rig moves a physical occluder in front of the subject's eye with a stepper motor under FPGA control while an infrared camera records refixation movements and software computes the deviation, demonstrating machine execution of the occlusion maneuver itself (horizontal deviation within 8 prism diopters in over 91% of cases).

tasks.label: Clean or sterilize ophthalmic or surgical instruments.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Between-patient disinfection of the Goldmann applanation tonometer prism in a clinic exam lane: remove the prism from the tonometer holder, wipe/rinse under running water, disinfect (3% hydrogen peroxide or 1:10 bleach soak, or manufacturer wipe system), rinse, dry with lint-free tissue, inspect for scratches, reinstall — dozens of times a day between patients, under clinic patient-flow time pressure. Prism is PMMA: no autoclaving, no temperatures above 60 C.

Cleaning and disinfecting non-immersible diagnostic optics and patient-contact equipment in exam lanes: gonioscopy and fundus contact lenses, 90D/78D lenses, trial contact lens sets, chin rests and forehead bands, occluders — hand-wiped with lens cleaner or approved disinfectant per each device's IFU, dried and returned to the lane between patients.

High-level disinfection / reprocessing of semi-critical contact probes in the clinic: A-scan biometry and pachymeter probes, B-scan ultrasound probes, tonometer tip covers-free devices — carried to the reprocessing area, cleaned, disinfected by the approved chemical or automated method, dried, logged, and returned for the next patient.

Reprocessing minor-procedure instruments in the clinic's sterilization/utility room: chalazion clamps, lid specula, fine forceps, punctal dilators, needle holders used for lid lesions and injections — rinse and scrub soil off, run ultrasonic cleaner, rinse, dry, inspect, pouch with indicator, run tabletop steam autoclave, log the cycle, store the sterile packs.

Intraocular instrument reprocessing between cataract/anterior-segment cases at an ambulatory surgery center: immediate point-of-use flushing of cannulas, I/A tips and phaco handpiece lumens with sterile water, manual/ultrasonic cleaning, automated washer cycle, inspection under magnification for residue and damage, tray assembly, steam sterilization (often short cycles) and documentation, with strict TASS-prevention protocols and short turnaround between cases.

sources.title: Miele Introduces Compact Washer-Disinfector Designed for Intraocular Surgical Instruments
sources.claim: Miele's G7899 is a commercial washer-disinfector built specifically for ophthalmic microsurgical instruments; it runs a machine-controlled cleaning/disinfection cycle and uses injector racks to flush the narrow lumens of phaco-emulsification handpieces and cannulated eye instruments once the load is presented in its racks.

sources.title: Compact Washer-Disinfector Designed for Intraocular Surgical Instruments (PRWeb release)
sources.claim: Testing under ISO guidelines showed the G7899 cleans and disinfects surgical instruments without pre-soaking or ..., i.e. the machine cycle itself delivers the cleaned/disinfected instrument that the surgery center accepts.

sources.title: Nanosonics Announces Commercial Availability of trophon2 High Level Disinfection System in US and Canada
sources.claim: The trophon2 is a benchtop automated high-level disinfection machine: a delicate handheld patient-contact probe is placed in its chamber and the device runs an unattended chemical (H2O2 mist) disinfection cycle with automatic cycle records; it is validated across more than 1,000 probe models.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated high-level disinfection of ultrasound transducers. Ophthalmic A-scan/pachymeter and B-scan probes are small handheld ultrasound probes requiring the same low-temperature chemical HLD output; the same load-and-run machine handles comparably delicate, heat-sensitive patient-contact devices.

sources.title: Nanosonics N05000-US Trophon 2 (product page)
sources.claim: trophon units are in routine everyday clinical use at scale, with more than 25,000 devices installed across North American healthcare facilities since 2011 — evidence the automated disinfection cycle is accepted as standard-of-care output, not a demo.
sources.transferJustification: Same related task as above: machine reprocessing of small semi-critical patient-contact probes, establishing deployment maturity of the cited disinfection machine.

sources.system: Gibotech Automated Central Sterile Supply Department (robot cells, conveyors, mobile robots)
sources.title: Automated Central Sterile Supply Department — Gibotech
sources.claim: Gibotech supplies fully automated central sterile supply departments in which robot arms, mobile robots and conveyors replace the manual handling around washing and sterilization of surgical instruments; the first was installed at Koge Hospital in 2011, with Rigshospitalet and Herlev following.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: mechanized instrument reprocessing lines in hospital CSSDs. It shows the presentation/transfer of instrument loads to washer-disinfectors and sterilizers is performed by machines in purpose-built lines, which is how the cleaning/sterilizing instance arises at E1.

sources.system: M-ATS Self-Driving Robot Transfer System; ATS Automatic Transfer System
sources.title: M-ATS Self-Driving Robot Transfer System — Steelco
sources.claim: Steelco/Belimed sell a self-driving transfer robot and automatic transfer shuttles that move washing loads and sterilization containers into and out of washer-disinfectors and sterilizers without direct human handling.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: loading/unloading and transport of instrument loads through the reprocessing chain. It substantiates that in a purpose-built line the workpieces are presented to and removed from cleaning and sterilizing machines by machine, closing the handling steps around the wash/sterilize cycles.

sources.system: Autonomous instrument tray assembly robot (UR-style arm with vision)
sources.developer: University of Louisville (Chitalia lab) with an SPD partner
sources.title: Towards Autonomous Instrument Tray Assembly for Sterile Processing Applications
sources.claim: A university group demonstrated a fully automated robotic cell that picks individual surgical instruments, classifies them by vision and packs them into sterile trays on a bench, with the technician retaining the inspection role.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic handling and sorting of individual soiled/clean surgical instruments. It shows machine handling of the same small delicate instruments in a fixtured bench cell, supporting E1-level manipulation around cleaning and sterilizing cycles, but only in a purpose-built setup.

sources.title: RIF Robotics pioneers autonomous surgical tray assembly — Catalyst by Wellstar
sources.claim: RIF Robotics ran a pilot with Wellstar (Windy Hill Hospital) using a vision-guided robotic arm to automate surgical instrument tray assembly and sterilization workflow, with the robot working alongside sterile processing technicians who trained it on hundreds of instruments.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: sterile processing tray assembly in a working hospital SPD. Cited only as context for the state of in-facility (E2) deployment; autonomy in routine operation is not established, so it supports no positive judgment.

tasks.label: Maintain ophthalmic instruments or equipment.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Between-patient and end-of-day cleaning/disinfection of exam-lane equipment in place: wipe chin rests, forehead bands, phoropter face pieces, joysticks, headrests and trial frames with disinfectant; clean slit-lamp and indirect-ophthalmoscope optics with lens tissue without scratching coatings or disturbing alignment; put on dust covers. Done in the minute or two between patients in an occupied clinic lane.

Cleaning and disinfecting removable patient-contact optics and tips between uses: Goldmann applanation prisms, gonioscopy and 90D/78D diagnostic lenses, pachymeter/tonometer tips. Remove from the instrument, rinse, clean, disinfect by soak or wipe per manufacturer protocol, rinse, dry, inspect for cracks, and return to service at the clinic workroom sink.

Reprocessing reusable minor-procedure/surgical instruments in an ophthalmology practice or ASC: gross pre-clean at the sink, ultrasonic cleaning, inspection for debris and damage, sorting and packing into peel pouches or trays, loading and unloading the autoclave, running and documenting cycles and spore tests.

Scheduled calibration and performance-verification checks with logging: Goldmann tonometer calibration-error check using the weight bar at set drum positions, lensmeter/keratometer/autorefractor verification against standards, perimeter and A-scan/biometer checks, recording results and flagging out-of-tolerance devices for service.

Preventive upkeep and minor repairs: replacing slit-lamp and indirect ophthalmoscope bulbs and fuses, changing printer paper, batteries and chin-rest papers, cleaning or replacing filters, tightening loose knobs, reseating cables, clearing error codes, and arranging vendor service when a device fails.

Stocking, organizing and inventorying: restocking lane supplies (drops, tonometer tip covers, wipes, tissues), organizing instrument drawers, laying up trays for in-office procedures, and tracking par levels of instrument consumables.

sources.title: Bryan Health Uses New Robotic Technology to Clean and Sterilize Surgical Instruments
sources.claim: STERIS ATLAS Workflow Automation Vehicle ('Bella') autonomously picks up racks of hand-cleaned surgical instruments and loads/unloads washer-disinfectors in a hospital sterile processing department, navigating with laser and sonar guidance; deployed at Bryan Medical Center.
sources.transferJustification: Same task family: machine handling and washer/disinfector processing of reusable medical instruments; the ophthalmic technician's reprocessing instance uses the same racks, washers and sterilizers.

sources.system: Autonomous instrument tray assembly system (Staubli TX2-60L)
sources.title: Towards Autonomous Instrument Tray Assembly for Sterile Processing Applications (arXiv:2602.01679)
sources.claim: A fully automated robotic cell (Staubli TX2-60L arm, dual electromagnetic gripper, YOLO12 + ResNet perception) sorts surgical instruments and packs them into sterile trays with 3D-printed dividers, with fewer tool-to-tool collisions than human-assembled trays.
sources.transferJustification: Directly covers instrument sorting, inspection-adjacent classification and tray packing/kitting, the assembly and organizing portions of ophthalmic instrument reprocessing and tray set-up.

sources.system: Robosonic robotic ultrasonic cleaning cell (Fanuc CR-7i)
sources.title: Ultrasonic Robotic Parts Cleaning Cell Provides Precision Cleaning and Maximum Efficiency
sources.claim: Blackstone-NEY's Robosonic is a commercial robotic precision cleaning cell in which a Fanuc CR-7i robot moves parts (up to 15 lb) through spray wash, ultrasonic immersion wash, ... and dryer stages, marketed for cleanroom and precision parts including medical devices.
sources.transferJustification: Related task is automated precision cleaning of small, delicate cleanroom/medical components; ophthalmic prisms, diagnostic lenses and small instruments are of comparable size, fragility and cleanliness requirement when presented fixtured in a cell.

sources.system: Getinge sterilizer loading automation (Automatiq / automatic loading systems)
sources.title: Surgical instrument reprocessing - Sterile Zone - Getinge
sources.claim: Getinge supplies fully automatic loading and transport systems for sterilizers in central sterile reprocessing, handling loading and unloading of sterilizer racks without an operator.
sources.transferJustification: Covers the autoclave loading/unloading step of instrument reprocessing that ophthalmic technicians perform for in-office procedure instruments.

sources.system: Intelligent Autonomous Wiping and UV-C Disinfection Robot
sources.developer: POSTECH (Keehoon Kim lab) with KIST, KIRO, Elphoton
sources.title: Transforming hospital sanitation: autonomous robots for wiping and UV-C disinfection (EurekAlert)
sources.claim: POSTECH's Intelligent Autonomous Wiping and UV-C ... uses a mobile manipulator to physically wipe hospital surfaces and then UV-C irradiate hard-to-reach areas; it was validated in repeated autonomous runs at Pohang St. Mary's Hospital.
sources.transferJustification: Related task is autonomous surface disinfection in a hospital; it marks the frontier for robotic wiping but is demonstrated only on room furniture surfaces, not on assembled optical instruments with coated lenses and removable prisms.

sources.system: UR5-based automated medical device test cell (ESAOTE probes)
sources.developer: BioRobotics Institute, Sant'Anna School / Universal Robots
sources.title: Automated testing improves precision and repeatability for medical device quality control
sources.claim: A UR5 collaborative-robot cell automates the functional test battery on ESAOTE ultrasound probes, precisely aligning the probe in a water bath and producing more precise and repeatable measurement data than the specialized technicians who previously did the tests by hand.
sources.transferJustification: Related task is robotic performance verification of a clinical diagnostic instrument: fixture the device, apply a standard stimulus, take a quantitative reading and judge conformance - the same physical acts as a technician's periodic tonometer/lensmeter calibration check when the device is presented fixtured.

sources.title: Swisslog Healthcare Partners with Diligent Robotics to Enhance Hospital Logistics
sources.claim: Diligent Robotics' Moxi mobile manipulator is deployed in more than 25 ..., autonomously performing over a million point-to-point deliveries of supplies, pharmacy items and specimens through corridors and elevators.
sources.transferJustification: Related task is hospital supply logistics; it shows deployed E2 mobile manipulation is limited to transport of totes and carts, not organizing drawers or laying up instrument trays inside clinic rooms.

tasks.label: Instruct patients in the care and use of contact lenses.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: New soft-lens wearer at the insertion-and-removal training visit in a clinic exam or dispensing room: the technician explains hand hygiene, demonstrates the insertion and removal technique, coaches the patient through repeated attempts on their own eyes, and reviews wear schedule, solutions, storage case care, and warning signs before the patient is released.

Established wearer being re-educated at a follow-up or annual visit: switching from monthly to daily disposables or to a toric/multifocal design, or correcting non-compliance such as sleeping in lenses, topping off solution, or overwearing; the technician reviews the replacement schedule, cleaning regimen, and risk of infection.

Specialty lens patient (rigid gas-permeable, scleral, or orthokeratology): the technician instructs on plunger/DMV use, filling the scleral bowl with preservative-free saline without bubbles, specific cleaners and conditioning solutions, overnight storage, and the different handling technique these lenses require.

Pediatric or teenage patient, often in myopia-control lenses, with a parent or caregiver present: the technician instructs both the child and the adult, gauges the child's dexterity and willingness to touch the eye, and repeats the session over a longer or second appointment.

Instruction delivered as a handoff or remotely: reviewing printed take-home care sheets and manufacturer instructions at checkout, or answering a patient's phone or portal question about a care product, lost lens, or discomfort after dispensing.

tasks.label: Assess refractive conditions of eyes, using retinoscopes.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Cooperative adult in a standard ophthalmology/optometry clinic exam lane: tech obtains objective refraction (streak retinoscopy at the phoropter, or autorefraction) as the starting point for the manifest refraction, records sphere/cylinder/axis in the chart for the physician.

Cooperative school-age child or teen in clinic, usually after cycloplegic drops: tech performs wet retinoscopy (or cycloplegic objective refraction) with the patient seated at the instrument/phoropter and able to follow instructions and fixate.

Preverbal infant, toddler, or developmentally disabled/nonverbal patient in a pediatric ophthalmology clinic: child sits on a parent's lap or squirms, fixates on a toy or video; tech performs cycloplegic retinoscopy with a handheld streak retinoscope and loose lenses or lens racks, chasing the reflex as the child moves.

Adult whose optics defeat automated measurement: dense cataract or other media opacity, keratoconus/irregular or post-surgical cornea, nystagmus or eccentric fixation, small pupils, very high ametropia, or a patient with dementia who cannot cooperate; tech uses retinoscopy to obtain a usable objective refraction.

Immobile patient examined outside the lane: hospital bedside consult, nursing-home visit, or wheelchair patient who cannot sit up to a table-mounted instrument or behind a phoropter; tech performs handheld retinoscopy with a trial frame or lens bars in whatever position the patient can hold.

Mobile/outreach screening: school vision screening in a gym, community health fair, church hall, or mobile clinic van; tech screens a queue of mostly cooperative patients with a portable retinoscope/lens bars under variable lighting and improvised seating.

sources.title: NIDEK launches the ARK-F/AR-F Auto Ref/Keratometer / Auto Refractometer
sources.claim: The Nidek ARK-F/AR-F auto ref/keratometer performs fully automatic objective refraction: once the patient's chin is on the rest, an eye-detection camera finds both eyes, the motorized head aligns itself and measurement is triggered with no operator input; voice guidance instructs the patient. Commercially sold and installed in clinics worldwide.
sources.transferJustification: Objective refraction by autorefraction is the same work product the retinoscope produces (sphere/cylinder/axis starting lens); clinics routinely use one in place of the other for cooperative patients.

sources.title: Evaluation of objective and subjective binocular ocular refraction with looking in type (BMC Ophthalmology)
sources.claim: The Topcon Chronos binocular refraction system uses eye trackers to detect each pupil and corneal reflex and then physically positions two auto-refractometer heads in front of the patient's eyes and measures refraction in both eyes; it also runs guided subjective refraction and can be driven from a tablet in another room.

sources.developer: Topcon Corporation (study: Clinique Honoré Cave, Montauban, France)
sources.title: Clinical validity of automated refraction with the Chronos binocular refraction system compared to standard refraction techniques - PubMed
sources.claim: In a clinical validation at an eye clinic, automated refraction with Chronos was compared against Nidek ARK-1 autorefraction plus manual subjective refraction in 361 eyes of 182 patients; agreement was good with clinically acceptable mean differences, supporting the automated device as an alternative in routine clinical practice.

sources.title: Walmart and Sam's Clubs launch Eyebot vision kiosks – Eyebot
sources.claim: Eyebot's S1/S1+ self-service kiosk measures refraction (wavefront) with no operator present and produces an eyeglass prescription; kiosks are deployed in malls, universities, grocery and retail stores, and since December 2025 in Walmart Vision Centers and Sam's ..., with each result reviewed remotely by a licensed eye doctor.
sources.transferJustification: The kiosk performs the objective refractive assessment that the technician's retinoscopy provides, and hands the result to the prescriber for review, mirroring the tech-to-ophthalmologist workflow.

sources.title: This AI Bot Has A Rapid View on Vision Testing - Techstrong.ai
sources.claim: Independent reporting describes the Eyebot kiosk as a fully autonomous, self-serve vision test completed in about 90 seconds without an on-site optometrist, and a comparison study found prescriptions generated from Eyebot sessions gave patients 20/20 acuity at the same rate as their optometrist's prescriptions.

sources.system: Autorefractors (device class, incl. table-mounted auto-aligning models)
sources.date: accessed 2026; text derived from optometry reference literature
sources.title: Autorefractor - an overview | ScienceDirect Topics
sources.claim: Reference text on autorefractors: under cycloplegia in children autorefraction is as accurate as (or more accurate than) retinoscopy, but autorefractor results are unreliable or unobtainable in patients ... error, small pupils, cataract, pseudophakia or nystagmus.
sources.transferJustification: Establishes where automated refraction can and cannot substitute for the technician's retinoscopy; used for the quality check on cooperative patients and for the negative judgments.

sources.title: Going Old School: A Refresher on Retinoscopy | Review of Optometry
sources.claim: Clinical trade article on retinoscopy: patients who cannot sit up to an autorefractor ... behind a phoropter, and those with nystagmus or eccentric fixation or pathology preventing accurate autorefraction, must be refracted by retinoscopy/trial frame instead.
sources.transferJustification: Directly delimits which instances of this task automated instruments cannot cover; used only for negative judgments.

tasks.label: Call patients to inquire about their post-operative status or recovery.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Assist patients to insert or remove contact lenses.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: New soft-lens wearer's insertion-and-removal training session in a clinic exam/training room: technician demonstrates, loads the lens on the patient's fingertip, checks for an inverted or torn lens, coaches lid control at the mirror, retrieves dropped lenses, often inserts or removes once to demonstrate, and certifies the patient can do both before discharge.

Technician inserts a diagnostic/trial soft or toric lens on a cooperative adult during a fitting: rinses the lens with saline, retracts upper and lower lids, places the lens on the cornea of a blinking eye, checks centration and movement at the slit lamp, and removes the trial lens afterward.

Removal for a patient who cannot get the lens out: dry or adherent soft lens, or lens decentered under the upper lid; technician instills saline, everts or lifts the lid, locates and pinches or slides the lens off the ocular surface without abrading the cornea, in the clinic lane.

Scleral or RGP lens insertion/removal assistance for a keratoconus or post-transplant patient with poor dexterity: filling the scleral bowl with preservative-free saline, bubble-free placement while holding both lids wide, or removal with a suction plunger placed on the lens edge.

Pediatric, elderly-frail, or cognitively impaired patient in the clinic who resists: technician calms and stabilizes the head, holds squeezing lids apart (sometimes with a second staff member), and places or removes the lens in the brief window between blinks and head movements.

Post-operative or urgent-visit bandage contact lens insertion or removal at the slit lamp in a procedure/post-op room: tender, photophobic, watering eye, freshly operated cornea, requiring very light touch and immediate verification of lens position.

sources.title: This robot will put your contact lenses in for you (Freethink)
sources.claim: The Cliara Lens Robot is a table-top self-service device on which the wearer places their own lens, rests their forehead, and voice-activates a suction cup that rises to the eye; it was a prototype in clinical testing and is described by its inventor as being controlled by the user, with no evidence of clinical deployment or worker-quality performance.
sources.transferJustification: Same task (contact lens insertion/removal) but performed by the wearer on themselves with the device as a tool: the patient positions their own head and eye and issues the command, and the device does not retract lids, verify lens condition or centration, or handle uncooperative patients, so it does not substantiate a technician-quality assist.

sources.system: CLIARA lens manipulator / CHIO handheld device
sources.title: Cliara receives US patent for contact lens measurement device (Eyes On Eyecare Glance)
sources.claim: As of 2024 CLIARA's shipping product is the CHIO, a ~$20 handheld manual inserter/remover; the robotic apparatus remains patent-stage and under study with BostonSight and LV Prasad Eye Institute, and the patent describes a lens manipulator controlled by the user.
sources.transferJustification: Directly on this task; shows the only commercially available CLIARA product is a manual hand tool and the robotic version is user-controlled and still under study, so it cannot support autonomous completion.

sources.title: Luum launches next-generation AI eyelash extension robot with faster application and national rollout
sources.claim: Luum's AI eyelash-extension robot autonomously applies individual lash extensions to reclining clients in commercial studios and retail shop-in-shops, with human lash artists prepping and evaluating — the closest deployed example of robotic manipulation immediately adjacent to a human eye.
sources.transferJustification: Related task (precision robotic work at the eye region inside a controlled facility). It does NOT transfer: lashes are applied to closed, taped eyelids with no ocular-surface contact, whereas this task requires retracting the lids of an open, blinking eye and placing or peeling a lens off the cornea.

sources.developer: Duke University (Draelos, Izatt, Kuo et al.)
sources.title: Contactless optical coherence tomography of the eyes of freestanding individuals with a robotic scanner (Nature Biomedical Engineering)
sources.claim: The state of the art in autonomous robotics acting on the eyes of awake humans is contactless imaging: a robot-mounted OCT scanner aligns itself to a freestanding person's eye without head stabilization, but never touches the eye or lids.
sources.transferJustification: Related task (autonomous robot targeting a live human eye). It shows eye tracking and alignment are solved only for non-contact imaging at a safe standoff; no lid retraction or ocular-surface contact is performed, so it does not substantiate lens insertion or removal.

sources.developer: OQrimo (initial clinical use in pars plana vitrectomy)
sources.title: Initial clinical use of the intraocular endoscope holding robot in pars plana vitrectomy (PubMed)
sources.claim: Ophthalmic robots that do contact the eye are surgical systems driven by a surgeon (foot controller or leader-follower) on an anesthetized, speculum-held, immobilized globe in an operating room, not autonomous assistants for awake patients.
sources.transferJustification: Related task (robotic instrument manipulation at the human eye). It is teleoperated and depends on anesthesia, a lid speculum and an immobilized globe, so it cannot support autonomous work on an awake, blinking patient.

tasks.label: Conduct binocular disparity tests to assess depth perception.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine adult comprehensive eye exam in an ophthalmology/optometry exam lane: technician places polarized glasses over the patient's habitual correction, holds a Titmus or Randot stereotest booklet at 40 cm under standard illumination, works down the circles/animals, reverses or rotates plates to rule out monocular cues, and records stereoacuity in seconds of arc in the chart.

Pediatric patient aged roughly 2-8 in a pediatric ophthalmology/strabismus clinic: technician selects Randot Preschool, Lang, or Stereo Fly, coaxes a restless or shy child, holds polarized glasses on a small face that keeps turning, accepts pointing or touching responses, repeats trials, and judges whether responses are reliable.

Strabismus/amblyopia workup or post-operative follow-up in an older child or adult: near plus distance stereo testing (Distance Randot, Frisby, or Worth-type suppression checks) interleaved with cover testing and prism measurement, results interpreted against prior visits and flagged to the ophthalmologist.

Occupational health, DOT physical, or DMV-style screening room: depth-perception subtest run on a stereoscopic vision screener (Titmus/Optec); the technician seats the person at the viewer, gives instructions, advances the depth-perception slide set, and records pass/fail or the graded score on the screening form.

Community, school, or mobile-clinic vision screening: portable stereo test (Random Dot E, Lang, or Stereo Fly) administered to a line of children in a school gym, health-fair booth, or mobile van with variable lighting and noise; quick pass/refer decision recorded on a screening sheet.

sources.title: This AI Bot Has A Rapid View on Vision Testing - Techstrong.ai
sources.claim: Eyebot S1 is a self-service, fully autonomous vision-testing kiosk deployed in retail locations that measures refraction and produces a prescription-grade result in about 90 seconds; the retrieved material describes acuity/refraction testing, with no depth-perception or stereoacuity subtest described.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated refraction/acuity screening in an institution-controlled retail optical setting. Cited only to show the frontier of autonomous eye testing; it does not present disparity stimuli, fit polarized eyewear, or output a stereoacuity value, so it does not substantiate completion of binocular disparity testing.

sources.title: Olleyes, Inc. Expands VisuALL Virtual Reality Platform With Breakthrough Stereopsis Test
sources.claim: Olleyes added a stereopsis (depth perception) test to its VisuALL virtual-reality platform for eye-care practices; the test is delivered through a head-mounted display worn by the patient, which a clinic staff member fits and starts, and is a screen/software-based instrument rather than a machine that manipulates the physical world.
sources.transferJustification: Same task (stereopsis assessment) but delivered by a head-worn display; under the stated definition a screen-based device is not a robotic system, and a human still positions the patient, fits the headset, and supervises, so it cannot substantiate robotic completion.

sources.title: Titmus Vision Tester V4 | e3 Diagnostics
sources.claim: Commercial stereoscopic vision screeners that include a depth-perception subtest are operator-driven instruments: the Titmus V4 changes slides automatically but is run from a remote-control panel by a technician who instructs the person at the viewer and records the responses.
sources.transferJustification: Same task (depth-perception screening) on the standard occupational-health instrument; cited to show that the machine only presents slides while a human operator conducts and scores the test, so it does not substantiate autonomous completion.

sources.system: Robotically aligned OCT scanner (contactless robotic OCT)
sources.developer: Duke University (Draelos, Izatt, Kuo et al.)
sources.title: Contactless optical coherence tomography of the eyes of freestanding individuals with a robotic scanner | Nature Biomedical Engineering
sources.claim: A robotic OCT scanner autonomously locates a freestanding patient's eyes with 3D cameras and a robot arm and acquires diagnostic-quality retinal images without a chin rest, demonstrating autonomous robotic alignment of an ophthalmic instrument to a human eye in a clinical research setting.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous robotic alignment of an ophthalmic imaging instrument to a patient's eyes in an eye clinic. It shows robots can find and track human eyes, but the task here is a subjective psychophysical test requiring stimulus presentation at a set distance, fitting polarized eyewear, eliciting and validating patient responses, and grading them - none of which this system does, so capability does not carry over.

tasks.label: Adjust or make minor repairs to spectacles or eyeglasses.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Dispensing new spectacles in the practice's optical area: the technician places the finished glasses on the seated patient, reads how they sit (level, pantoscopic tilt, vertex distance, temple pressure), then repeatedly removes them, warms the acetate front/temples in a frame warmer, bends temples and end pieces with pliers or fingers, sets nose pads, and re-checks on the face until the patient reports comfort and the optical centers line up.

Walk-in comfort adjustment of a patient's existing glasses that slip, sit crooked, pinch behind the ears or rub the nose: the technician diagnoses the problem from how the frame sits on that patient's face, alternates bench bends (temple angle, splay, curl, pad arms) with on-face checks, and finishes in a few minutes at the front desk or exam lane.

Bench screw repair on a patient-owned frame handed over at the counter: a loose or missing hinge/pad-arm screw is re-seated or replaced with a stock screw, driven to correct tightness with a jeweler's screwdriver, hinge action checked, and the frame handed back within minutes.

Bench small-part repair: replacing worn, discolored or missing push-in or screw-in nose pads, slipping on new temple tips, or re-seating a lens that has popped out of a plastic frame or a rimless/nylon-cord mount, on an assortment of patient-owned frames of unknown make.

Pre-adjustment of new or stock frames at the bench with no patient present: bringing the frame to standard alignment - equal temple curl and spread, correct temple angle, level fronts - using the frame warmer, pliers and an alignment reference before the glasses are dispensed.

Awkward or specialty repairs and adjustments: tightening a rimless mount without cracking the lens, replacing a broken temple or nylon cord, adjusting wrap-around safety or sports eyewear and small pediatric frames on a squirming child, or adjusting on a post-operative patient with a shield or tender periocular skin.

sources.system: RA Single Head Platform Glasses Hinge Automatic Locking Screw Machine
sources.developer: Dongguan Rongan Electromechanical Equipment Co., Ltd.
sources.title: Ra Automatic Robot Screw Locking/Fastening/Tightening Equipment for Glasses Hinges
sources.claim: A commercially sold automatic screw-locking machine is built specifically to drive and tighten eyeglass hinge screws: the frame is held on a fixtured platform, screws (M1-M5) are fed automatically by blow/suction feeder and driven by a multi-axis motorized head under PLC control, with alarms for missing, floating or cross-threaded screws, at 1.0-2.5 s per screw.
sources.transferJustification: Related task is factory hinge-screw fastening on spectacle frames rather than clinic screw repair; the object (a spectacle hinge and its ~1.4 mm screw), the driving torque and the precision are identical to the technician's screw tightening/replacement, and the machine is sold specifically for eyewear frames.

sources.system: RA-DNW-01 Glasses Temple Automatic Bending Machine
sources.developer: Dongguan Rongan Electromechanical Equipment Co., Ltd.
sources.title: Ra Auto-Temple Bending Press / High-Speed Optical Frame Former / Medical Grade Eyewear Production Machinery
sources.claim: A commercially sold automatic bending machine bends the temples of finished eyewear to programmed angles and arcs under PLC/multi-axis motor control, storing thousands of product parameters, at about 12 seconds per piece.
sources.transferJustification: Related task is production bending of temples on finished eyewear rather than bench pre-adjustment; the workpiece (a mounted spectacle temple), the deformation (setting temple angle and curl to a specified geometry) and the fixtured bench presentation match the operation the technician performs with pliers and a frame warmer.

sources.system: UR10e vision-guided unscrewing cell for e-waste disassembly
sources.developer: academic group, published in Robotics and Computer-Integrated Manufacturing
sources.title: Robotic system for automated disassembly of electronic waste: Unscrewing
sources.claim: A research robot autonomously locates, identifies and removes screws of several head types on varied consumer electronics presented in a workcell, using a UR10e arm, a RealSense ... mechatronic screwdriver.
sources.transferJustification: Related task is vision-guided screw removal on varied electronic devices; it shows a robot can find and engage small screws on items it was not pre-programmed for, which is the perception half of tightening or replacing a hinge screw on an unfamiliar spectacle frame presented in a fixtured cell.

sources.system: ESTIC ERS robotic workcell / Nitto Seiko PD400UR screwdriving cell (UR5e)
sources.developer: ESTIC America; Nitto Seiko America with Universal Robots
sources.title: New Tech for Robotic Fastening | ASSEMBLY
sources.claim: Off-the-shelf robotic screwdriving workcells with automatic screw feeders handle fasteners down to M1.7 and are sold as standardized cells built around cobots and precision drivers.
sources.transferJustification: Related task is industrial small-fastener driving in a purpose-built cell; it corroborates that torque-controlled driving of miniature screws on fixtured parts is routine commercial practice, supporting only the E1 (work brought to the machine) presentation of spectacle screw repair.

tasks.label: Assist patients to select eyewear.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Adult patient in the practice's optical dispensary immediately after a routine refraction: the technician reviews the new prescription, asks about lifestyle (computer work, driving, sports), walks the patient through the frame boards, suggests shapes/colors suited to face shape and coloring, lets the patient try frames at the mirror, and talks through lens material, coatings, price and insurance until the patient decides.

Patient with a complex or strong prescription (high myopia, astigmatism, progressive addition, prism, aphakia): the technician steers the patient away from frames incompatible with lens thickness, decentration or minimum fitting height, explains high-index/aspheric lens options and edge-thickness trade-offs, and confirms the chosen frame will work optically before the patient commits.

Pediatric or teen patient with a parent present: the technician recommends durable, appropriately sized frames (spring hinges, wrap cable temples, polycarbonate lenses), balances the child's style preference against fit and safety, and mediates the parent/child decision, often against a school or Medicaid-covered frame selection.

Medically driven eyewear selection: post-cataract-surgery readers or single-vision distance glasses, post-op or post-dilation UV/sunwear, occupational or sports safety eyewear, low-vision magnifying or filter lenses. The technician explains what the physician ordered and helps the patient pick among the limited compliant options.

Benefit-constrained or replacement selection: patient chooses from an insurance-covered frame board, or replaces lost/broken glasses on an existing prescription, sometimes handled at the front desk, by phone, or via an online/virtual try-on portal with the technician advising remotely on fit, size and lens choices.
