instances.label: Bedside in-service on a rehab unit: the orthotist/prosthetist shows inpatient nurses and physical therapists a newly delivered lower-limb prosthesis, explaining donning/doffing sequence, sock ply management, skin-check schedule, and weight-bearing limits, answering staff questions.

Clinic fitting appointment with a referring physician or treating therapist present: the practitioner shows the custom orthosis (e.g., AFO, spinal orthosis, fracture brace), points out trim lines, alignment and adjustment features, and explains the wear schedule and precautions to the clinician.

Scheduled staff in-service/education session in a hospital or clinic conference room: sample braces and prosthetic components are laid out and demonstrated to a group of nurses, therapists, or residents, covering indications, application technique, and troubleshooting.
Off-site explanation to school nurses, home-health aides, or skilled-nursing-facility staff during a delivery or follow-up visit, showing how the appliance is applied and monitored in that setting.
Vendor/exhibit or professional-meeting setting: showing a device line and explaining its function and candidacy criteria to visiting clinicians at a booth or teaching table.

Remote explanation: phone or video call, emailed photos/short videos, or written instructions sent to a nurse or therapist who is applying or monitoring the appliance, with verbal walkthrough of use and precautions.

tasks.label: Train and supervise support staff, such as orthopedic and prosthetic assistants and technicians.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: In the fabrication lab, the practitioner reviews a technician's in-progress work (a modified positive model, a laminated prosthetic socket, a thermoformed AFO) against the prescription and cast measurements, points out where trimlines or reliefs are wrong, and directs rework. Output is corrective direction and sign-off, not the fabrication itself.

Hands-on instruction of a newly hired technician, assistant, or resident in a fabrication technique (plaster modification, lamination and resin handling, thermoplastic draping, CAD carving), by explaining, demonstrating, watching the trainee attempt it, and critiquing the result. Occurs in the lab over multiple sessions.

During a patient appointment in the clinic room, the practitioner directs an assistant: assigning strap or pad adjustments, verifying alignment work, instructing on patient transfer and gait-check protocol, and coaching on chart documentation and coding while the patient is present.

Administrative supervision in an office or conference room: assigning caseload and workload, setting production priorities, conducting performance reviews and competency sign-offs, and delivering required safety, infection-control, and compliance training to lab and clinic staff.

In-servicing the staff on new componentry, materials, or software (scanner and CAD/CAM workflow, a new liner or knee system, EMR changes), often jointly with a manufacturer's representative, then verifying staff can apply the new procedure.

tasks.label: Update skills and knowledge by attending conferences and seminars.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Research new ways to construct and use orthopedic and prosthetic devices.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Practitioner scans new construction/use methods without hands-on work: reads JPO/Prosthetics & Orthotics International, reviews AAOP/AOPA meeting content and manufacturer technical bulletins, attends CE courses and trade-show booths, handles sample components, and synthesizes what is worth adopting in the practice. Setting: clinic office, classroom, convention hall.

Bench exploration in the practice's fabrication lab of a new material or fabrication parameter set (new filament/resin, print orientation, infill or lattice geometry, thickness schedule): make test coupons or dummy sections, load/flex/impact them, compare stiffness, strength and durability against the current standard, and record which parameters to adopt. Setting: institution-controlled O&P fab lab with standard equipment.

Devising and building a novel device construction for a specific unmet patient problem: capture the shape (cast or scan), iterate a CAD or plaster modification, carve/print/laminate a prototype orthosis or socket, then check it on the patient, note where the new approach fails, and rework it. Setting: clinic fitting room plus fab lab.

Clinical trialing of new componentry or a new way of using a device (e.g., a new microprocessor knee, elevated-vacuum suspension, a new AFO trimline strategy) on selected patients: fit it, observe gait, collect outcome measures and patient feedback over follow-up visits, and document whether it outperforms the usual approach. Setting: clinic and gait area.

Participating in a formal bench research campaign with a manufacturer, university or VA lab: prepare specimens of new component constructions, mount and run static/cyclic structural and durability tests (ISO 10328-type or robotic gait simulator), analyze the resulting data, and write up findings. Setting: institution-controlled test/research laboratory.

sources.developer: Boston University (Snapp, Gongora, Brown et al.)
sources.title: Autonomous Discovery of Tough Structures
sources.claim: BEAR is a self-driving lab that autonomously selects, 3D-prints, handles, mechanically tests and interprets >25,000 additively manufactured polymer structures to discover better load-bearing/energy-absorbing constructions, in a dedicated closed-loop robotic research cell.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous mechanical-structure discovery. It transfers to the bench portion of 'research new ways to construct' devices because the objects (3D-printed polymer parts of the same size and material class used for printed sockets, AFO shells and test coupons), the measurements (mass, geometry, stiffness/strength under load) and the accept/reject judgment are the same, and the system closes the design-fabricate-test-analyze loop that a practitioner's bench trial consists of.

sources.developer: Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory / UC Berkeley
sources.title: An autonomous laboratory for the accelerated synthesis of novel materials - PubMed
sources.claim: The A-Lab ran autonomously for 17 days, planning, executing and interpreting robotic synthesis experiments and producing 41 novel compounds, demonstrating an end-to-end autonomous physical research loop in a purpose-built robotic laboratory.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous materials-discovery experimentation. It supports the general claim that a robotic system can carry a physical research loop (hypothesis selection, sample preparation, measurement, interpretation, next experiment) to accepted output without step-by-step human control, but only inside a purpose-built robotic lab; the chemistry domain differs from device construction, so it is corroborating rather than decisive.

sources.developer: Roboticom (Italy); deployed at WCBL and other O&P fabricators
sources.title: Prosthetic Orthotic Central Fabrication Services | WCBL
sources.claim: A 7-axis robotic carving cell is commercially deployed in O&P central fabrication and clinic labs, milling patient-specific positive models and prosthetic/orthotic shapes from a digital file to ~0.1 mm inside an enclosed, floor-fixed robot cell.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated fabrication of O&P positive models. It shows a robot can realize a prototype shape from a digital design in an enclosed purpose-built cell, but it executes a supplied design and does not generate, evaluate or fit a new construction, so it supports only the making step of a research instance.

sources.system: Robotic Gait Simulator (6-DOF parallel robot, iterative learning control)
sources.developer: VA RR&D Center of Excellence for Limb Loss Prevention and Prosthetic Engineering / University of Washington (Aubin et al.)
sources.title: Gait simulation via a 6-DOF parallel robot with iterative learning control - PubMed
sources.claim: Robotic gait simulators built on 6-DOF parallel manipulators and dedicated prosthetic test rigs apply physiological loads and motions to lower-limb prostheses in a laboratory to evaluate new designs and alignments.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: mechanical evaluation of prosthetic components. It transfers to the testing portion of bench research on new device constructions because the specimens are exactly the devices in question and the machine applies and records the loading regimes a researcher would use; it does not cover specimen preparation or interpretation.

tasks.label: Publish research findings or present them at conferences and seminars.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

roles.title: Hearing Aid Specialists
aliases: Board Certified Hearing Instrument Specialist (Board Certified HIS)
National Board Certified Hearing Instrument Specialist (National Board Certified HIS)
roles.description: Select and fit hearing aids for customers. Administer and interpret tests of hearing. Assess hearing instrument efficacy. Take ear impressions and prepare, design, and modify ear molds.

tasks.label: Train clients to use hearing aids or other augmentative communication devices.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: New-fitting orientation in the dispensing office: specialist teaches an older first-time user how to insert and remove the aid, distinguish left/right, change or charge batteries, clean the dome/wax filter, and follow a daily wear-time acclimatization schedule; the client practices while the specialist coaches and corrects.

Follow-up visit teaching connectivity and controls: pairing the aids to a smartphone, using the manufacturer's app for volume/programs, Bluetooth call and TV streaming, and telecoil/loop use; specialist walks the client through menus and has them repeat the steps.

Instruction directed at a spouse, adult child, or care-facility staff member for a client with arthritis, low vision, or cognitive decline: teaching the helper to insert, charge, clean, and troubleshoot the devices and to set up communication strategies, in the office or at the client's residence/facility.

Remote or telephone coaching after delivery: talking a client through feedback/whistling, a dead battery, a plugged wax guard, moisture problems, or app re-pairing, sometimes with video and remote programming support.

Training on accessories and other augmentative communication devices: remote microphones, TV streamers, amplified/captioned telephones, alerting systems, and personal amplifiers, including when and where to use each and how to charge and store them.

tasks.label: Counsel patients and families on communication strategies and the effects of hearing loss.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Select and administer tests to evaluate hearing or related disabilities.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Comprehensive in-office hearing evaluation at a retail hearing aid clinic (Miracle-Ear/Beltone/Costco-type office): specialist performs otoscopy, seats the cooperative adult client in a sound-treated booth, places supra-aural or insert earphones and the bone oscillator on the mastoid, runs pure-tone air and bone thresholds with masking as needed, plus SRT and word recognition, then interprets the audiogram and screens for red flags.

Immittance and supplementary test battery in the clinic: selecting and running tympanometry/acoustic reflexes (inserting and sealing a probe tip in each ear canal), otoscopic wax/perforation check, and optional speech-in-noise (QuickSIN) or loudness discomfort measures on an adult client, with referral decisions based on findings.

Screening-level testing away from the booth but on premises controlled by an institution: retail floor or store hearing-screening station, employer/worksite hearing conservation event, health fair, or company mobile hearing van, using a portable/tablet audiometer with insert phones amid ambient noise; brief pass/refer screen and otoscopy.

Bedside/room testing on rounds at a nursing home or assisted-living facility: portable audiometer set up in a resident's room, frail elderly client who may be hard of hearing, seated in a wheelchair or bed, requiring hands-on placement of transducers, removal of existing hearing aids, repeated instruction and coaxing, plus otoscopy for wax.

In-home hearing test by a mobile hearing aid specialist: equipment carried into a private residence with unknown layout, pets, TV noise and no sound treatment; specialist positions the client, does otoscopy, places transducers and runs an abbreviated pure-tone and speech battery, judging validity given ambient noise.

Atypical or difficult client in the clinic: a young child, a client with dementia or a language barrier, a tinnitus/asymmetry/dizziness complaint, or a suspected non-organic loss — requiring modified or additional test selection (conditioned response methods, re-instruction, cross-checks) and a referral judgment to a physician or audiologist.

sources.developer: University of Southern Denmark / Lifeline Robotics collaborators
sources.title: Autonomous swab robot for naso- and oropharyngeal COVID-19 screening
sources.claim: An autonomous robot station physically performs naso- and oropharyngeal swabbing on seated human subjects at a purpose-built sampling station, validated in two small clinical studies; the closest demonstrated case of a robot autonomously contacting a patient's head region for a diagnostic procedure.
sources.transferJustification: Cited as the nearest patient-contact analogue (autonomous instrument placement on a seated person's head). It does not substantiate this task: swabbing is a single scripted reach into the mouth, whereas administering a hearing test requires otoscopic inspection of each canal, seating earphones/foam tips and a mastoid oscillator, an adaptive patient-response protocol with masking, and interpretation; no such capability is demonstrated.

sources.developer: Tsinghua University / Beijing Tsinghua Changgung Hospital collaborators
sources.title: Beyond hospital reach: Autonomous lightweight ultrasound robot for liver sonography
sources.claim: An autonomous ultrasound robot was deployed in a hospital ultrasound department and autonomously acquired standard abdominal imaging planes on volunteers, but the robot is mounted on the subject by a human and the anatomy is the abdomen, not the ear.
sources.transferJustification: Cited as evidence of the current frontier for autonomous robotic patient examination. Transfer to hearing testing fails: the device is human-mounted on a large body surface, does not perform ear-canal otoscopy or transducer placement, and does not run or interpret an audiometric battery.

sources.system: GSI AMTAS Pro / AMTAS Flex automated audiometry
sources.title: Automated Audiometry | GSI AMTAS Pro | Grason-Stadler
sources.claim: Automated audiometry products administer self-paced pure-tone and speech threshold tests and produce audiograms with minimal supervision, but they are software plus headphones and a response interface — the client or clinician physically places the transducers, and otoscopy and probe insertion remain manual.
sources.transferJustification: Included to show why automation of this task is non-robotic: AMTAS is software running an audiometer with headphones and a screen, explicitly excluded from the definition of a robotic system, and the physical acts of the task (otoscopy, seating earphones/bone oscillator, sealing an immittance probe) are still done by a person.

sources.system: HEARO robotic system (robotic cochlear implantation access)
sources.title: First Study in Men Evaluating a Surgical Robotic Tool Providing Autonomous Inner Ear Access for Cochlear Implantation
sources.claim: Autonomous robotic work on the ear that exists is surgical drilling of the temporal bone for cochlear implantation under CT-based planning in the operating room — not non-invasive audiometric assessment.
sources.transferJustification: Cited to show the only autonomous ear-directed robotics found is intraoperative drilling on an anesthetized, rigidly head-fixed patient with preoperative CT planning; it performs none of the steps of selecting and administering hearing tests on an awake client.

tasks.label: Administer basic hearing tests including air conduction, bone conduction, or speech audiometry tests.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine air-conduction pure-tone audiometry on an adult new customer in a sound-treated booth or quiet test room at a hearing-aid retail office: visually/otoscopically check the ears, seat the customer, place insert or supra-aural earphones with correct right/left orientation and canal seating, give and re-give verbal instructions, run the threshold search at 250-8000 Hz in both ears watching for false or delayed responses, and record a clean audiogram.

Bone-conduction testing with masking in the clinic booth: position the bone oscillator on the mastoid (or forehead) with correct contact force and no pinna contact, place the masking earphone on the non-test ear, obtain bone thresholds, decide when and how much narrow-band masking to apply, and resolve air-bone gaps, re-seating the oscillator when readings look implausible.

Speech audiometry in the clinic booth: familiarize the patient with spondees, obtain speech reception threshold, present recorded or monitored-live-voice word lists at suprathreshold levels (sometimes with contralateral masking or in noise), listen to and score the patient's spoken repetitions, and record word-recognition scores.

Testing an atypical or difficult patient in the clinic: an elderly customer with cognitive slowing, tremor or a wheelchair, a current hearing-aid wearer whose devices must be removed, collapsed ear canals, severe tinnitus confused with test tones, or a patient who cannot follow the response task — requiring re-instruction, re-conditioning, repositioning of transducers, and judgment about test validity.

Off-site testing without a booth: nursing-home room, customer's living room on a home visit, a mobile hearing van, a community health fair or a big-box store floor, using a portable audiometer; the specialist manages ambient noise, improvised seating and lighting, sets up the equipment, places transducers and obtains screening/threshold results good enough to act on.

sources.system: SR-NOCS autonomous swab robot (Lifeline Robotics lineage / University of Southern Denmark)
sources.developer: University of Southern Denmark / Lifeline Robotics
sources.title: Autonomous swab robot for naso- and oropharyngeal COVID-19 screening | Scientific Reports
sources.claim: SR-NOCS is an autonomous, force-controlled robot station that performs combined naso- and oropharyngeal swabbing on patients; it was evaluated in two clinical studies with 52 suspected COVID-19 patients, showing an autonomous manipulator can place a tool on/in a seated patient's head region in a clinic with minimal supervision.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic tool placement on a seated patient's head/mouth in a clinic. It shows vision- and force-guided contact with a live patient, but the robot executes one short swab trajectory; it does not place supra-aural/insert earphones or a bone oscillator, does not seat transducers to audiometric tolerance, and does not run an adaptive threshold or masking protocol, so it does not substantiate completing a hearing test.

sources.system: GSI AMTAS / AMTAS Pro / AMTAS Flex
sources.title: GSI AMTAS: Automated Hearing Assessment - AudiologyOnline
sources.claim: GSI AMTAS is a commercial patient-directed automated audiometry product that produces a diagnostic audiogram including air conduction, bone conduction with masking, and speech SRT/WRS, with quality indicators; the test is self-paced and unsupervised, meaning the patient — not any machine — dons and positions the earphones and bone transducer.
sources.transferJustification: This is an automated audiometer — a computer, screen and calibrated transducers — not a physically embodied machine that manipulates the world; the physical acts of the task (placing earphones, seating the bone oscillator, adjusting a poorly fitting transducer, removing hearing aids) are performed by the patient, so it cannot support a positive robotic judgment.

sources.title: Hearing Conservation Without Compromise | WAHTS USA
sources.claim: WAHTS is a deployed wireless automated audiometry headset with a built-in audiometer used for boothless occupational hearing testing, again requiring a person to don the headset and a technician to set up and supervise; no manipulator is involved.
sources.transferJustification: Relevant to the off-site instance, but it is an instrumented headset (transducers plus software), not a robotic system; a human still places the headset on the head and manages the patient, so it does not substantiate robotic completion of the instance.

sources.title: Experience with an Affective Robot Assistant for Children with Hearing Disabilities
sources.claim: A humanoid social robot (Pepper) has been used in a clinical setting as the interface for gamified audiometry with hearing-impaired children, presenting the test and interacting with the child, while transducer placement and clinical control of the audiometer remained with the clinical staff.
sources.transferJustification: Closest robotic evidence in audiometry itself: the robot serves as a social/interaction front end in a research study; it does not place or adjust audiometric transducers, decide masking, or produce a validated diagnostic audiogram, and its autonomy in the sessions is not established.

tasks.label: Maintain or repair hearing aids or other communication devices.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Walk-in/appointment routine maintenance in the dispensing office: specialist inspects the patient's RIC or BTE aid under a 10x microscope, vacuums wax and debris from receiver, microphone ports and vents, extracts and replaces the ~1 mm cerumen wax guard with a pre-loaded tool, swaps the silicone dome or cleans/replaces the thin tubing and earhook, dries the device, does a listening check with a stethoset, and returns it working.

Bench-level component repair in the clinic's in-house repair lab: diagnose a dead or weak aid (battery contacts corroded, receiver wire broken, microphone port clogged, battery door hinge broken, faceplate/shell cracked), open or disassemble the miniature housing, replace the plug-in receiver/wire, contacts, mic cover or battery door, reassemble and reseal, then verify; or determine it must be packaged and mailed to the manufacturer's repair lab.

Earmold/custom shell maintenance and modification at the workbench: re-tube a mold, replace tubing retention rings or removal lines, buff and grind an acrylic or silicone mold to relieve a pressure point identified from otoscopy and patient feedback, drill or plug a vent, glue a cracked shell, then re-check fit and feedback in the ear.

Diagnostic and verification bench work: run electroacoustic analysis in a hearing-aid test box against manufacturer specs, listening checks, moisture/desiccant treatment, reconnect or re-pair Bluetooth accessories, restore or update firmware and reload the patient's program after a repair, replace batteries/charger contacts on rechargeable devices, and document the outcome.

Off-site service: nursing home, assisted-living room, house call, or community outreach event where the specialist cleans and repairs residents' aids on a portable kit at a bedside or folding table — devices arrive dirty and unlabeled, lighting and surfaces vary, and patients often keep the aid in the ear until it is removed.

sources.title: UR5 handles tiny hearing aid components with precision — Universal Robots case story
sources.claim: A UR5 six-axis cobot is deployed in Oticon's hearing-aid moulding shop, autonomously suctioning millimetre-scale hearing-aid plastic parts out of injection moulds in a fixed, purpose-built machine cell — showing that robots handle hearing-aid-sized parts only when the parts are new, identical, and presented in a known position by the machine.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: manufacturing part handling of hearing-aid components. It shares object scale (~1 mm parts) but not the task's content: no diagnosis of a used device, no disassembly, no wax removal, no reassembly or verification, and the parts are presented in a fixture rather than arriving as an arbitrary fouled patient device.

sources.title: Hearing care market and supply chain — Sonova Report 2018/19
sources.claim: Sonova, the largest hearing-aid manufacturer, states that while some of its processes (hybrid circuit production) are fully automated, the assembly of hearing aids remains highly-skilled manual work — indicating that even inside purpose-built factories the fine manipulation involved in putting hearing aids together (and hence taking them apart to repair them) is not robotically automated.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: hearing-aid assembly in a factory. If the easier, fully-specified assembly of new devices is still manual at the industry's most automated site, robotic completion of the harder repair/disassembly of used devices is not substantiated.

sources.system: toolcraft automated micro-injection moulding cell with robotics for Sonova cerumen filters
sources.title: Cerumen filter | Sonova | mould making | injection moulding | robotics | case study | toolcraft AG
sources.claim: Sonova's cerumen (wax) filters — the consumable the specialist replaces during routine maintenance — are made on an automated micro-injection-moulding line with robotics at toolcraft; the automation makes the filters, it does not fit them into a patient's used hearing aid.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: production of the wax-guard part. Manufacture of the filter in a fixtured mould cell does not transfer to extracting a wax-clogged guard from an arbitrary patient device and inserting a new one, which requires locating the receiver port on an unknown, soiled device.

sources.title: PerfectClean Hearing Aid Cleaning System — ADCO Hearing Products
sources.claim: The closest automation to in-clinic hearing-aid maintenance is a push-button benchtop appliance (PerfectClean) that ultrasonically cleans, disinfects and dries hearing systems; it performs no manipulation — it cannot inspect, extract and replace a wax guard, change a dome or tube, or run a listening check, so it cannot complete the maintenance instance.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated cleaning of hearing aids. It covers only the wax/moisture-removal sub-step of the maintenance instance and involves no robotic manipulation, so it cannot substantiate whole-instance completion.

sources.system: Clinic repair bench workflow (human technicians, MedRx/Jodi-Vac style vacuum tools)
sources.title: Hearing Aid Repair - Bend, OR - Kenyon Audiology
sources.claim: In-clinic hearing-aid maintenance and repair is described by practices as human technician work performed under a 10-power microscope with hand-held vacuum tools, with no robotic system in the loop.
sources.transferJustification: Baseline/negative context: documents that the task as performed today is manual microscope bench work; no robotic system was found performing it.

tasks.label: Perform basic screening procedures, such as pure tone screening, otoacoustic screening, immittance screening, and screening of ear canal status using otoscope.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Otoscopic inspection in the hearing aid office: specialist seats the client, selects and attaches a speculum, retracts the pinna to straighten the canal, advances the otoscope a few millimeters without touching canal walls or eardrum, judges canal status (wax occlusion, debris, drainage, foreign body, perforation, collapsing canal) and documents it before testing or ear impressions.

Pure-tone air-conduction screening in the office sound booth/quiet room: specialist instructs the client, places supra-aural headphones or inserts foam-tip earphones correctly in each canal, presents screening tones at fixed levels, watches the client for valid vs. false responses, re-instructs or re-seats transducers as needed, and records pass/refer per ear.

Immittance/tympanometry screening in the office: specialist chooses an eartip of the right size, seats the probe in the canal to obtain an airtight seal, runs the pressure sweep, re-seats after leaks or blocked-probe errors (common with wax or a moving client), and interprets the tympanogram type and ear-canal volume.

Otoacoustic emission screening in the office (often for difficult-to-test adults or children): specialist inserts the OAE probe, verifies probe fit/calibration in the canal, keeps the client still and quiet, repeats the run when noise-rejected, and reads the pass/refer result per frequency band.

Off-site screening at a community health fair, employer site, nursing home room or client's residence: portable otoscope and screening audiometer/OAE unit carried in, ambient noise and seating vary, clients may be in wheelchairs or beds, layout differs at every site; specialist performs otoscopy plus pure-tone (and sometimes OAE) screening and records results.

sources.title: Autonomous swab robot for naso- and oropharyngeal COVID-19 screening (Scientific Reports)
sources.claim: A force-controlled robot autonomously inserted naso- and oropharyngeal swabs into real patients in two clinical studies (52 patients), the closest demonstrated analogue to autonomously introducing an instrument into a patient's body orifice; nothing comparable exists for the ear canal.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: swab sampling of a body orifice. Cited as the nearest analogue, but transfer to ear screening is NOT granted: the swab is a flexible probe entering a large nasal passage against a head rest, whereas otoscopy/tympanometry/OAE require pinna traction, tip-size selection, sub-millimetre advance in a curved ~7 mm canal and an airtight seal, with eardrum-perforation risk; no ear-canal demonstration was found.

sources.system: auto-RUSS (7-DoF autonomous robotic ultrasound scanning system)
sources.developer: Lin et al., hospital/university research group (China)
sources.title: Autonomous robotic ultrasound scanning system: a key to enhancing image analysis reproducibility and observer consistency in ultrasound imaging (Frontiers in Robotics and AI)
sources.claim: An autonomous robotic ultrasound system with force control and visual servoing acquired thyroid images on a human volunteer, showing autonomous placement of a diagnostic probe against a human body surface in a clinical research setting.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous diagnostic probe placement on a patient. Transfer to this task is NOT granted: contact is on flat external skin with a large probe and no insertion, whereas ear screening requires inserting a speculum or sealed eartip into a narrow, curved, pain-sensitive canal.

sources.title: Automated Audiometry and the Changing Role of the Audiologist
sources.claim: Hearing screening is automated today only in its stimulus/threshold logic: automated audiometers such as Luna run school, occupational and military screening from a laptop, headphones and a patient response switch, with a clinician placing the headphones on the patient; the system is not an embodied robot and performs no otoscopy or probe insertion.
sources.transferJustification: Same task (pure-tone screening) but software-only automation running on an audiometer with headphones; per the definition used here it is not a robotic system, and the physical acts of transducer placement and patient handling remain human.

sources.title: Robot-Assisted Middle Ear Endoscopic Surgery: Preliminary Results on 37 Patients (Frontiers in Surgery)
sources.claim: Robotics acting inside the human ear is confined to teleoperated surgical assistance in the operating room: the RobOtol system held an endoscope for middle-ear surgery in 37 patients under continuous surgeon control via a space mouse.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic instrument manipulation through the external ear canal. It cannot support a positive judgment because it is continuously teleoperated by a surgeon and is a surgical, not a screening, procedure.

tasks.label: Create or modify impressions for earmolds and hearing aid shells.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine silicone ear impression on a cooperative adult in a hearing-center exam room: otoscopy, select/place an otoblock past the first bend, syringe or gun-inject two-part silicone filling canal and concha, wait for cure while managing patient anxiety and jaw position, remove atraumatically, inspect for voids/blunt tip, trim excess, label and package for the earmold lab.

Impression on a difficult ear in the clinic: young child, very narrow or sharply bent canal, post-surgical/mastoid cavity or perforated TM, ears with cerumen requiring management first, or deep-canal impressions for CIC aids, musician monitors and hearing protection; includes retakes after a rejected impression (short canal, void, block displacement).

Digital ear scan taken in place of a silicone impression (e.g., Otoscan/Lantos): otoscopy, guiding the laser/optical probe through the canal to the second bend while watching the live 3D build, filling gaps by rescanning, trimming/cleaning the digital model and submitting it to the manufacturer.

Bench modification of an earmold or hearing-aid shell to a defined specification at the office lab bench: shorten the canal by a set amount, add or enlarge a vent, remove a helix/sharp edge, buff and polish back to a smooth gloss, re-tube or re-cement tubing — a specified geometric change delivered on a small acrylic/silicone part.

Diagnose-and-relieve fit modification with the patient in the chair: insert the mold, find the sore or reddened contact area from patient report and ear inspection (marking with lipstick/indicator), grind that spot, reinsert, and iterate until seating is comfortable and feedback-free.

Impression taken off-site during a house call, assisted-living room or mobile hearing unit: variable seating and lighting, patient may be bed-bound or have dementia, materials carried in a case, with the same otoblock/inject/cure/remove sequence performed in a setting taken as found.

sources.system: Sonova custom shell 3D printing production (with Materialise Rapid Shell Modelling)
sources.title: 3D printing technology for improved hearing | Sonova International
sources.claim: Custom hearing-aid shells and earpieces are manufactured automatically by 3D printers from digitized ear impressions in Sonova's production facilities, showing machine fabrication of the exact custom in-ear geometry class in a purpose-built production environment.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: producing the custom shell geometry rather than taking the impression. It transfers only to bench-side production/modification of a fixtured custom earpiece to a specified digital geometry, not to capturing the impression in the ear.

sources.title: 3D printing technology for improved hearing | Sonova International
sources.claim: Despite full automation of downstream shell manufacturing, the ear impression itself is still taken manually by a clinician in the hearing-care office.

sources.title: Fully Integrated CEREC System - CAD/CAM | Patterson Dental
sources.claim: A chairside CAD/CAM system in dental offices automatically mills a custom anatomical restoration to sub-millimetre accuracy inside an enclosed milling unit from a digital design, demonstrating automated custom small-part material removal at worker quality.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated shaping of a small custom acrylic/ceramic anatomical part to a specified geometry inside a machine enclosure. Comparable object size, sub-mm precision and finish requirements to shortening/venting/polishing an earmold presented fixtured at E1.

sources.system: FerRobotics Active Contact Flange / AOK905 robotic sanding-polishing kit
sources.title: Grinding, sanding, polishing, deburring - FerRobotics
sources.claim: Commercial force-controlled robotic end-effectors perform grinding, sanding, polishing and deburring on plastic and other parts with constant contact force, compensating surface tolerances without operator guidance.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: force-controlled abrasive material removal and polishing on plastic parts. Transfers to buffing/grinding a fixtured earmold to a defined spec, where contact force control prevents breaching the thin shell.

sources.title: First Study in Men Evaluating a Surgical Robotic Tool Providing Autonomous Inner Ear Access for Cochlear Implantation
sources.claim: The only clinically deployed autonomous in-ear robotic procedure is surgical drilling of a preplanned trajectory through the temporal bone with the head rigidly fixed in an operating room, under continuous surgeon supervision and CT-based planning; it does not perform any soft-tissue ear-canal impression work.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous robotic work inside the ear. It does NOT transfer to impression taking: it drills fixed bone along a CT-planned path in an OR, whereas an impression requires otoblock placement against a mobile eardrum, silicone injection, cure and atraumatic removal in soft tissue.

sources.title: A Novel Ear Impression-Taking Method Using Structured Light Imaging and Machine Learning: A Pilot Proof of Concept Study
sources.claim: As of 2024 the literature review in a peer-reviewed pilot study found no developed contactless (non-contact, automated) method of capturing ear-canal geometry; the authors' structured-light prototype produced only partial ear-canal matching in a proof-of-concept trial.

sources.title: Perceptive Completes World's First Fully Automated Dental Procedure on a Human Using AI-Driven Robotic System
sources.claim: The closest autonomous robotic work inside a patient's head is a single first-in-human automated dental crown preparation; it is a one-off demonstration in a dental clinic on rigid tooth structure, not a deployed, reliability-proven capability, and no equivalent exists for ear-canal impressions.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous instrument work in a confined human orifice. Transfer fails for ear impressions: rigid teeth versus a compliant canal with an eardrum, no silicone injection/cure/atraumatic removal shown, and only a single unpublished first-in-human case.

tasks.label: Read current literature, talk with colleagues, and participate in professional organizations or conferences to keep abreast of developments in audiology.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Demonstrate assistive listening devices (ALDs) to clients.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: In a private hearing-care office/fitting room, the specialist demonstrates a personal amplifier or hearing-aid accessory (pocket talker, remote microphone, TV streamer): retrieves the demo unit, checks/installs battery, powers it on, places the headset or earbuds on the seated client (or couples it to the client's aids), plays speech or TV audio, adjusts volume/tone to the client's spoken reaction, and answers questions.

In the same office, a connectivity/accessory demo: pairing a streamer, remote mic, phone app or telecoil program to the client's own hearing aids or smartphone, then showing live streaming of a phone call or audio, switching programs, and letting the client try the controls while the specialist coaches.

At a retail hearing-center showroom counter, demonstrating alerting/communication devices — amplified or captioned telephone, TV listening headset, bed-shaker alarm clock, doorbell/smoke-alarm signaler — including cabling/plug-in setup and a live trial with the client and often a family member present.

Office demo for an elderly client with dexterity, vision or cognitive limitations: repeated hands-on placement and removal of the device on the client's ears/head, guiding the client's hands over small buttons and battery doors, judging comprehension from body language, and coaching an accompanying caregiver.

Off-site demonstration — a home visit, nursing-home resident room, senior-center program or health-fair booth — where the specialist brings a demo kit, sets up on whatever table/outlet space is available, works around ambient noise and the client's own TV/phone equipment, and runs the trial.

sources.system: RoboRehab (Pepper humanoid + tablet, Gazi/Galatasaray University consortium)
sources.developer: Uluer et al. / RoboRehab project (SoftBank Robotics Pepper platform)
sources.title: Experience with an Affective Robot Assistant for Children with Hearing Disabilities (PMC8594648)
sources.claim: The RoboRehab system places a Pepper social humanoid alongside a tablet in an audiology clinic/lab to run gamified hearing tests with children who wear hearing aids or cochlear implants; the robot only speaks and gestures — it does not handle, fit, or demonstrate any listening device, and its behaviour is triggered through an intermediary device monitored by ....
sources.transferJustification: Closest robotic system operating in the hearing-care workflow (audiometry/hearing-aid adjustment sessions). It shows the state of the art there is social/verbal support only: no manipulation of hearing devices, no fitting on the client, no volume adjustment from client feedback, so it cannot substantiate completing an ALD demonstration.

sources.system: Galbot G1 autonomous retail clerk / Galaxy Space Capsule store
sources.title: The Humanoids Have Arrived! At CES 2026 — KraneShares
sources.claim: Galbot's autonomous retail clerk operates in real-world store environments (its 'Galaxy Space Capsule' consumer-goods stand in Beijing), autonomously retrieving packaged products for customers; it performs item pick-and-hand-over, not device setup, fitting on a person, or interactive product demonstration.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: customer-facing retail item retrieval and handover in a purpose-built store. It is the nearest demonstrated capability to presenting a product to a client, but it involves only rigid packaged goods from known shelf slots and no powering-up, ear-placement, or subjective benefit verification, so it does not transfer to demonstrating an ALD.

sources.title: Lio-A Personal Robot Assistant for Human-Robot Interaction and Care Applications (PMC8043496)
sources.claim: Lio, a mobile manipulator for personal-care tasks, has been deployed and operates autonomously in health-care facilities, handling and manipulating objects — showing that autonomous object handling by robots in structured care institutions exists, but for fetch/carry and simple handover rather than client-facing device demonstration and fitting.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous object handling and human interaction inside care institutions (an E2 setting comparable to a hearing clinic). Cited to show the frontier of deployed clinical manipulators is fetch/carry and light interaction, not setting up small electronics on a client's head and adjusting them to the client's reported hearing.

tasks.label: Assist audiologists in performing aural procedures, such as real ear measurements, speech audiometry, auditory brainstem responses, electronystagmography, and cochlear implant mapping.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Real-ear/probe-microphone verification in a dispensing office or clinic fitting room: otoscopy first, then mark and thread a soft probe tube ~28-30 mm down an adult ear canal to within ~5 mm of the tympanic membrane, insert the hearing aid without displacing or kinking the tube, seat and orient the patient to the loudspeaker, run REUR/REAR/REAG sweeps, and repeat after the audiologist adjusts the fitting. Patients flinch, canals are narrow or tortuous, cerumen is common.

Speech audiometry in a sound-treated booth: seat and instruct the patient, place insert earphones (foam tips compressed and inserted) or supra-aural headphones squarely over the canals, present recorded SRT/word-recognition lists at levels the audiologist directs, apply contralateral masking, score each spoken response live over talkback, and re-seat transducers on elderly or restless patients.

ABR/ASSR/OAE session in a hospital or ENT clinic, frequently on a sleeping infant or young child: abrade and prep skin, apply and secure surface electrodes at vertex, forehead and mastoids, check impedances, insert foam ear tips, keep the patient asleep and artifact-free, re-prep electrodes that drift, and hand clean waveforms to the audiologist.

Vestibular testing (ENG/VNG) in a darkened balance lab: fit and tighten VNG goggles (or apply periorbital electrodes), calibrate eye tracking, guide the patient through oculomotor, Dix-Hallpike and positional maneuvers on the table or rotary chair, set up and assist with warm/cool caloric irrigations, and monitor for nausea and fall risk while helping the patient on and off the table.

Cochlear implant mapping support in a CI clinic: place the coil/headpiece on the patient's head, connect the programming interface and cables, run impedance and neural-response sweeps under the audiologist's direction, condition and reinforce a young child's behavioral responses (VRA/play audiometry), swap coils and processors, and verify the device on the ear at the end.

sources.system: SR-NOCS autonomous swab robot (Lifeline Robotics / University of Southern Denmark)
sources.title: Autonomous swab robot for naso- and oropharyngeal COVID-19 screening (Scientific Reports)
sources.claim: The closest autonomous robot to inserting a probe into a patient's head orifice is a swab station that drives a swab into the nose/throat of a seated awake patient; it was tested on 52 patients in two clinical studies, and does one insertion only.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous insertion of a slender flexible probe into a body orifice of a seated, awake patient in a clinic. Cited as the nearest analog to probe-tube/insert-tip placement, but it does not transfer: the nasal cavity is far more forgiving than an ear canal, the robot performs a single insertion with no otoscopy, no depth control relative to a delicate tympanic membrane, no hearing-aid insertion, and no multi-step test protocol. It therefore does not substantiate completion of any instance.

sources.system: Vitestro Aletta Autonomous Robotic Phlebotomy Device
sources.title: Northwestern Medicine and Vitestro Collaborate to Advance Autonomous Robotic Phlebotomy
sources.claim: Autonomous patient-contact procedural robots exist in structured clinical facilities, but are confined to a single narrow act (a needle stick) with the patient's arm placed in a device cradle, and are still in multicenter validation trials.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: an autonomous invasive patient-contact clinical procedure. It establishes that such robots exist in E2 facilities, but the objects, precision and workflow differ entirely from aural procedures: one imaged vein on a fixtured forearm versus otoscopy, ear-canal probe placement, scalp electrode prep, goggle fitting and multi-step protocols on a mobile, instructed head. It supports no positive judgment here.

sources.system: Audioscan Probe Guide (Verifit2) / Natus Aurical ProbeTube Assistant
sources.title: Evaluation of Probe Guide: Software-assisted Probe Tube Placement in Hearing Aid Fittings (The Hearing Review)
sources.claim: The state of the art for real-ear probe-tube placement is on-screen software guidance for a human clinician who still performs the insertion; no robotic probe-tube placement system is in use.
sources.transferJustification: Negative/context evidence. This is software, not a robotic system: the clinician still inserts the probe tube by hand. It shows that even the most automated commercial REM workflow leaves the entire physical act to a human.

sources.title: First Study in Men Evaluating a Surgical Robotic Tool Providing Autonomous Inner Ear Access for Cochlear Implantation
sources.claim: The only ear-related robot performing an autonomous physical act on a patient is a surgical drilling robot that executes a preplanned trajectory through the temporal bone of an anesthetized, rigidly head-fixed patient in an operating room.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous robotic action on the ear. It does not transfer to this task: it operates on an anesthetized patient with bone-anchored fiducials and preoperative CT planning in an OR, whereas the aural procedures here are performed on awake, moving, instructed patients in a clinic with no registration frame, and involve sensor placement and behavioral testing rather than drilling.

sources.title: Robot-Assisted Middle Ear Endoscopic Surgery: Preliminary Results on 37 Patients (Frontiers in Surgery)
sources.claim: Otologic robots used clinically outside the drilling step are teleoperated endoscope/instrument holders driven by the surgeon, not autonomous.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot manipulation at the ear. Explicitly teleoperated, so under the autonomy rule it cannot support a positive judgment for any instance.

sources.system: TRV mechanical rotation chair (mechanical rotation chairs for BPPV)
sources.title: A mechanical rotation chair provides superior diagnostics of benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (Frontiers in Neurology)
sources.claim: For vestibular positional testing, motorized multi-axis chairs move the patient through diagnostic head positions, but the chair is driven by the clinician and does not fit goggles, calibrate eye tracking, or run caloric irrigations.
sources.transferJustification: Directly related to the vestibular instance: a machine repositions the patient for Dix-Hallpike/positional testing. It covers only the positioning sub-step, is clinician-commanded rather than autonomous, and leaves goggle fitting, calibration, caloric irrigation and patient monitoring to the human, so it does not substantiate whole-instance completion.

tasks.label: Diagnose and treat hearing or related disabilities under the direction of an audiologist.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Diagnostic hearing evaluation in a retail hearing center or ENT/audiology clinic sound booth: greet and history-take, perform otoscopy with a handheld otoscope, place supra-aural headphones or insert foam-tip earphones and a bone oscillator, run air/bone pure-tone and speech testing with masking decisions, plot and interpret the audiogram for the supervising audiologist's review.

Hearing aid selection and fitting appointment: physically insert the aid/dome or custom shell into the patient's ear canal, thread a real-ear probe tube past the canal bend for real-ear measurement, adjust gain/programming to target, check feedback and physical fit, and instruct the patient on insertion, removal and care.

Follow-up treatment visits in the office: otoscopic check for cerumen or drainage, clean and de-wax the instrument, replace wax guards/domes/tubing, re-insert and re-verify, and fine-tune programming based on patient complaints of comfort, occlusion or loudness.

Taking a silicone ear impression for a custom mold or earmold: otoscopy, placing a cotton/foam otoblock at the correct depth in the canal, injecting impression material to fill canal and concha, waiting for cure, extracting the impression atraumatically and checking it for defects before sending to the lab.

Off-site service in a nursing home room, assisted-living facility or private residence (mobile hearing care): portable/boothless audiometry, otoscopy, hearing aid fitting or repair with a frail, sometimes cognitively impaired patient in a bed or armchair, working around furniture, lighting and ambient noise taken as found.

sources.title: First Study in Men Evaluating a Surgical Robotic Tool Providing Autonomous Inner Ear Access for Cochlear Implantation
sources.claim: The HEARO robotic system performs an autonomous, image-guided drilling of a tunnel to the inner ear during cochlear implantation, but it operates in an operating room on an anesthetized, head-fixed patient under continuous surgeon supervision, and it addresses surgery rather than audiometric diagnosis, hearing aid fitting or ear impressions.
sources.transferJustification: Closest robotic capability acting on the human ear. It does not transfer: it drills bone under CT-based navigation with the head rigidly fixed under anesthesia, and covers none of the awake-patient steps (otoscopy, transducer placement, audiogram interpretation, aid insertion, probe-tube placement, impression taking) that constitute this task.

sources.system: Lifeline Robotics automatic throat swab robot
sources.developer: Lifeline Robotics (University of Southern Denmark spin-out)
sources.title: Throat swabbing robot developed for COVID-19 testing by Danish startup
sources.claim: A robot that autonomously inserts a swab into a conscious person's mouth/throat has been built as a prototype, showing that autonomous instrument insertion into a human orifice remains at demonstration stage rather than clinical routine.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous insertion of an instrument into a conscious patient's orifice, analogous to otoblock/probe-tube/earmold insertion. It does not substantiate this task: it is a four-week prototype for a single sampling motion in the mouth, not millimetre-precise ear-canal work near the tympanic membrane, and no ear-canal equivalent was found.

sources.system: NAO humanoid robot 'Sam' auditory testing interface
sources.developer: University Medical Center Groningen / University of Groningen
sources.title: Use of a humanoid robot for auditory psychophysical testing (PLoS ONE 18(12): e0294328)
sources.claim: A humanoid NAO robot named ... has been used as an interface to administer auditory psychophysical tests to normal-hearing adults in a laboratory, presenting stimuli through its own loudspeakers and logging responses, with no physical contact with the listener's ears and no clinical diagnosis.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-administered hearing testing. It does not transfer to diagnostic audiometry: the robot only plays sounds over built-in speakers and collects responses in a research lab; it performs no otoscopy, no calibrated transducer placement, no masking or clinical interpretation, and the authors report sound-quality and timing limitations.

roles.title: Health Technologists and Technicians, All Other
roles.description: All health technologists and technicians not listed separately.

roles.title: Neurodiagnostic Technologists
aliases: Certified Intraoperative Neurophysiology Technologist (Certified Intraoperative Neurophysiology Tech)
roles.description: Conduct electroneurodiagnostic (END) tests such as electroencephalograms, evoked potentials, polysomnograms, or electronystagmograms. May perform nerve conduction studies.

tasks.label: Indicate artifacts or interferences derived from sources outside of the brain, such as poor electrode contact or patient movement, on electroneurodiagnostic recordings.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Monitor patients during tests or surgeries, using electroencephalographs (EEG), evoked potential (EP) instruments, or video recording equipment.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Intraoperative neuromonitoring (IONM) during spine, cranial, or vascular surgery in a hospital OR: the technologist stays with the patient for hours running SSEP/MEP/EMG on an EP instrument, delivering stimulation, watching for real waveform changes versus anesthesia/electrocautery artifact, reaching under drapes to re-seat or re-tape dislodged subdermal/needle electrodes, observing limb twitch responses, and calling alerts to the surgeon in seconds.

Routine 20-40 minute outpatient EEG in a hospital or clinic EEG lab (adult or pediatric): technologist watches the live tracing and the patient simultaneously, annotates behavior (eye opening, movement, drowsiness, clinical events), positions and runs the photic stimulator, coaches hyperventilation, checks/repairs impedances and popping electrodes mid-record, and calms or repositions a restless or uncooperative patient.

Long-term video-EEG monitoring in an epilepsy monitoring unit or continuous EEG in the ICU: technologist supervises live traces and video from a central station across a shift, verifies camera framing and audio, responds to alarms and seizures by going to the bedside, ensures patient safety, performs seizure testing (responsiveness, language, motor commands), pushes the event button, replaces electrodes that fail over days, and documents events.

Attended overnight polysomnography in a sleep lab: technologist monitors 16+ channels plus infrared video and audio for 6-8 hours on 1-3 patients, re-applies fallen oximeter/thermistor/EEG leads in the dark, fits and adjusts CPAP masks and titrates pressure to events, scores/annotates events in real time, and assists patients who wake or need to get up.

Home/ambulatory monitoring: patient wears an ambulatory EEG with home video or a home sleep test; the technologist checks signal quality remotely or at a home visit, coaches the patient/family by phone or video, and reviews and annotates the incoming record, occasionally traveling to the residence to repair electrodes.

sources.system: Human IONM workflow (SpecialtyCare clinical service description)
sources.title: Intraoperative Monitoring: Protecting Patients Through Real-Time Neurological Assessment - SpecialtyCare
sources.claim: The IONM technologist role that this task describes combines continuous vigilance with hands-on equipment work at the patient throughout the case (stimulation delivery, artifact/technical troubleshooting), establishing what a machine would have to replace.
sources.transferJustification: Not a robotic system; cited only to characterize the task content that a robot would need to perform. It cannot support a positive judgment.

sources.title: World first: researchers develop completely automated anesthesia system | McGill University Newsroom
sources.claim: The closest machine analogue to continuous EEG-based patient surveillance with autonomous action in an operating room is a closed-loop anesthesia drug-delivery robot, which titrates drugs from an EEG-derived depth-of-hypnosis index but performs no neurodiagnostic monitoring, no patient observation, and no electrode maintenance.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: closed-loop anesthesia control in an OR using an EEG-derived index. Transfer is limited: it controls drug infusion from a single processed index and does not interpret SSEP/MEP/EMG, discriminate artifact, observe the patient, or repair electrodes, so it does not complete the monitoring task.

sources.system: Stereotactic robot arm for sEEG implantation (e.g., ROSA)
sources.title: Contributions of Robotics to the Safety and Efficacy of Invasive Monitoring With Stereoelectroencephalography (Frontiers in Neurology)
sources.claim: Robots used in neurological ORs are stereotactic arms that position and place sEEG depth electrodes under surgeon direction; they perform a rigid, image-registered placement step, not continuous monitoring of a patient's neural signals.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic electrode implantation in the OR. It shows robots can be registered to a fixed patient head frame, but the work is a surgeon-directed placement step with no vigilance, signal interpretation, or response to patient events, so it does not transfer to monitoring.

sources.title: Diligent Robotics Unveils Moxi 2.0 ... — Diligent Robotics
sources.claim: The largest deployed fleet of hospital mobile manipulators performs logistics (delivering medications and lab samples) in hospital corridors; no deployed hospital robot performs patient neurodiagnostic monitoring.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous mobile manipulation in hospitals (an E2 facility). It establishes that hospital robots handle transport errands, not bedside physiological surveillance or patient interaction, so it cannot substantiate completion of this task at any tier.

sources.developer: Foxconn with NVIDIA (Taichung Veterans General Hospital trial)
sources.title: Foxconn Taps NVIDIA to Accelerate Physical and Digital Robotics for Global Healthcare Industry
sources.claim: Nursing-assistant robots piloted on hospital wards perform delivery, patrol, and guidance roles alongside nurses; they do not conduct or supervise neurodiagnostic recordings.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous ward assistance in a hospital (E2). The demonstrated duties are transport, patrol and guidance, not physiological monitoring or bedside intervention, so it does not transfer to monitoring patients during tests or surgeries.

sources.system: Automated online seizure detection software in epilepsy monitoring units
sources.developer: Various (e.g., Persyst-class detectors evaluated in EMU studies)
sources.title: Yield of conventional and automated seizure detection methods in the epilepsy monitoring unit (ScienceDirect)
sources.claim: Even the purely informational detection component of long-term monitoring is only partially automated by software, and human staff must still respond at the bedside; the automation that exists is software-only, not an embodied system.
sources.transferJustification: Software-only, therefore not a robotic system and unable to support a positive judgment; cited to show that the monitoring alert function is not fully automated and that physical bedside response remains human.

tasks.label: Conduct tests or studies such as electroencephalography (EEG), polysomnography (PSG), nerve conduction studies (NCS), electromyography (EMG), and intraoperative monitoring (IOM).

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine 20-40 minute outpatient/inpatient EEG in a hospital or clinic EEG lab: greet and interview the patient, measure the head and mark the 10-20 positions, abrade skin and apply ~21 cup electrodes with paste/collodion plus ECG and eye leads, verify impedances, run the record with hyperventilation and photic stimulation, coach the patient, annotate behavior and artifacts, then remove electrodes and clean up.

Overnight polysomnography in a sleep lab: full hookup of scalp EEG, EOG, chin and leg EMG, ECG, nasal pressure/thermistor, thoracic and abdominal effort belts, oximeter and snore sensor; biocalibrations; all-night monitoring with electrode/sensor repair, patient assistance, and CPAP mask fitting and titration.

Bedside EEG in an ICU, ED or NICU: portable machine at a crowded bedside, uncooperative, sedated, agitated or critically ill patient with lines, dressings and head wraps; collodion-applied long-term continuous EEG hookup, daily electrode maintenance and troubleshooting in a high-artifact electrical environment.

Nerve conduction study in a neurology/EDX clinic: position and warm the limb, palpate landmarks, place recording and ground electrodes, measure and mark distances, hand-hold the stimulator over each nerve site, escalate to supramaximal stimulation, obtain clean CMAP/SNAP waveforms, reposition for artifact or anomalous responses, and assist the physician during needle EMG.

Intraoperative neuromonitoring in an operating room: insert subdermal needle electrodes for SSEP/MEP/EMG/EEG on a draped anesthetized patient, obtain baselines, maintain the montage through positioning and drapes, monitor continuously during surgery, distinguish true signal change from anesthetic/technical artifact, and alert the surgical team.

Portable/ambulatory studies outside the lab: 24-72 hour ambulatory EEG hookup or home sleep apnea test setup performed at the patient's home, a school, or a nursing facility, with instruction of the patient/family and equipment retrieval.

sources.system: Robotic microjet e-tattoo printer (on-scalp printed EEG electrodes)
sources.developer: University of Texas at Austin / UCLA (Nanshu Lu, Jose del R. Millan labs)
sources.title: Ink-Based E-tattoo Can Decode Brainwaves - UT Austin News
sources.claim: A robotic inkjet printer, guided by a camera-based head scan and a layout algorithm, deposits conductive-ink 'e-tattoo' EEG sensors directly onto a volunteer's scalp; it works only on short-haired subjects, places sensors rather than conducting a clinical study, and remains a laboratory research demonstration.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: applying EEG sensors to the scalp, the first step of a routine EEG. Transfer is limited: it is a lab demo on short-haired volunteers, does not prepare skin, apply a full 10-20 collodion/paste montage, verify impedances, or run activation procedures, patient coaching and event annotation, so it does not substantiate completing an EEG study.

sources.system: NovaGuide Intelligent Ultrasound / Lucid Robotic System (robotic transcranial Doppler)
sources.date: 2022-02 (Scientific Reports study); FDA-cleared and in hospital use
sources.title: Safety and efficacy of a novel robotic transcranial doppler system in subarachnoid hemorrhage - Scientific Reports
sources.claim: The NovaGuide/Lucid robotic transcranial Doppler system autonomously searches for and optimizes cerebral artery signals in hospitalized patients, but a human clinician positions the patient in the head cradle and engages the robotic probes on the temporal region; it involves no electrode application and none of the EEG/PSG/NCS/EMG/IOM studies.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic acquisition of a neurodiagnostic signal from a patient's head in a hospital. It shows autonomous signal search is feasible once a human sets up the interface, but it performs no scalp preparation, multi-electrode application, or any of the listed studies, so it cannot substantiate completing them.

sources.date: commercial product in clinical/research use; page retrieved 2026
sources.title: Axilum Robotics TMS-Robot | Neurolite Advanced Medical Solutions
sources.claim: A commercial robot positions a TMS coil against a patient's head at neuronavigated targets, maintains contact and compensates for head motion during clinical sessions, showing robots can safely contact the scalp under supervision, but it places a single coil and performs no electrode work or diagnostic recording.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated placement of an instrument on a human scalp in a clinic. Safe, precise head contact transfers partially, but it does not part hair, abrade skin, apply or secure multiple electrodes, run a recording protocol, or annotate a study.

tasks.label: Collect patients' medical information needed to customize tests.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Explain testing procedures to patients, answering questions or reassuring patients, as needed.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Set up, program, or record montages or electrical combinations when testing peripheral nerve, spinal cord, subcortical, or cortical responses.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine outpatient/inpatient EEG in a hospital or clinic neurodiagnostic lab: after the 10-20 electrodes are on, the tech connects the electrode leads/jackbox to the amplifier, selects and programs the recording montages (longitudinal bipolar, transverse, referential) plus sensitivity/filter settings in the acquisition software, verifies impedances and channel integrity, then records the study, switching montages and adjusting settings live to display findings and suppress artifact.

Evoked potential study (SSEP, BAEP, VEP) in a neurodiagnostic lab: tech connects recording electrode leads to the specified amplifier inputs to build the required derivations (e.g., Erb's point, cervical, cortical channels), hooks up and positions the peripheral nerve stimulator / insert earphones / pattern screen, programs stimulus rate, intensity, polarity, sweep and averaging parameters, and records replicable averaged waveforms, adjusting when responses are poor.

Intraoperative neuromonitoring in an operating room: tech sets up multimodality montages (SSEP, transcranial MEP, spontaneous/triggered EMG, EEG), plugs dozens of subdermal needle leads into designated headbox inputs per the montage map, connects and programs stimulators, establishes baselines, and records continuously through the case while re-derivating channels and troubleshooting electrical interference.

Continuous EEG / long-term monitoring at the bedside in an ICU or epilepsy monitoring unit: tech configures the acquisition unit and headbox, programs recording and review montages (including reduced-lead or quantitative trends), sets spike/seizure detection and video sync, records over hours to days, and reformats derivations remotely as clinical questions change.

Nerve conduction study in an EMG/neurodiagnostic lab: tech sets up the recording electrode pair and reference/ground combination for each nerve tested, connects and applies the handheld stimulating probe, programs sweep, gain, filter and stimulus parameters, incrementally raises stimulus to supramaximal, and records responses at each stimulation site with acceptable latency/amplitude quality.

sources.title: Performance, Safety, and Patient Experience of an Autonomous Robotic Phlebotomy Device: A Multicenter Trial | Clinical Chemistry
sources.claim: The Aletta device autonomously performs venipuncture on patients in outpatient blood-collection settings, with one supervising staff member overseeing several devices; it is the closest example of an autonomous robot performing a patient-contact diagnostic procedure, but it performs a single fixed procedure and does nothing resembling multi-channel montage configuration or signal-quality-driven neurophysiologic recording.
sources.transferJustification: Related task (robotic venipuncture) cited only to bound the state of the art in autonomous patient-contact diagnostic robotics; it does not transfer, because it does not connect electrode leads to amplifier inputs, program derivations, or judge recorded waveform quality.

sources.title: Axilum - TMS Robot By SYNEIKA
sources.claim: A commercial robot automatically positions and maintains a transcranial magnetic stimulation coil against a patient's head under neuronavigation, compensating for head movement; it positions a stimulating device on a patient but does not set up recording montages, program electrical derivations, or acquire and validate evoked responses.
sources.transferJustification: Related task (robotic positioning of a stimulator on the head) is the nearest neurophysiology-adjacent robot; it does not transfer because the montage task requires connecting/assigning many recording channels, programming acquisition parameters, and interpreting live signal quality, none of which this system performs.

sources.system: Clinical evoked potential / IONM amplifier headbox setup (human practice reference)
sources.title: Neurophysiologic Tests in the Operating Room | Springer Publishing
sources.claim: Setting up montages for evoked potentials and intraoperative monitoring involves physical connection of recording and stimulating electrode leads into specific amplifier/stimulator headbox inputs, confirming the task has a hands-on hardware component beyond software configuration.
sources.transferJustification: Context source, not a capability claim: establishes that montage set-up requires physical lead-to-input connections, so the task has a physical component that a robot would have to perform.

sources.title: Reliability of a novel point of care device for monitoring diabetic peripheral neuropathy | Scientific Reports
sources.claim: The NC-stat/DPNCheck point-of-care device automates stimulation, recording and measurement for a single sural nerve conduction test, but the probe is hand-held and manually positioned by a clinician, so no machine performs the physical set-up or electrode-combination placement.
sources.transferJustification: Related task (automated single-nerve conduction measurement) shows the signal-processing side can be automated, but the device is manually placed and covers one fixed derivation, so it cannot support a positive judgment for robotic montage set-up and recording.
