sources.developer: CenterVue (study by Fogagnolo et al., University of Milan)
sources.title: Compass: Clinical Evaluation of a New Instrument for the Diagnosis of Glaucoma | PLOS One
sources.claim: The clinical protocol for the automated perimeter still requires a person to patch the fellow eye and place the patient's forehead and chin on the instrument's rests before the automated test begins - the patient-handling step that no cited machine performs.

sources.system: Nao humanoid robot perimetry assistant (Octopus 900 via Open Perimetry Interface)
sources.developer: University of Melbourne (McKendrick, Turpin et al.); robot by SoftBank Robotics
sources.title: Robot Assistants for Perimetry: A Study of Patient Experience and Performance | TVST | ARVO Journals
sources.claim: A Nao humanoid robot took the in-test supervision role during perimetry on an Octopus 900: a script triggered by fixation losses, false-positive catch trials and test progress delivered encouragement and instructions, and across 40 adults there was no significant difference ... mean sensitivity, fixation losses or false positives versus feedback from a trained human operator.

sources.developer: Duke University (Draelos, Izatt, Kuo et al.)
sources.title: Contactless optical coherence tomography of the eyes of freestanding individuals with a robotic scanner | Nature Biomedical Engineering
sources.claim: A robot-mounted OCT scanner autonomously locates and aligns to the eye of a freestanding person and acquires retinal volumes without a chinrest or a technician positioning the patient; later piloted on emergency-department patients.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: retinal imaging rather than perimetry. It shows a robot can autonomously align an ophthalmic instrument to a patient's eye in a clinic without a chinrest, but it presents no stimuli, collects no patient responses, does not occlude the fellow eye and does not coach or reposition the patient, so it does not substantiate completing a visual field test outside a fixtured station.

sources.title: CenterVue DRS Operating Manual (Directions for Use)
sources.claim: Instruments from the same manufacturer as COMPASS include a motorized chin rest that automatically adapts to the patient's head plus an auto-alignment module, showing machine-controlled physical actuation of the patient support and optics in a clinic room.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated fundus photography at the same class of chinrest-fixtured patient station. It substantiates that the machine, not the technologist, can perform the positioning/alignment actuation once the patient's head is at the instrument - the presentation assumed for perimetry at E1.

tasks.label: Measure corneal thickness, using pachymeter or contact ultrasound methods.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine glaucoma/ocular-hypertension workup in an ophthalmology exam lane: cooperative seated adult, tech measures central corneal thickness (handheld ultrasound pachymeter or the practice's non-contact tono-pachymeter/specular pachymeter), checks reading spread and quality, records CCT in the chart for IOP correction.

Refractive-surgery, cataract or cornea-clinic evaluation: cooperative seated adult needing a full pachymetric map/thinnest-point value (Scheimpflug tomography, anterior-segment OCT or specular microscope with integrated pachymetry), sometimes with an ultrasound confirmation reading.

Difficult or uncooperative patient in the clinic: young child, patient with dementia, tremor, nystagmus, blepharospasm or wheelchair/limited mobility; tech physically steadies the head, holds lids, coaxes fixation and usually uses a handheld ultrasound probe between blinks.

Abnormal cornea where contact ultrasound is the clinically required method: edema, dense scar/opacity, post-graft or irregular epithelium; anesthetic drop instilled, probe held perpendicular on the central cornea, several readings averaged, probe disinfected, care taken not to abrade.

Supine or non-seated patient: exam under anesthesia, intraoperative/pre-procedure pachymetry in the OR, hospital bedside or reclined post-op/injured patient; handheld ultrasound pachymeter applied to the eye of a lying patient.

sources.developer: Duke University (Draelos, Ortiz, McNabb, Kuo, Izatt)
sources.title: Contactless optical coherence tomography of the eyes of freestanding individuals with a robotic scanner (Nature Biomedical Engineering)
sources.claim: Duke's robot-mounted OCT scanner autonomously positions itself to a freestanding person's eye without any headrest or operator intervention and acquires anterior-segment (corneal) OCT volumes of quality comparable to clinical tabletop instruments.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous anterior-segment ocular OCT imaging (the paper reports autonomous anterior segment results in freestanding individuals). Corneal thickness is a standard automated readout of anterior-segment OCT volumes, so autonomously acquiring a well-aligned corneal OCT scan yields the same measurement an optical pachymeter produces, on the same object at micrometre resolution.

sources.title: Robotic, optical coherence tomography retinal imaging for emergency department patients: a pilot study (Annals of Emergency Medicine)
sources.claim: The same robotic OCT system was used on emergency-department patients who sat freely with no chin or head rest; the robot located the eye and held alignment by itself, with a minimally trained operator only triggering acquisition remotely.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic ocular OCT imaging of unselected patients in a working hospital. It establishes that robotic eye-finding and alignment holds up on real, unrestrained patients in a clinical facility, which is the patient-handling portion of a pachymetry measurement.

sources.system: Tomey EM-4000 specular microscope with integrated non-contact pachymetry
sources.date: product page accessed 2026-07; device marketed since ~2018
sources.title: EM-4000: Specular Microscope – TOMEY GmbH
sources.claim: The Tomey EM-4000 is a commercially sold non-contact specular microscope that performs alignment and measurement automatically and reports central corneal thickness (integrated non-contact pachymetry) with every exam, in about four seconds per eye.

sources.title: Intradevice Repeatability and Interdevice Comparison of Two Specular Microscopy Devices in a Real-Life Setting: Tomey EM-4000 and Nidek CEM-530 (Medicina)
sources.claim: A peer-reviewed real-life clinical comparison (112 eyes of 56 patients in an anterior-segment practice) confirms the EM-4000 measures non-contact in seconds with central auto-alignment and integrated pachymetry, and quantifies its repeatability against a manually aligned competitor.

sources.date: 2022-03 listing; device in clinical use since ~2009
sources.title: Tonometer - TONOPACHY NT-530P - NIDEK - pachymeter / air tonometry / tabletop (MedicalExpo)
sources.claim: The Nidek Tonopachy NT-530P, a widely sold clinic instrument, uses 3-D auto tracking and auto ... to find the eye and fire without operator joysticking, and automatically measures the patient's central corneal thickness alongside IOP.

sources.system: OCULUS Pentacam Scheimpflug tomographer (and Tomey CASIA2 AS-OCT)
sources.date: accessed 2026-07; products in clinical use for over a decade
sources.title: OCULUS Pentacam Anterior Eye Segment Tomographer (Clarion Medical)
sources.claim: Commercial anterior-segment tomographers used for pre-refractive-surgery pachymetry maps run the measurement themselves once the patient is at the instrument: the Pentacam releases the scan automatically with a built-in quality test, and the CASIA2 AS-OCT offers auto-alignment and auto-scan capture with pachymetry output.

sources.developer: Duke University (Hurley, Foust, Izatt, Kuo, McNabb)
sources.title: Multi-angle refraction corrected robotically aligned anterior eye OCT (Proc. SPIE)
sources.claim: A robot-mounted multi-angle anterior-eye OCT with robotic pupil alignment images the whole anterior segment and applies dual-surface refraction correction to visualise the cornea (demonstrated on an anterior eye phantom).
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-aligned corneal (anterior segment) OCT with refraction correction — the same optical measurement chain from which corneal thickness maps are computed, showing robotic alignment being developed specifically for corneal imaging.

tasks.label: Measure corneal curvature with keratometers or ophthalmometers to aid in the diagnosis of conditions, such as astigmatism.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine pre-test in an ophthalmology/optometry practice: cooperative adult seated at an auto kerato-refractometer in the pretest lane. Tech adjusts table/chin-forehead rest, instructs the patient to fixate and blink, captures K1/K2 and axis for both eyes, checks the confidence/quality flags, and sends values to the chart/EMR.

Pre-operative keratometry for cataract or refractive-surgery planning: cooperative adult at an optical biometer or Scheimpflug/Placido topographer in the clinic. Higher precision demands, repeat captures, comparison between eyes, and quality vetting before the K values feed an IOL calculation.

Keratometry/topography on irregular or unstable corneas: keratoconus, post-graft, post-LASIK, dry eye, or contact-lens fitting. Poor tear film and fixation; tech coaches blinking, sometimes holds lids, repeats scans and discards artifact-laden readings before recording.

Patients who are hard to position at a table-mounted instrument: wheelchair users, frail or kyphotic elderly, tremor, hard-of-hearing or non-English-speaking patients. Tech physically repositions the patient and instrument, steadies the head, or falls back on a manual/handheld keratometer in the lane.

Young children and uncooperative or sedated patients: handheld autokeratometer used on a squirming toddler in clinic, or keratometry during an exam under anesthesia on a supine patient in the operating room.

Off-site screening/outreach: mobile vision van, nursing home dayroom, school or community screening event; portable auto kerato-refractor set up on whatever table is available, variable lighting and seating.

sources.title: Chronos Automated Binocular Refraction System
sources.claim: Topcon Chronos is a commercial clinic instrument combining binocular autorefraction and keratometry; with SightPilot NAVi the patient completes the measurement steps under the device's own guided prompts, with the device performing the objective measurement and reducing technician involvement.

sources.title: Topcon Announces the European Launch of Chronos
sources.claim: Chronos, launched commercially in the US and Europe, integrates keratometry with autorefraction in one fully automated device used in eye-care practices.

sources.system: Kestrel 3100m fully automatic fundus camera with self-service module (Shanghai Top View Industrial)
sources.developer: Shanghai Top View Industrial / Shanghai Eye Disease Prevention & Treatment Center
sources.title: Service Quality and Residents' Preferences for Facilitated Self-Service Fundus Disease Screening: Cross-Sectional Study (JMIR)
sources.claim: In Shanghai primary health-care screening sites, a fully automatic non-mydriatic fundus camera let residents run their own ocular imaging: the machine found the eyes and pupils, moved its lens, focused, shot and reviewed image quality by itself, with service quality statistically indistinguishable from optometrist-operated imaging.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated ocular imaging at a chin-rest instrument. It transfers because the physical act is the same class — a motorized head-rest instrument that finds the eye, aligns and focuses its optics in three axes, captures, and gates the result on an automatic quality check, on a self-positioned patient inside a health facility. Imaging the retina through an undilated pupil is at least as demanding an alignment as reading mires reflected off the anterior cornea, and the study found no significant difference in image-quality pass rate versus an operator.

sources.title: Optical Biometer AL-Scan M | NIDEK
sources.claim: The NIDEK AL-Scan M optical biometer, which measures keratometry alongside axial length in cataract and myopia practice, uses 3D auto-tracking and auto-shot so the instrument locates the eye and fires the measurement itself once the patient is at the headrest.

sources.date: 2025 (undated manufacturer product site; Pentacam commercial since 2002)

sources.title: Effectiveness and satisfaction of fully self-service fundus disease screening among middle-aged individuals: a cross-sectional study
sources.claim: A 2025 Shanghai community study of fully self-service fundus photography reports that the device independently performs alignment, focusing and capture, with imaging quality comparable to photography by experienced operators.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated ocular imaging on a self-positioned patient in a community health facility. Same instrument class (chin-rest, motorized three-axis alignment, auto-capture) and same patient population as clinic keratometry, so autonomous alignment-and-capture performance carries over to obtaining keratometric readings from a cooperative seated adult.

tasks.label: Supervise or instruct ophthalmic staff.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: In an ophthalmology clinic, the technologist orients and trains a newly hired ophthalmic assistant: explaining clinic protocols, walking through how to run visual field, OCT, and autorefraction workflows, answering questions, and observing the trainee's practice runs to give verbal correction and feedback.

Day-to-day oversight of technicians during clinic hours: assigning patients and rooms, monitoring workup pace and patient flow, answering technicians' clinical questions, and stepping in verbally to redirect when a workup is incomplete or a measurement looks inconsistent.

Reviewing completed work for quality: checking charted refractions, tonometry, and imaging studies for accuracy and completeness, flagging repeat scans, and counseling the responsible technician on how to correct technique or documentation errors.

Formal in-service or continuing-education instruction: preparing and delivering a teaching session or competency check-off (e.g., new perimeter software, infection-control or aseptic technique review, JCAHPO certification prep) to a group of ophthalmic staff, including written or oral evaluation.

Administrative supervision: completing performance evaluations, documenting competencies, setting schedules and coverage, and holding corrective or coaching conversations with staff, often in an office or via clinic messaging systems.

tasks.label: Measure the thickness of the retinal nerve, using scanning laser polarimetry techniques to aid in diagnosis of glaucoma.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine baseline RNFL/optic-nerve scan on a cooperative adult glaucoma suspect in an ophthalmology or optometry clinic: tech enters patient data, seats patient at the tabletop scanner (GDx-type polarimeter historically, now almost always spectral/swept-source OCT disc cube), aligns to the pupil, captures both eyes undilated, checks signal strength/centration/segmentation, repeats if poor, and files the RNFL thickness report to the chart.

Follow-up progression scan on an established glaucoma patient: same-location registration to the baseline scan, both eyes, then screening the printout for motion artifact, blink lines, decentration and segmentation errors before releasing it for trend/GPA analysis at the same visit.

Difficult but cooperative patient in the clinic: elderly, cataract or other media opacity, small pupil, poor or wandering fixation, wheelchair or limited neck mobility; requires coaching, extra attempts, occasional dilation and manual repositioning to get an acceptable-quality RNFL scan.

Poorly cooperative patient in the clinic: advanced dementia or confusion, nystagmus or severe tremor, very low vision unable to fixate, ptosis/small lids needing manual eyelid retraction, or a young child; the technologist physically steadies the head, holds lids, improvises fixation, and often accepts a partial study.

Off-site glaucoma screening: portable/automated OCT set up at a community health event, senior center or nursing-home dayroom, or a mobile eye van, with variable lighting, tight space and untriaged walk-up patients; images captured for later remote reading.

sources.system: Robotically Aligned OCT (RAOCT), Universal Robots UR3e + custom swept-source OCT

sources.claim: Duke's robotically aligned OCT (RAOCT), a UR3e arm carrying a custom OCT engine with face- and pupil-tracking, autonomously aligned to and imaged the eyes of 25 seated patients (healthy and diseased retinas, ages 25-91) at Duke Eye Center with no chin/forehead rest; foveal thickness matched technician-acquired Spectralis (mean difference -1 um, p>0.7) with lower intra-session variation, and volumes captured both fovea and optic nerve head.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous OCT acquisition and retinal thickness quantification. It transfers to RNFL measurement because it is the same modality, same organ and same alignment/fixation problem; the acquired volumes include the optic nerve head, and layer thickness was measured to within ~1 um of a clinical technician-operated OCT.

sources.title: Contactless, autonomous robotic alignment of optical coherence tomography for in vivo evaluation of diseased retinas
sources.claim: The same Duke robot imaged an 81-year-old patient with Parkinsonian tremor whose eye the technician could not capture on the clinical tabletop OCT, using face- and pupil-tracking motion compensation while the patient sat unrestrained; the paper notes local non-specialized staff act only as chaperones placing the patient in front of ... system.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous retinal OCT capture in hard-to-image patients (tremor, elderly, dilated/undilated). Transfers because the failure mode that defeats technicians on RNFL scans is the same - patient motion and alignment loss during a ~1 s acquisition.

sources.title: Topcon Maestro2 - The Robotic OCT Fundus Camera with OCTA
sources.claim: The Maestro2's automation extends to difficult eyes: a cataract mode automatically moves the scanning position to work around media opacities, and the OCT can image through pupils as small as 2.5 mm, with a 12x9 mm wide scan covering macula and optic disc plus a glaucoma (Hood) report.

sources.claim: Peer-reviewed measurement of quantitative retinal layer thickness on the Topcon Maestro in eyes with retinal disease showed repeatability coefficients of variation under 3.4% and reproducibility under 3.5%, indicating the automatically acquired scans meet clinical precision expectations.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated layer-thickness quantification on the same device used for RNFL reports; establishes that the auto-aligned, auto-captured scans yield thickness values with clinical-grade repeatability.

sources.claim: Notal Vision's SCANLY Home OCT, granted FDA De Novo authorization in May 2024, lets wet-AMD patients perform technician-free spectral-domain OCT scans at home with self-guided fixation; 97% of patients in the pivotal study successfully obtained images, averaging 48 seconds per self-scan.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: OCT image capture without a trained operator. Only corroborative here - the scan is a 10-degree macular scan, not a peripapillary RNFL scan, and the human patient performs the positioning, so it cannot by itself support a positive judgment.

tasks.label: Assist physicians in performing ophthalmic procedures, including surgery.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Scrub/assist role during routine cataract or anterior-segment surgery in an ambulatory surgery center OR: verify the eye/IOL, position and drape the patient, prep the lids and fornix with povidone-iodine, set up the phaco tray and console tubing, prime handpieces, load the IOL cartridge and viscoelastic, hand and take back microsurgical instruments and sutures on the surgeon's cue, wipe/irrigate the cornea, change console settings on verbal request, and place the shield at the end.

Assisting in-office intravitreal injections in a clinic exam/procedure lane: seat and recline the patient, instill anesthetic and dilating drops, prep lids and lashes with povidone-iodine, open the sterile injection kit, draw/hand the loaded syringe and lid speculum, hold lids or steady the patient's head, apply post-injection drops and count fingers, and turn the room over between the 10-20 patients on the injection day.

Assisting in-office laser procedures (YAG capsulotomy, SLT, panretinal photocoagulation, laser retinopexy): power up and check the laser, instill anesthetic/miotic drops, seat and align the patient at the chin rest, apply coupling gel and hand the gonio/fundus contact lens, adjust power and spot settings on the physician's verbal instruction during the treatment, steady the patient's head, and clean/disinfect the lens afterward.

Assisting minor lid and ocular-surface procedures at the slit lamp or in a minor procedure room (chalazion incision and drainage, corneal foreign body and rust ring removal, punctal plug insertion, suture removal, lash epilation): set up the sterile tray and anesthetic, hand instruments (blade, chalazion clamp, curette, burr, forceps), hold lids or gauze, apply pressure and ointment, patch the eye, and clean up sharps and specimens.

Assisting complex hospital-OR ophthalmic surgery (pars plana vitrectomy, scleral buckle, corneal transplant, strabismus, oculoplastics): operate and troubleshoot the vitrectomy console, exchange fragile 25-gauge instruments and light pipes, manage infusion, gas/silicone oil and tamponade, hand sutures and load donor tissue, reposition the microscope and viewing system, and respond to intraoperative complications.

sources.title: RoboNurse-VLA: Robotic Scrub Nurse System based on Vision-Language-Action Model
sources.claim: RoboNurse-VLA is a research robotic scrub nurse that autonomously grasps and hands over surgical instruments on voice command, evaluated in laboratory bench experiments rather than on patients.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: instrument handover is one sub-step of the ophthalmic technologist's procedure-assist role. It does not cover patient prep, draping, lid holding, console operation, or the delicate microsurgical instrument set used in eye surgery, and it is demonstrated only on a laboratory bench.

tasks.label: Perform fluorescein angiography of the eye.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine FA in a retina/ophthalmology clinic on a cooperative dilated adult: verify consent and allergy/renal history, capture baseline color and red-free photos, perform antecubital venipuncture with butterfly needle, inject ~5 mL of 10% sodium fluorescein as a rapid bolus while starting the timer, capture transit-phase frames at ~1/s, then mid and late phases of both eyes, monitor for nausea and extravasation, label and upload the study.

Hospital/academic eye clinic FA where a nurse or physician places the line and injects the dye and the technologist runs only the photography: seats and positions the patient at the mydriatic fundus camera, coaches fixation, coordinates timer with the injection, captures the timed transit/mid/late sequence over both eyes, culls and quality-checks images.

Ultra-widefield or combined FA/ICG study (Optos, Clarus, Eidon FA, Spectralis) for diabetic retinopathy, vein occlusion or vasculitis: steered peripheral sweeps with fixation targets, filter/laser mode switching, montage capture, plus the IV bolus and timing as above.

Difficult patient: frail or elderly, wheelchair or gurney-bound, poor fixation, small pupil or media opacity, difficult venous access requiring several attempts or a hand vein; patient becomes anxious, nauseated or vasovagal mid-study, requiring the tech to pause, reassure, hand an emesis basin, or summon help while preserving the timed sequence.

Pediatric/infant or exam-under-anesthesia FA (RetCam or handheld camera in the OR or NICU) and bedside inpatient studies: dye dosed by weight, contact imaging with a lid speculum and coupling gel, scleral depression for peripheral views, tight coordination with the anesthesia team and surgeon.

sources.title: iCare EIDON FA Fluorescein Angiography Confocal Fundus Imaging System
sources.claim: iCare (CenterVue) EIDON FA is a commercial confocal fundus imaging system marketed as a highly automated fluorescein angiography platform with motorized chin rest, auto-alignment, auto-focus, auto-exposure and auto-capture, but it images only: the human staff still dilate, cannulate, inject the dye and manage the patient, and it is operated by a person at the device.
sources.transferJustification: Related task is automated retinal image capture, the photography half of FA. Transfer is only partial: the same objects (retina, seated patient) and precision, but the device performs no venipuncture, no dye injection, no patient positioning and no patient monitoring.

sources.title: NEW PRODUCT APPLICATIONS: Bringing Automation to Fluorescein Angiography Systems
sources.claim: Trade-press description of the most automated FA camera on the market shows the exam is run step-by-step by a human operator who presses record while a clinician injects the dye; no machine sequences the angiogram or delivers the injection.
sources.transferJustification: Same task (FA image capture); cited to establish the level of machine autonomy actually available in FA systems, i.e. operator-initiated capture rather than autonomous execution of the study.

sources.title: Contactless, autonomous robotic alignment of optical coherence tomography for in vivo evaluation of diseased retinas
sources.claim: Duke's robotically aligned OCT autonomously finds and tracks a freely seated patient's eye and acquires diagnostic-quality retinal volumes in healthy and diseased eyes without a technician touching the patient, in an eye-clinic and emergency-department research setting.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous retinal image acquisition on a seated patient. It transfers to the alignment/focus portion of FA photography, but it is dye-free OCT, involves no intravenous injection, no timed multi-phase sequence, and remains a research prototype.

sources.title: Vitestro unveils Aletta robotic phlebotomy device – CAP TODAY
sources.claim: Vitestro's Aletta is a CE-marked autonomous robotic phlebotomy device that performs the whole venous blood draw — tourniquet, skin prep, ultrasound vein selection, needle insertion, sample collection — in outpatient blood-collection clinics and hospitals in the Netherlands under staff supervision.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous venipuncture, the vascular-access step of FA. Transfer is partial: it withdraws blood at its own draw station rather than delivering a timed 5 mL dye bolus into a patient seated at a fundus camera, and it is limited to routine easy-access veins.

sources.developer: University of Miami Miller School / Ivy (Michael Ivan)
sources.title: A Serial Entrepreneur: Miller School Neurosurgeon Leads World's First Robotic-Assisted IV Catheterization
sources.claim: The Ivy platform performed the first robotic-assisted IV catheterization in a human in late 2025; it is described as semi-autonomous and remains an early clinical demonstration rather than a deployed autonomous injector.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: intravenous access for drug delivery, the injection step of FA. Cited as a negative bound: as of 2026 human IV placement for injection is only semi-autonomous and first-in-human, not worker-quality autonomous.

tasks.label: Photograph patients' eye areas, using clinical photography techniques, to document retinal or corneal defects.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine posterior-pole color fundus photography in the clinic imaging room: a cooperative seated adult (often pharmacologically dilated) is positioned at a table-mounted camera on chin/forehead rest; the tech aligns on the pupil, focuses, captures disc- and macula-centered fields of both eyes, checks for artifacts/reflexes, retakes as needed, and files images to the chart to document retinal pathology (DR, AMD, disc changes).

Widefield / multi-field or montage retinal documentation of a cooperative seated adult: ultra-widefield or 7-field montage, autofluorescence or stereo disc pairs, steering fixation to capture peripheral lesions (tears, lattice, vein occlusion, peripheral DR), then reviewing and assembling the set.

Anterior segment / corneal photography at a slit lamp or anterior-segment camera: documenting an ulcer, abrasion, foreign body, graft, scar or dystrophy — requires eyelid retraction or patient gaze direction, choosing slit width/angle, diffuse vs. slit vs. retroillumination vs. cobalt-blue after fluorescein instillation, and multiple magnifications.

Fluorescein or ICG angiography session: consent and dye administration (IV injection performed or assisted by the technologist), then a timed sequence of transit, mid- and late-phase frames on both eyes with fixation changes and peripheral sweeps, while monitoring the patient for adverse reactions.

Hard-to-image patient in the clinic, operating room, or at the hospital bedside: a child, a wheelchair-bound or reclined patient, a post-op or poorly cooperative patient with unsteady fixation, small pupil or media opacity, imaged with a handheld/portable camera or with heavy coaching and repositioning.

External / adnexal clinical photography: standardized views of lids, ptosis, strabismus, orbital or ocular-surface lesions with a hand-held or mounted camera, including multiple gaze positions, scale reference, and consistent lighting/background for pre- and post-treatment comparison.

sources.system: Topcon Maestro2 (robotic OCT + true-color fundus camera)

tasks.label: Maintain ophthalmic instruments or equipment.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Daily/between-patient in-situ care of exam-lane equipment in an ophthalmology clinic: wipe and disinfect slit-lamp chin and forehead rests, joystick, phoropter face pieces, keratometer, B-scan probe; clean oculars, objective lenses, mirrors and instrument optics with lens tissue/cleaner; dust covers, empty waste, restock supplies at each of several lanes.

Reprocessing reusable detachable patient-contact accessories: Goldmann applanation prisms, gonioscopy/fundus contact lenses, lid specula, calipers, pachymeter tips - remove from device, pre-clean, disinfect or sterilize per IFU, rinse, dry, inspect for scratches/cracks, return to lane storage.

Reprocessing minor-surgical/procedure instrument sets after in-office lid, lacrimal or intravitreal procedures (or ophthalmic ASC sets): point-of-use treatment, ultrasonic/washer cleaning, inspection and lubrication of delicate microsurgical instruments, pouch or tray packing, autoclave cycle, indicator verification, documentation and sterile storage.

Scheduled calibration and quality checks of diagnostic equipment: Goldmann tonometer weight-bar calibration check and adjustment, lensmeter/autorefractor/keratometer accuracy checks, visual-field perimeter calibration and stimulus checks, A-scan/biometer verification, projector and acuity chart checks, logging results.

Minor troubleshooting, repair and preventive maintenance: replace slit-lamp/illumination bulbs, fuses and batteries, printer paper and chin-rest tissue, clean or change filters, tighten/align optics and joystick, lubricate chair and table mechanisms, tag out failed units and coordinate vendor service.

sources.title: Bryan Health Uses New Robotic Technology to Clean and Sterilize Surgical Instruments

tasks.label: Conduct tests, such as the Amsler Grid test, to measure central visual field used in the early diagnosis of macular degeneration, glaucoma, or diseases of the eye.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine standard automated static perimetry (Humphrey 24-2/30-2 SITA or Octopus) on a cooperative adult in a glaucoma/comprehensive eye clinic testing room: greet and explain the test, patch the fellow eye, seat the patient and adjust table and chin/forehead rest, enter data and set trial-lens/liquid-lens correction, hand over the response button, start the test, watch the live eye monitor for alignment and fixation, coach and pause as needed, save and print the reliable result.

Automated perimetry on a challenging patient: frail elderly or wheelchair-bound, low vision, hearing-impaired, cognitively impaired, non-English-speaking or pediatric. Requires hands-on transfer and positioning, holding or re-seating the head, ptosis taping, repeated re-instruction, frequent pauses, and often a repeat run when reliability indices are poor.

Chairside Amsler grid / quick central field check at the exam lane for a macular patient: put near correction in place, hand or hold the grid card at about 30 cm, occlude one eye, question the patient about missing, wavy or distorted lines, have the patient mark the chart, repeat for the second eye, and document findings in the chart.

Specialized central field testing in a retina or neuro-ophthalmology clinic: 10-2 macular threshold fields or microperimetry (MP-3/MAIA/COMPASS) with fundus alignment and retinal tracking, on patients with central scotomas and unsteady fixation who need extra coaching and often repeat acquisitions.

Manual or kinetic central field testing: Goldmann or semi-automated kinetic perimetry, tangent screen, or confrontation-style central field checks, where the technologist controls stimulus size, intensity and movement in real time and judges the validity of each response while mapping isopters and scotomas.

Off-site or portable central field screening: health fair, mobile clinic, nursing home or bedside, using a portable perimeter, tablet-based screener or printed Amsler grid in a room with uncontrolled lighting, improvised seating and no fixed equipment layout.

sources.system: Robotic OCT scanner (robot-mounted, active pupil tracking)
sources.title: Contactless optical coherence tomography of the eyes of freestanding individuals with a robotic scanner | Nature Biomedical Engineering
sources.claim: A robot-mounted OCT scanner autonomously positions itself and images the eyes of freestanding people without operator intervention or head ..., producing volumes comparable to clinical tabletop systems.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: acquiring an ophthalmic diagnostic measurement from a patient's eye in an eye-clinic setting. It shows a robot can align safely and precisely to a live patient's eye, but the acquisition is passive for the patient; it does not cover fellow-eye occlusion, refractive correction, response-button interaction or the minutes-long reliability coaching a visual field test requires.

sources.claim: A mobile robotic OCT prototype was built and characterized for imaging patients in outpatient and inpatient clinical settings across standing, seated and reclined postures.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-acquired ophthalmic imaging of patients in real clinic rooms. Establishes robot mobility and eye alignment in an eye-clinic environment, but it is an imaging prototype; it does not administer psychophysical field tests or perform patient set-up (patching, chin rest, trial lens).

sources.transferJustification: Directly related sub-step: robot-delivered patient instruction and encouragement during visual field testing. It substantiates only the coaching component, not the whole task; the robot performed no set-up, occlusion, alignment or instrument operation, and autonomous triggering could not be confirmed.

sources.title: iCare COMPASS Automated Perimeter with Retinal Tracking
sources.claim: A commercial automated perimeter offers motorized auto-alignment, real-time retinal tracking that corrects fixation losses, and trial-lens-free correction, but is operated by a technician ... positions the patient and runs the exam.
sources.transferJustification: Same task (central visual field measurement). It automates parts of the instrument workflow but is a diagnostic instrument the technologist operates, not a robot that seats, patches, aligns, instructs and monitors the patient; unattended end-to-end operation is not established.

sources.transferJustification: Same task; negative context establishing that current perimetry instruments do not complete the test unattended at worker quality.

tasks.label: Conduct binocular disparity tests to assess depth perception.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine adult comprehensive eye exam in a clinic lane: technologist seats the patient, places polarized (or red-green) glasses over the patient's habitual correction, holds a Titmus or Randot booklet at 40 cm under controlled lighting, asks which circle stands out, rotates/inverts the plate to check for guessing, and records stereoacuity in seconds of arc.

Pediatric patient (roughly 3-8 years, suspected amblyopia/strabismus) in a pediatric ophthalmology clinic: coaxes the child to keep polarized glasses on, presents the Titmus fly / Randot Preschool / Lang cards, asks the child to pinch the fly's wings or point to shapes, coaches and repeats with a moving, sometimes uncooperative child, and judges whether responses are genuine or guessed.

Strabismus / binocular-vision workup before or after surgery or during vision therapy: near stereo test plus distance stereo testing (e.g., distance Randot or Frisby-Davis at 3 m), performed with prism or occluder manipulation and paired with cover testing, on adults and older children in the exam lane.

Off-site screening: school vision screening, community health fair, or occupational/driver vision screening; portable stereo test or screener carried in, variable lighting and seating, high patient throughput, brief instructions to each person.

Difficult patient: elderly, low-vision, wheelchair-bound, cognitively impaired, or non-verbal patient; requires adapted stereo testing (Lang two-pencil test, preferential-looking cards), physical support/positioning of the patient's head, and interpretation of behavioral responses.

Instrument- or chart-based stereo testing in an automated refraction lane: technologist positions the patient at a digital acuity chart or vision screener, inserts/fits polarizing filters, runs the stereo slide sequence, and records the result in the chart.

sources.title: Contactless, autonomous robotic alignment of optical coherence tomography for in vivo evaluation of diseased retinas
sources.claim: A robot-mounted OCT scanner autonomously tracks a seated patient's face and pupil and aligns an ophthalmic imaging instrument to the eye without chin rest or operator intervention, validated on patients recruited from Duke Eye Center clinics.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: performing an ophthalmic diagnostic test on a seated clinic patient. It shows a robot can safely approach a patient's eye autonomously in an eye clinic, but binocular disparity testing additionally requires placing polarized filters on the patient's face, presenting physical stereo plates at a controlled distance, coaching (often a child), and judging subjective/behavioral responses. RAOCT does none of these, so it does not substantiate completion of this task.

sources.title: Automated vision-testing kiosks face concerns amid national expansion
sources.claim: Automated vision testing that does exist in clinics and retail is delivered as self-service touchscreen kiosks and camera/sensor software rather than by a physically embodied robot, and covers refraction rather than a technologist-administered stereopsis test.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated administration of vision tests. Excluded as a robotic system under the stated definition (software running on hardware with cameras, sensors and screens, with no manipulation of the physical world), and its measured outputs are refractive, not stereoacuity elicited with polarized plates.

sources.system: EyeSwift (NovaSight) and PDI Check on autostereoscopic Nintendo 3DS
sources.title: Pediatric Non-Refractive Vision Screening with EyeSwift, PDI Check and Blinq
sources.claim: Automated/objective stereoacuity measurement is implemented as screen-based digital tests (eye-tracking displays and autostereoscopic handheld games), not by machines that handle test plates, filters, or the patient.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: measuring stereopsis in children. These are display-and-eye-tracking software systems, explicitly outside the definition of a robotic system, and correlation with clinical stereo tests was modest; no cited embodied machine sets up the patient, fits filters, or presents the physical stereo targets.

tasks.label: Assess abnormalities of color vision, such as amblyopia.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine adult screening in an ophthalmology exam lane: tech retrieves the Ishihara pseudoisochromatic plate book, seats the patient under standard daylight-balanced illumination at ~75 cm, has the untested eye occluded, flips plates on a ~3-second cadence, records the numbers read, scores and charts the result.

Pediatric/amblyopia or strabismus workup: a young, poorly cooperative child is tested with unlettered/shape plates or HRR; the child traces winding lines with a finger or brush, the tech holds or applies an occluder patch, coaxes attention, repeats plates, and judges partial or ambiguous responses.

Quantitative arrangement testing (Farnsworth D-15 or FM 100-hue) for suspected acquired defect or drug-toxicity monitoring: tech scrambles the caps on the tray, instructs the patient, times the arrangement, reads the cap order off the backs, re-scrambles for the second eye, and plots/scores the result.

Computerized color vision testing in the clinic (e.g., cone contrast test or tablet-based ColorDx): tech positions the calibrated display at the specified distance, verifies refractive correction, occludes the untested eye, runs practice trials, watches for guessing or head movement, then exports and charts results.

Screening away from the exam lane but inside an institution: occupational-health/pre-employment or school/DMV screening room, or a hospital bedside/wheelchair-bound patient; tech carries the plate book or vision screener to the patient, improvises positioning and lighting, tests each eye, and records results.

sources.system: Duke robotic OCT scanner (robotic arm + OCT head)
sources.developer: Duke University (Draelos, Izatt, Kuo et al.)
sources.title: Robotic scanner automates diagnostic imaging in the eye | EurekAlert!
sources.claim: Duke's robotic OCT system uses a robot arm with face and pupil tracking to autonomously align an imaging scanner to a patient's eyes and acquire clinical-quality scans without an operator, the closest demonstrated robotic capability in patient-facing ophthalmic assessment.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous ophthalmic imaging of a seated patient. It shows a robot can align hardware to a patient's eye, but color vision assessment is a subjective psychophysical test requiring presentation of graded plates or caps, verified monocular occlusion and correction, elicitation and judgment of patient responses, and scoring; none of that is demonstrated by this imaging system, so it does not transfer.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated in-store vision screening. It is the nearest deployed automation of technician-run vision testing, but its validated test set excludes color vision, so it cannot substantiate completion of this task.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: pediatric color vision testing. It is excluded as a robotic system under the stated definition (software running on a screen), so it cannot support a positive robotic judgment; cited to document that no robotic implementation exists.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-mediated eye examination. It shows that even the robotized parts of the eye exam are human-supervised and teleoperated with a technician handling the patient, so it cannot support autonomous completion of color vision testing.

tasks.label: Conduct low vision blindness tests.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Distance visual acuity on a low-vision patient in a clinic exam lane: technologist seats and aligns the patient, occludes one eye, presents a low-vision chart (ETDRS/Feinbloom/tumbling E), walks the chart in from 4 m to 1 m or 25 cm as needed, coaches an often elderly or hearing-impaired patient, scores letter-by-letter and records acuity with test distance.

Quantifying ultra-low vision when no chart letters are seen: counting fingers at measured distances, hand-motion presentation, and light perception/projection testing with a transilluminator shone from four quadrants in a darkened room, alternating occlusion and recording per-eye results.

Near/reading assessment and low-vision device trial: presenting near reading cards at a ruler-measured working distance, determining required add/magnification, then handing the patient hand and stand magnifiers, telescopes or a CCTV, adjusting focus and lighting, and recording reading acuity and performance with each aid.

Functional vision measures: contrast sensitivity with a Pelli-Robson or Mars chart at fixed distance under controlled illumination, plus glare/brightness acuity testing with a hand-held BAT held against the patient's orbit while acuity is re-read.

Visual field assessment supporting legal-blindness determination in the clinic's testing station: patching the fellow eye, seating the patient at an automated perimeter (or Goldmann bowl), aligning chin and forehead, instructing on the response button, monitoring fixation and reliability indices, and printing/recording the field.

Portable low-vision testing away from the standard lane: bedside in a hospital room, a nursing-home lounge, a school, or a home visit, using hand-held charts, a penlight and portable near cards in whatever lighting and seating the room offers.

sources.title: Contactless, autonomous robotic alignment of optical coherence tomography for in vivo evaluation of diseased retinas - PMC
sources.claim: A robot-aligned OCT system (Duke) autonomously aligns and focuses an imaging scanner on a seated patient's eye without an operator at the patient's side, but performs retinal imaging only — no psychophysical vision measurement, chart presentation, or patient coaching.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic ophthalmic imaging of a seated clinic patient. It shows a robot can safely approach and align to a human eye, but it measures optics, not the patient's subjective visual function, so it does not substantiate conducting low-vision acuity/field testing.

sources.system: Robotic eye examination system (NIH/National Robotics Initiative project)

sources.claim: An NIH-funded university robotic eye examination system automatically positions sensors to scan eyes; extending it to perform most steps of a standard eye exam is still an open research problem, with safety of close-proximity operation unresolved.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automating routine ophthalmic examination steps. It is the closest robotic effort to this task and is explicitly still under development, so it cannot substantiate completion of low-vision testing today.

sources.system: Humphrey Field Analyzer 3 (HFA3) with Liquid Trial Lens and Head Tracking
sources.title: The New Humphrey Field Analyzer 3 From ZEISS Sets a New Standard for Efficient Visual Field Testing | Business Wire

Once the patient is presented at the instrument the machine runs the threshold test and produces the recorded output.

sources.claim: The iCare COMPASS automated perimeter performs threshold visual field testing with auto-alignment and continuous infrared retinal tracking that repositions stimuli for eye movement, compensating for fixation loss without operator intervention during the test.

sources.title: Eyebot - Crunchbase Company Profile & Funding
sources.claim: Self-service automated vision kiosks measure visual acuity and refractive error for eyeglass prescriptions, but they are screen-based terminals aimed at prescription-eligible adults and do not perform low-vision protocols (variable-distance low-vision charts, counting fingers/hand motion/light perception, magnifier trials).
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated visual acuity/refraction measurement. It shows the automated end of acuity testing is a screen kiosk for near-normal vision, not a robotic system, and it does not cover the low-vision range that defines this task.

tasks.label: Perform advanced ophthalmic procedures, including electrophysiological, electrophysical, or microbial procedures.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Contact ophthalmic ultrasonography in a clinic exam lane: after instilling topical anesthetic, the technologist applanation- or immersion-A-scans an awake patient for axial length/biometry, and performs B-scan through the closed lid with coupling gel, orienting the probe in specific meridians, judging echo spikes/gain in real time and repeating until readings meet quality criteria.

Full-field electroretinography on a cooperative adult: dilate, dark-adapt, prep and apply lower-lid skin sensors or a DTL fiber/corneal contact-lens electrode plus reference and ground electrodes, verify impedances, seat the patient at the ganzfeld, run the ISCEV flash series while coaching fixation and blink control, reject artifacts and repeat runs.

Visual evoked potential, pattern ERG or EOG testing: abrade and prep scalp (Oz/Cz) and periocular sites, apply paste electrodes and check impedance, position the patient at the pattern-reversal display with correct refraction and fixation, monitor cooperation, average trials and re-run channels with poor signal.

Microbial specimen collection for suspected ocular infection: at the slit lamp, retract the lid, swab the conjunctival fornix/lid margin, or assist with corneal scrapings using a spatula/blade at the ulcer edge, then directly inoculate blood/chocolate/Sabouraud plates in C-streaks, inoculate broth, and spread smears onto glass slides for staining.

Lab-side processing of already-collected ocular specimens in the clinic/hospital microbiology bench: load swabs/liquid transport devices, inoculate and streak agar plates for isolation, inoculate broth, prepare and stain Gram/Giemsa slides, label and place plates in the incubator.

Advanced testing on difficult patients: handheld/skin-electrode ERG or flash VEP on infants and young children, or B-scan ultrasonography during an exam under anesthesia, where the patient cannot cooperate, the head must be steadied, and the technologist adapts positioning and timing to the patient's state.

sources.system: Copan WASP DT / WASPLab (Walk-Away Specimen Processor)
sources.title: Copan WASP DT: Walk-Away Specimen Processor | Beckman Coulter
sources.claim: Copan WASP DT is a commercially sold automated instrument that performs the bench microbiology steps a technologist would do with a collected specimen: plating and streaking agar, broth inoculation, and Gram slide preparation.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: clinical microbiology pre-analytic specimen processing. Transfer holds because the objects are identical to the ophthalmic technologist's lab-side work (swab in transport medium, agar plates, broth, glass slides) and the accepted output (isolated colonies, stained smear) is the same.

sources.title: Copan Walk Away Specimen Processor (WASP) Automated System for Pathogen Detection in Female Reproductive Tract Specimens
sources.claim: The Copan WASP automated processing system has been evaluated against manual methods on clinical patient swab specimens inside a hospital microbiology laboratory, i.e. it is in real laboratory use rather than a bench prototype.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated culture set-up from swab specimens in a clinical lab. Same consumables and streaking technique an ophthalmic technologist uses when plating ocular swabs; comparable precision demands (inoculum volume, quadrant streaking).

sources.system: Robotic OCT (robot-arm mounted OCT with 3D-camera pupil tracking); mobile robotic OCT cart
sources.developer: Duke University (Draelos, McNabb, Kuo, Izatt); University of Michigan Image-Guided Medical Robotics Lab

sources.claim: The most advanced autonomous robot-to-eye system demonstrated is a robotic-arm OCT scanner that aligns to and images a free-standing person's cornea and retina without an operator; it is non-contact optical imaging only and does not touch the eye, place electrodes, or apply an ultrasound probe.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automated ophthalmic imaging in a clinic. Cited to bound the frontier: it establishes autonomous alignment to a human eye, but not contact with the globe or lid (ultrasound probe, DTL/contact-lens electrode, swab), so it does not substantiate the contact procedures in this task.

sources.developer: Technical University of Munich / Lifeline Robotics collaborators (Haddadin et al.)
sources.title: Autonomous swab robot for naso- and oropharyngeal COVID-19 screening | Scientific Reports
sources.claim: An autonomous force-controlled robot has taken naso- and oropharyngeal swab samples from patients in two clinical studies, showing robots can collect mucosal specimens from a person, but only from the mouth/nose, without eyelid manipulation or work near the cornea.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous specimen collection from a patient's mucosa. Cited to test transfer to conjunctival swabs/corneal scraping; transfer fails because the eye requires lid retraction, sub-millimetre targeting at an ulcer edge under slit-lamp magnification, and corneal-abrasion risk far beyond the throat's tolerance.

tasks.label: Perform slit lamp biomicroscopy procedures to diagnose disorders of the eye, such as retinitis, presbyopia, cataracts, or retinal detachment.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine anterior-segment slit lamp examination of a cooperative adult in an ophthalmology clinic exam lane: patient seated at the table-mounted slit lamp with chin/forehead rest, technologist varies beam width, angle, filters and magnification to survey lids, lashes, conjunctiva, cornea, anterior chamber, iris and crystalline lens (e.g., cataract grading, pterygium, post-op check), and documents findings for the physician.

Slit lamp evaluation requiring instillation of dye/drops: technologist instills fluorescein (and often topical anesthetic), then examines under cobalt blue with a barrier filter for corneal staining, tear break-up time, abrasion/foreign body, Seidel test, or contact-lens fit assessment; the timing-sensitive dynamic observation is part of the procedure.

Slit lamp biomicroscopy of the posterior segment or angle using an auxiliary lens on a dilated patient: technologist holds a 78D/90D non-contact condensing lens a few millimetres from the cornea (or applies a Goldmann three-mirror/gonio contact lens with coupling gel) while coordinating slit beam and joystick to sweep disc, macula and peripheral retina for retinal detachment, tears or retinitis.

Slit lamp photography/imaging documentation in an ophthalmology practice or eye hospital: capturing high-resolution stills and video of anterior-segment findings (corneal ulcer, lens opacity, lid lesion, post-op wound) under prescribed illumination/magnification protocols for the chart, referral or asynchronous physician review.

Slit lamp examination of a patient who cannot be positioned normally: young child, patient with dementia or tremor, wheelchair user who cannot reach the chin rest, or an inpatient/ED consult examined at the bedside with a portable or hand-held slit lamp; requires coaxing, manual head/lid holding and improvised positioning.

sources.title: Aetheia | Auto-Optometry | Tele-Optometry | UK
sources.claim: Aetheia:Auto can initiate and complete slit lamp exams entirely through its automation engine, capturing 4K images/video and handling patient positioning prompts and device fine tuning, deployed from optical retail to decentralised care networks.

sources.title: SpaMedica's Nationwide Rollout of Aetheia:Auto - EYOTO
sources.claim: Aetheia:Auto was piloted in 100 SpaMedica clinics with more than 2,000 patients and then rolled out across SpaMedica's entire UK hospital network in December 2025 — real clinical deployment of automated slit lamp examination in eye hospitals.

sources.claim: A robot-mounted OCT scanner autonomously finds and tracks the eye of freestanding human subjects using face and pupil cameras and acquires clinical-quality ocular volumes without operator intervention or head ....
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous ophthalmic imaging (OCT rather than slit lamp). Transfer is limited to the alignment problem — locating and tracking a live human eye at millimetre precision in a clinic exam room — which is the same sensing/positioning problem an automated slit lamp must solve; it does not substantiate dye handling, auxiliary-lens work, or uncooperative patients.

tasks.label: Create three-dimensional images of the eye, using computed tomography (CT).

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine volumetric (3D) macular/optic-nerve OCT on a cooperative ambulatory adult in an ophthalmology clinic imaging lane: greet and seat the patient, set chin/forehead rest, instruct on fixation and blinking, align and capture both eyes, check scan quality/signal strength, repeat if artifacted, label and export volumes to the EHR before the physician's exam.

3D OCT on a cooperative but hard-to-position patient who cannot use a standard chin rest: wheelchair-bound, kyphotic, obese, or an inpatient/post-op patient imaged reclined or bedside with a portable unit; the technologist brings the instrument to the patient and works around posture and reach limits.

3D OCT on a poorly cooperative patient: young child, dementia or tremor, very low vision with no steady fixation, ptotic lids or small pupil. Technologist coaxes and steadies the head, physically holds the lid open, re-instructs repeatedly, and salvages a readable volume from many attempts.

Anterior-segment 3D tomography for cataract/refractive/glaucoma work-up: AS-OCT or Scheimpflug corneal tomography of cornea, angle and lens; patient positioned, several captures taken, quality/centration verified, maps generated for surgical planning.

Follow-up/advanced 3D series on a returning retina patient: widefield or montaged OCT plus OCT-angiography, registered to the prior visit's scan location, multiple repeat acquisitions for motion-free volumes, quality review and export/comparison reporting.

Orbital/ocular CT study in a hospital or imaging suite (trauma, mass, thyroid eye disease): escort and transfer the patient onto the CT table, position and immobilize the head, confirm safety/contrast screening, run the scan and produce the 3D orbital reconstructions for the ophthalmologist.

sources.developer: Duke University (Draelos, Ortiz, McNabb, Kuo, Izatt)
sources.title: Contactless optical coherence tomography of the eyes of freestanding individuals with a robotic scanner (Nature Biomedical Engineering)
sources.claim: Robot-mounted OCT scanner autonomously aligns to and images the eyes of freestanding people without an operator or chin rest, producing volumetric (3D) retinal and anterior-segment datasets comparable in quality to clinical tabletop OCT.

sources.claim: Autonomous robotic alignment acquired OCT and OCT-angiography volumes in healthy and diseased eyes of 17 seated patients at Duke Eye Center with no chin/forehead rest, with the human imager 10.8 km away giving instructions and checking image quality.

roles.title: Athletic Trainers
roles.description: Evaluate and treat musculoskeletal injuries or illnesses. Provide preventive, therapeutic, emergency, and rehabilitative care.

tasks.label: Conduct an initial assessment of an athlete's injury or illness to provide emergency or continued care and to determine whether they should be referred to physicians for definitive diagnosis and treatment.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: On-field/sideline acute musculoskeletal injury during a practice or game (football field, basketball court, wrestling mat): athlete goes down, the trainer runs out, checks responsiveness and mechanism, palpates the joint, runs special tests (Lachman, anterior drawer, talar tilt), checks neurovascular status, decides remove-from-play vs. return, applies ice/wrap/crutches, and decides on physician referral — all in minutes with crowd noise, teammates, coaches and weather.

Athletic training room evaluation of a reported injury (post-practice or next-day walk-in): history-taking, observation of gait/swelling, palpation of bony landmarks and soft tissue, goniometric ROM, manual muscle testing, joint-specific special tests, comparison to uninvolved side, treatment plan and referral/imaging decision, documented in the EHR.

Suspected head injury/concussion: sideline screening for red flags and cervical spine involvement, symptom checklist, cognitive screen, cranial nerve and ocular-motor testing, tandem/balance testing, serial re-checks in a quiet room, removal from play and referral decision.

General medical/illness complaint in the training room or clinic: fever, sore throat, skin lesion (MRSA/tinea), abdominal pain, asthma exacerbation, dehydration — vital signs, temperature, auscultation/otoscopy or visual inspection, symptom history, decision to hold from participation and refer to team physician.

True emergency on the field or in the venue: exertional heat stroke, cardiac arrest, obvious fracture/dislocation, spine injury, severe bleeding, anaphylaxis — rapid primary survey, airway/breathing/circulation, CPR/AED, rectal temperature and cold-water immersion, splinting/spine motion restriction, EAP activation and EMS handoff.

Off-site/travel setting with no facility: cross-country course, road race, away-game visiting sideline, ski hill, parking lot or team bus — assessment performed on grass, gravel or a bus seat with only a kit bag, variable lighting and weather, no controlled premises.

sources.system: FARUS fully autonomous robotic ultrasound system (thyroid scanning)
sources.developer: Su, Liu, Ren et al. (academic consortium, China)
sources.title: A fully autonomous robotic ultrasound system for thyroid scanning | Nature Communications
sources.claim: The most advanced autonomous robot-patient physical contact for diagnosis is autonomous robotic ultrasound: a fully autonomous thyroid scanning system positioned a probe on volunteers' necks with force control and acquired diagnostic images, but it performs one imaging protocol on a stationary, cooperative, supine subject rather than a hands-on musculoskeletal examination or a care/referral decision.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous diagnostic imaging with a robot arm contacting a human body. It is the closest demonstrated autonomous robot-on-patient examination, so it bounds what is possible; it does not transfer to injury assessment because it involves no history-taking, palpation, ligament stress testing, emergency care, or referral judgment, and requires a cooperative subject positioned in a laboratory rig.

sources.title: AI-Powered Massages? Automated Massage Robots Already at Work — Associated Bodywork & Massage Professionals
sources.claim: Commercially deployed autonomous hands-on human body contact exists in fitness/wellness settings: Aescape's robotic table autonomously scans a client's body and delivers targeted massage strokes in Equinox gyms, but it only applies pre-planned soft-tissue pressure to a prone client on its own fixture and performs no injury evaluation, testing, or clinical decision.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous force-controlled contact with a human body in a structured facility (gym spa room). It shows safe robot-human contact is commercially viable, but not assessment: the machine works on a fixtured, still, uninjured client and produces no diagnostic finding, emergency care, or referral decision.

sources.title: The Reliability of the GNRB® Knee Arthrometer in Measuring ACL Stiffness and Laxity — International Journal of Sports Physical Therapy
sources.claim: Instrumented/automated ligament testing exists as a bench device: the GNRB knee arthrometer motorizes anterior tibial translation to quantify ACL laxity, but a clinician must position and strap the limb and it measures a single parameter of one joint — it is a sub-step of, not a substitute for, the athletic trainer's injury evaluation.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: instrumented ligament stress testing, the mechanical core of one special test used in knee injury assessment. It does not transfer to the whole task: a human must set up and align the patient, and the device yields a number rather than an assessment, care plan, or referral decision.

sources.developer: Journal of Robotic Surgery review authors
sources.title: Technical challenges in autonomous robotic ultrasound examinations: perception, planning, and control | Journal of Robotic Surgery
sources.claim: Autonomous robotic examination of patients remains a research field as of 2026, with open problems in perception, planning and control; no fielded autonomous system performs a general clinical physical examination.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous robotic examination of patients generally. Cited only as a negative bound — the state of the art in autonomous robot-on-patient examination is still a research literature focused on imaging, with no system performing hands-on injury assessment.

tasks.label: Assess and report the progress of recovering athletes to coaches or physicians.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Athletic training room, mid-rehab check on an injured athlete (e.g., 6 weeks post ankle sprain or ACL reconstruction): hands-on re-assessment — goniometric ROM, manual muscle testing, palpation for effusion/tenderness, special/ligament tests, watching the athlete perform rehab exercises — then a verbal progress update to the sport coach and a note for the team physician.

Functional progression testing on the practice field, court, or weight room: the trainer runs the athlete through jogging, cutting, hop/agility tests and sport-specific drills, judges movement quality, compensation, pain response and confidence, and reports where the athlete stands on the return-to-play progression to the coach.

Quick status check and verbal update during a practice or game: brief check of the recovering athlete on the sideline (pain report, quick ROM/strength spot-check, tape/brace check) amid ongoing play, followed by an immediate verbal report to the coach on availability and limits.

Office/EMR work: compiling accumulated objective and subjective findings into a formal written progress report or SOAP documentation, and communicating it to the team physician (electronic note, phone call, or accompanying the athlete to a physician follow-up clinic visit).

Instrumented objective testing session in a sports medicine clinic or testing lab (isokinetic dynamometer strength/limb-symmetry test, knee arthrometer laxity test, force-plate hop testing) run at milestone points, with the quantitative comparison to prior sessions delivered to the physician to support clearance decisions.

sources.title: DYNEELAX Robotic Arthrometer Reliability and Feasibility on Healthy and Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injured/Reconstructed Persons
sources.claim: The DYNEELAX robotic/motorized arthrometer automatically applies anterior-posterior translation and axial rotation loads to a knee strapped into the device and records objective laxity metrics with high intrarater reliability, and such laximetry devices are used to compare a patient's knees at different time points during recovery.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: instrumented follow-up measurement of knee ligament laxity. It transfers only to the instrumented-testing instance of this task, where the recovering athlete's limb is fixtured in the device and the machine produces the serial objective measure reported to the physician.

sources.title: Western University thesis (knee laxity arthrometry), figure caption
sources.claim: The GNRB knee arthrometer is a fully automated device that fixes the limb, applies a controlled anterior force and measures resulting tibial translation with a displacement sensor, i.e., a motorized measurement of a joint without a clinician performing the manual test.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: objective joint-stability measurement. Comparable object (an athlete's knee) and precision (0.1 mm displacement) to the instrumented progress test an athletic trainer orders; the workpiece must be strapped into the purpose-built device.

sources.title: Talking Tech: RTP with Biodex System 4
sources.claim: The Biodex System 4 isokinetic dynamometer is marketed and used to assess limb strength symmetry and hamstring-to-quadriceps ratios as objective return-to-play criteria for recovering athletes, with the athlete strapped into the motorized chair.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: objective strength testing at rehabilitation milestones. It substantiates only the fixtured, instrumented portion of progress assessment; the device supplies numbers a clinician interprets, and the athlete must be positioned and strapped by a human.

tasks.label: Care for athletic injuries, using physical therapy equipment, techniques, or medication.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Cryotherapy/thermotherapy/compression in the athletic training room: fill and mold an ice bag or ice cup over a swollen ankle/knee, secure it with plastic and elastic wrap or a compression sleeve, or apply a moist heat pack with towel layers; monitor skin for 15-20 minutes and remove.

Instrument modality session on a treatment table: set up and deliver a dosed treatment to a localized injury (therapeutic ultrasound sweep with gel, electrode placement for e-stim/TENS, or class IV laser) to the athlete's knee, shoulder, hamstring or low back; set parameters, run 8-20 minutes, check response.

Hands-on soft-tissue work in the training room: massage/myofascial release of a tight or strained back, hamstring, calf, quad or shoulder for a post-practice athlete lying on a treatment table, with pressure adjusted to tolerance.

Rehabilitation session for an injured athlete (e.g., post-ACL, ankle sprain, rotator cuff): guide a multi-exercise program of ROM, band/weight strengthening, balance and proprioception drills and sport-specific progressions, plus manual stretching, PNF, joint mobilization and manual resistance; cue form, spot, and progress the load.

Acute injury care on the field, court or sideline during practice or competition: respond to a downed athlete, apply ice and compression wrap, splint a suspected fracture, control bleeding, apply a sling, and help the athlete off the playing surface amid other players, coaches, weather and crowd.

Wound care and medication in the training room: clean and dress turf burns, abrasions and blisters, apply antiseptic/topical analgesic and adherent dressings, and administer or dispense single-dose OTC medication under the team physician's protocol.

sources.title: Equinox, Aescape Launch Pre and Post-Workout Massages - Athletech News
sources.claim: Aescape's autonomous robotic massage tables are commercially deployed in more than 50 Equinox fitness clubs delivering coach-designed pre-workout and recovery massage sessions to members, i.e., soft-tissue recovery work on athletes in an institution-run facility.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: recovery/soft-tissue massage of the same body regions (back, legs, shoulders) an athletic trainer treats for muscle soreness and strain, on a treatment table, with pressure titrated to the client.

sources.title: AI-Powered Massages? Automated Massage Robots Already at Work | Associated Bodywork & Massage Professionals
sources.claim: The Aescape system scans each body and delivers targeted bodywork fully automatically through two robotic arms mounted on its table, without a human therapist operating it.
sources.transferJustification: Same as above: establishes that the soft-tissue treatment itself is machine-controlled and adapts to each body, not teleoperated.

sources.developer: ASA Laser (clinic deployment: Arthritis & Sports Orthopaedics/PT)
sources.title: What Is MLS (Multiwave Locked System) Laser Therapy? | Arthritis & Sports
sources.claim: In sports-medicine and orthopaedic clinics the robotic MLS laser head guides the beam over the skin and completes the multi-pass treatment itself while the patient stays still and positioned.
sources.transferJustification: Same task in a sports-medicine setting: an energy modality applied over an injured area for a timed dose, equivalent to a trainer's ultrasound/laser modality treatment, once the patient is positioned under the head.

tasks.label: Evaluate athletes' readiness to play and provide participation clearances when necessary and warranted.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Game-day sideline evaluation of an acute injury (ankle/knee sprain, shoulder, hamstring) at a high school or college contest: the AT goes onto the field, palpates, performs manual special tests (Lachman, anterior drawer, talar tilt) and manual muscle testing, runs a quick functional sideline test (jog, cut, hop), and decides on the spot whether to clear the athlete back into the game. Noise, crowd, weather, time pressure, uncooperative/emotional athlete.

Daily reassessment of rehabbing athletes in the athletic training room before practice: symptom interview, goniometric ROM, manual strength grading, palpation for tenderness/swelling, joint stability tests, then setting participation status (full, limited, non-contact, held out) and communicating it to the coach.

Concussion/head-injury evaluation and graduated return-to-play clearance: sideline SCAT-style symptom and cognitive screen, cranial nerve and balance (BESS) testing, serial daily symptom checks and exertion-stage progression over days, culminating in clearance in coordination with the team physician.

Criterion-based return-to-sport testing battery in a sports medicine clinic or athletic performance lab (post-ACL or other major injury): isokinetic/handheld dynamometry, hop-test battery, force-plate jump symmetry, sport-specific agility drills, plus psychological readiness questionnaire; AT scores the battery, interprets limb symmetry indices, and recommends clearance to the physician.

Pre-participation screening/clearance day: mass pre-participation physical exam stations in a school gym — history review, vitals, vision, orthopedic screening exam, review of prior injury records — with the AT flagging athletes for physician review and issuing/withholding participation clearance paperwork.

sources.developer: research group, deployed at Beijing Tsinghua Changgung Hospital
sources.title: Beyond hospital reach: Autonomous lightweight ultrasound robot for liver sonography
sources.claim: Autonomous robotic ultrasound systems can acquire diagnostic images on human subjects in a hospital department with force-controlled probe contact; this is the closest existing autonomous robot–on–human physical assessment, but it produces images only, not a musculoskeletal clinical exam or a participation clearance decision.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous robotic contact-based examination of a human body in a clinical facility. It bears on this task only as an upper bound on robot–patient physical assessment; it does not include history taking, manual strength/laxity testing, functional testing, or the clearance judgment that define readiness-to-play evaluation.

sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous robot-applied probe contact on a human in a controlled clinical room. Cited to show the frontier of autonomous robot–human physical examination; it does not transfer to manual orthopedic special testing or return-to-play clearance.
