tasks.label: Assign firefighters to jobs at strategic locations to facilitate rescue of persons and maximize application of extinguishing agents.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Company officer or first-arriving battalion chief at a residential/commercial structure fire: sizes up the building, then assigns arriving engine and truck companies to tasks and positions by radio and face-to-face order (e.g., Engine 2 take a line to the second floor, Truck 1 primary search on Division 2, RIT staged side Alpha), adjusting assignments as conditions and reports change.

Routine, smaller incidents (vehicle fires, dumpster/brush fires, alarm activations, automatic-aid single-unit responses): supervisor verbally assigns a handful of firefighters to hoseline, water supply, overhaul, and traffic/scene-safety positions, usually a short standard set of assignments.

Rescue-driven incidents (vehicle extrication, water/ice rescue, confined space, structural collapse, victim rescue at a fire): supervisor allocates crews to patient access, stabilization, cutting/lifting, and backup safety positions while coordinating with EMS on the scene.

Large or expanding incidents run under formal ICS (multi-alarm fire, wildland/WUI fire, hazmat, mass-casualty): division/group supervisor or IC assigns strike teams, task forces, and crews to divisions, geographic branches, and functions from a command post or incident action plan, tracking accountability and rotating crews.

Non-emergency assignment of personnel to positions during drills, live-fire training evolutions, pre-incident planning walkthroughs, and standby/event details (parades, sporting events, fireworks), where the supervisor designates who covers which position or sector.

Station-level, pre-incident riding-position and staffing assignments made at shift change or during move-ups: supervisor designates nozzle, backup, irons, driver/operator, and apparatus/coverage assignments so crews arrive at scenes with strategic roles already set.

tasks.label: Communicate fire details to superiors, subordinates, or interagency dispatch centers, using two-way radios.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

tasks.label: Serve as a working leader of an engine, hand, helicopter, or prescribed fire crew of three or more firefighters.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Wildland engine boss (ENGB) on initial/extended attack: drives and positions a Type 3/6 engine on a two-track or roadside anchor point, sizes up fire behavior, assigns and works alongside 3-4 crew members on progressive hose lays, pump-and-roll, and mop-up in brush and slope, with radio traffic to division/IC and changing weather and fire behavior.

Hand crew squad boss / crew boss on a 20-person Type 1 or Type 2 crew: leads a squad of 3-8 sawyers, swampers and diggers building direct or indirect handline in steep timber or chaparral, sets tool order and spacing, falls hazard trees or bumps line himself, enforces LCES and watch-out situations, in smoke, heat and darkness.

Prescribed fire crew leader / firing boss on a planned burn unit: briefs the crew, checks spot weather against the burn plan, leads 3+ ignitors with drip torches along a strip-head or ring pattern, coordinates holding forces and mop-up of the perimeter, adjusts firing rate to observed fire behavior and smoke.

Helitack / helicopter crew leader: manages a crew of 3+ at a helibase or remote helispot, rigs cargo nets and longlines, supervises hooking loads and helicopter bucket dips, cuts and improves helispots, briefs passengers, works alongside the crew while maintaining aviation safety accountability.

Municipal engine company officer working as a leader of 3 firefighters at a structure fire or other emergency: rides the seat, gives the size-up, then stretches and advances an attack line with the crew, directs forcible entry, primary search and ventilation inside a private dwelling or commercial occupancy, tracks crew accountability and air supply.

Non-emergency crew leadership at the station or training ground: leads 3+ firefighters through apparatus and pump checks, hose testing, ladder and SCBA drills, physical training and station/project work at an institution-controlled fire station, training tower or district yard.

sources.title: LAFD Debuts the RS3: First Robotic Firefighting Vehicle in the United States
sources.claim: The only robotic firefighting vehicle in US municipal service, the Thermite RS3 operated by LAFD since 2020, is a remote-controlled water-delivery platform; it neither works autonomously nor supervises firefighters.
sources.transferJustification: Closest fielded system to structural/industrial fireground work by a crew leader; cited to show the state of the art is a teleoperated nozzle platform, not an autonomous working crew leader.

sources.title: Paris Firefighters Used This Remote-Controlled Robot to Extinguish the Notre Dame Blaze
sources.claim: Colossus, the best-known fireground ground robot in service with the Paris Fire Brigade, is remote-controlled and functions as a tool directed by firefighters rather than as an autonomous crew member or leader.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: interior/structural fire attack. Cited to establish that fielded fireground robots operate under continuous human control and cannot substitute for a working company officer.

sources.system: Wildfire Mission Autonomy System on Sikorsky autonomous Black Hawk (MATRIX)
sources.title: Rain and Sikorsky Test Advanced Aerial Firefighting Technologies Using Autonomous Black Hawk Helicopter
sources.claim: Autonomy in wildfire suppression has been demonstrated only for aerial water delivery by an optionally piloted helicopter in flight tests, not for ground crew leadership or hand/engine crew work.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: wildfire initial attack suppression. Cited because it is the most advanced autonomous wildfire system, yet it performs only aerial water drops and does not lead or supervise a ground crew.

sources.title: Igniting the future: Technology on prescribed fire | US Forest Service
sources.claim: In operational prescribed fire, drone aerial ignition is flown by a remote pilot and the crew is still led by human firing and holding bosses, with a 30-person crew on the ground.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: prescribed fire ignition. Cited to show that even where robotic tools are routine in prescribed burning, the working leader roles (firing boss, holding boss) remain human and the aircraft is remotely piloted.

tasks.label: Evaluate size, location, and condition of fires.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: First-due company officer at a single-family dwelling fire performs the initial exterior size-up: walks the 360 lap of the house, reads smoke volume/color/velocity and visible flame, judges which floor/room is involved, how far it has spread and what stage it is in, then transmits the initial radio size-up. Night, weather, bystanders, parked cars, fenced yards.

Continuing size-up from inside the burning structure: officer advancing with the crew in heavy smoke and heat uses a handheld thermal imager and hand/foot cues to find the seat of the fire, check ceilings, walls and voids for hidden extension, and judge whether conditions are improving or deteriorating (flashover/collapse risk).

Larger commercial, industrial or multi-family building fire: incident commander sustains an evaluation over 20-90 minutes from a command post plus division reports - where the fire is inside a large compartmented building, how much of it is involved, whether it is extending to exposures, and whether conditions justify going defensive.

Small, directly visible fire in the open: vehicle fire on a roadway, dumpster or trash fire, small outbuilding or fence fire, or a quarter-acre grass fire on a lot. Officer sizes up extent, exact location, what is burning and whether it is spreading to exposures, usually within a minute of arrival.

Wildland/vegetation fire initial size-up: officer or battalion chief arriving at a brush or grass fire estimates acreage, precise location and access, fuel type, terrain, wind-driven spread direction and rate, and threatened structures, reporting conditions to dispatch/IC.

sources.system: Unifire FlameRanger (IR array flame detectors + Force robotic nozzle, TARGA PLC)
sources.title: Automatic Fire Fighting System Detects & Extinguishes Fires in Seconds
sources.claim: Unifire's FlameRanger is a commercially sold robotic fire monitor system whose paired IR array detectors autonomously detect a fire and triangulate and continuously track its three-dimensional size and location, driving the nozzle until the fire is out; installed in waste/recycling plants, warehouses and hangars.
sources.transferJustification: Same task content: the system's detectors and software perform the evaluation of a fire's size, location and burning status (and track its condition until extinguishment); it is embedded in a suppression product rather than reported verbally.

sources.title: Automated Waste and Recycling Fire Fighting Technology - Asia Pacific Fire
sources.claim: The same FlameRanger system is distributed and installed in waste and recycling facilities, where it operates completely autonomously around the clock, reporting the presence of a fire with its size and location data and handling up to four simultaneous fires.
sources.transferJustification: Same task content (determining a fire's size and location); establishes that the autonomous evaluation runs in real human work facilities, not only in test rigs.

sources.title: Dryad Networks Unveils Silvaguard Drone Prototype for Detecting, Locating and Monitoring Wildfires
sources.claim: Dryad's Silvaguard drone, dispatched automatically by the Silvanet sensor network, flew itself to a controlled forest fire and pinpointed the fire's location and size from the air in a March 2025 demonstration in a managed forest in Eberswalde, Germany.

sources.system: Sikorsky MATRIX autonomy + Rain wildfire mission autonomy on an optionally piloted Black Hawk
sources.title: Rain and Sikorsky Test Advanced Aerial Firefighting Technologies Using Autonomous Black Hawk Helicopter
sources.claim: In April 2025 live-fire tests near Hesperia, California, an optionally piloted Black Hawk running Sikorsky MATRIX plus Rain's wildfire mission autonomy autonomously found and tracked burning brush piles, generated a suppression plan and executed water drops.
sources.transferJustification: Related task (autonomous initial-attack water drops); the cited autonomy performs the evaluation step - finding, localizing and tracking the fire - on outdoor vegetation fires, the same judgment a wildland size-up requires.

sources.system: Skydio X10 / Skydio Dock DFR for fire service
sources.developer: Skydio (with Oklahoma City Fire Department and others)
sources.title: Skydio autonomous drone programs for fire departments
sources.claim: Drone-as-first-responder programs put autonomously launching drones over structure fires ahead of the engines, but the drone streams EO/thermal video while human officers and chiefs perform the 360 assessment and make the tactical judgment.
sources.transferJustification: Cited to show what is actually fielded at real firegrounds: autonomous flight plus human evaluation, i.e. the machine does not itself produce the size-up.

sources.title: Future of Firefighting Robots | WFCA
sources.claim: Mobile firefighting robots fielded by fire departments (e.g., Thermite RS3 at LAFD, Shark Robotics Colossus) still depend on human operators for navigation and decision-making in unpredictable fire environments.
sources.transferJustification: Cited only to support negative judgments about autonomous fireground reconnaissance.

tasks.label: Instruct and drill fire department personnel in assigned duties, including firefighting, medical care, hazardous materials response, fire prevention, and related subjects.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Station-based company drill / classroom session: the captain or battalion chief delivers a required monthly training topic (SOP review, building construction, fire behavior, prevention/code topics) to a crew of 3-8 in the station classroom or day room, using slides, props and discussion, answers questions, and documents attendance and competencies in the training records system.

Hands-on firefighting skills drill on the apparatus floor or station lot: officer sets up the evolution (hose loads, ladders, forcible-entry door prop, SCBA), physically demonstrates the technique, then coaches, times and corrects each firefighter's hands-on repetitions (hoseline advance, ladder throw, SCBA emergency procedures, tool operation) in full PPE, and critiques the crew afterward.

EMS/medical skills drill: officer runs a patient-care competency session in the station or training room using manikins and airway/CPR/IV trainers, demonstrates the skill, plays or scripts the scenario, watches each member's hands-on performance, physically corrects hand placement and technique, and signs off skill sheets.

Training-ground evolution at the department or regional academy: officer acts as instructor-in-charge or safety officer for a live-fire burn-tower evolution, hazmat prop (leaking drums, chlorine A-kit), or vehicle extrication/rope prop; sets and inspects props, controls ignition/fuel, works in PPE and SCBA inside heat, smoke and zero visibility with the crews, intervenes physically for safety, and leads the after-action critique per NFPA 1403.

Off-site drill in the community: multi-company evolution in an acquired vacant structure, target-hazard walkthrough/pre-incident drill at a business or apartment complex, or extrication and water-supply drill in a parking lot or on a public street, where layout, access, hazards and weather are taken as found and civilians/traffic may be present.

sources.title: TeachBot: Towards teaching robotics fundamentals for human-robot collaboration at work
sources.claim: TeachBot is an autonomous robotic ... (a Sawyer-type arm with screen and voice) that delivers interactive lecture modules and physical demonstrations to teach manufacturing workers robotics fundamentals; it is a research prototype evaluated in a study, teaching a single technical topic to one learner at a time.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-delivered workforce instruction. It is the closest robotic analogue to 'instruct personnel', but transfer fails: it teaches one scripted robotics topic in a lab/production-line cell, does not observe or grade a crew's psychomotor performance, cannot set up or supervise firefighting, hazmat or EMS evolutions, and cannot provide safety oversight of trainees, so it cannot complete any instance of this task.

sources.title: Secret Service uses robotic targets to improve live-fire training realism
sources.claim: Marathon autonomous robotic targets navigate a live-fire range on their own and react to hits, and are used in large numbers of law-enforcement and USMC training events; they serve as training aids within a human instructor's drill rather than instructing or evaluating trainees.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous robots supporting live-fire tactical training on an institution-controlled range. Transfer fails because the robots supply a moving target stimulus only; a human instructor still designs the drill, demonstrates technique, corrects trainees and documents competency, which is the substance of this task.

sources.system: Computer-controlled Class B burn simulator / Dräger Interior Live Fire Training System
sources.developer: Westchester County Fire Training Center / Dräger
sources.title: Fire Training Props - Westchester County Emergency Services
sources.claim: Fire-service live-fire training buildings use computer-controlled propane burners and theatrical smoke to generate drill conditions, but the props are configured and operated by human instructors (including wireless handheld remotes) and do not teach, assess or supervise trainees.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: machine-generated live-fire drill conditions on a training ground. It shows the scenario hardware is automatable, but the prop is instructor-controlled and performs none of the instruction, demonstration, performance evaluation or safety supervision the task requires.

sources.title: HAL® S5301 | Gaumard
sources.claim: High-fidelity patient simulators such as Gaumard HAL breathe, speak and answer assessment questions using AI, providing a physically actuated simulated patient for EMS scenario training; the scenario is still authored, run and debriefed by a human instructor.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic manikin used in medical-care drills. Transfer fails because the simulator is the training object, not the trainer: it does not demonstrate skills to the crew, judge hand placement or compression technique, correct trainees, or sign off competency.

tasks.label: Assess nature and extent of fire, condition of building, danger to adjacent buildings, and water supply status to determine crew or company requirements.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Single-family residential structure fire: first-arriving company officer performs an on-arrival size-up (reads smoke and fire conditions, building construction/occupancy, life hazard, exposure distance to neighboring homes, confirms hydrant location and water supply), then transmits an initial radio report and states whether additional companies or alarms are needed.

Commercial, industrial, or multi-family building fire: officer/battalion chief sizes up a larger occupancy (fire location and extent within the building, sprinkler/standpipe and FDC status, roof and truss construction concerns, collapse potential, adjoining attached exposures, hydrant flow adequacy) and determines how many engine, truck, and rescue companies plus special resources to request.

Minor incident: vehicle fire, dumpster or trash fire, grass strip, smoke odor, or automatic alarm. Officer makes a rapid assessment on arrival and determines that the assigned crew is sufficient, often releasing or downgrading other responding units.

Wildland, brush, or wildland-urban-interface fire: officer assesses fuel type, fire behavior and rate of spread, wind and topography, structures threatened, access, and non-hydrant water supply (tenders, drafting sites), then orders additional engines, tenders, dozers, or air support.

Continuing size-up as incident commander at a working fire: repeated re-assessment of changing fire and building conditions (extension, structural degradation, exposure ignition, tank/hydrant supply status) to decide offensive/defensive strategy and to call for or release additional alarms and companies.

tasks.label: Perform maintenance and minor repairs on firefighting equipment, including vehicles, and write and submit proposals to modify, replace, and repair equipment.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Start-of-shift / weekly apparatus check and servicing in the fire station apparatus bay: walk-around of engine or truck, open hood and check engine oil, coolant, DEF, foam and hydraulic fluid levels and top off; check tires, batteries, shoreline, warning lights, siren, air brakes; engage and test the pump and onboard generator; verify compartment inventory; correct small deficiencies and log findings.

Minor repairs and parts replacement at the station workbench or bay: diagnose and fix a leaking hose coupling or nozzle (replace gaskets/O-rings/swivels), replace broken latches, brackets, bulbs, radio and flashlight batteries; inspect, clean and change SCBA facepiece and regulator parts; inspect, clean and lubricate ground ladders and hardware.

Small-engine and power-tool maintenance in the station: chainsaws, rotary rescue saws, positive-pressure fans, portable pumps, generators and hydraulic extrication tools — fuel/oil mixing, spark plug and filter changes, chain sharpening or replacement, blade changes, belt and fluid checks, weekly test-run under load.

Fire hose care after an incident or on the annual schedule: pull dirty/wet hose off the apparatus, wash and decontaminate it, pressure-test it to NFPA 1962, detect and mark leaks, dry it, roll or coil it and record results before returning it to service.

Documenting a deficiency and writing/submitting a proposal, work order or budget justification at the station office computer to modify, replace or repair equipment — gathering specs and quotes, writing the justification memo, and routing it to the fleet shop or chief.

Field servicing and minor repair away from the station: at an incident scene, on the roadside, or at a wildland base camp — swapping a burst hose section, changing a saw chain or blade, clearing a clogged nozzle, replenishing fuel and fluids, securing a loose fitting, under time pressure and in whatever conditions are found.

sources.title: Product Showcase 2025 — Firehouse
sources.claim: Hosemaster is a commercially sold, fully automatic fire-hose care unit built for fire stations that washes, pressure-tests, detects and marks leaks, dries and coils hose automatically in one cycle, with an NFPA 1962-compliant testing module for US departments.

sources.title: Hose Master – Revolutionizing the maintenance of fire hoses — Gulf Fire
sources.claim: The Hosemaster cycle begins with the hose loaded into a dedicated carriage that is inserted into the machine ... coupled to it — i.e. the workpiece is fixtured and presented to the machine, which then runs the wash/test/dry/coil program itself.

sources.title: IFS and Boston Dynamics Collaboration Combines the Power of Robotics with Agentic AI to Transform Field Operations
sources.claim: Boston Dynamics Spot performs autonomous inspection rounds inside industrial facilities, reading analog gauges, checking indicator lights, thermal-imaging for overheating and listening for leaks, but it produces inspection data rather than performing servicing or repair.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: routine equipment condition rounds in a facility. It substantiates only sensing-and-reporting; the fire-apparatus check additionally requires opening hoods and compartments, dipstick checks, fluid top-off and operating the pump, which Spot is not shown to do.

sources.title: UVeye Expands AI-Powered Vehicle Inspections to Trucks, Buses, and Commercial Fleets

sources.title: RoboTire Launches Tire Changing System in Second Discount Tire Location

sources.transferJustification: Related task: robotic servicing of a road vehicle. It marks the frontier of deployed vehicle-service robotics — one fixtured operation on a positioned vehicle — and therefore does not extend to multi-step apparatus checks or heterogeneous minor repairs.

instances.label: Daily apparatus-bay housekeeping at the fire station: crew assigned to sweep and scrub/mop the large sealed-concrete bay floor, squeegee wash water to drains, and clear road grit, ash and debris tracked in after runs; officer assigns and works alongside.

Living-quarters floor care between calls: vacuum dayroom, dorm, office and hallway carpet; dust-mop and wet-mop kitchen, corridor, stairwell and locker-room hard floors in a furniture-filled, occupied station.

Station restroom/shower detail: scrub toilets, urinals, sinks, mirrors and shower stalls, mop and disinfect the floor, restock paper and soap, empty trash - small residential-scale bathrooms inside the station.

Kitchen and common-area detail: wash pots/dishes after crew meals, wipe counters, stove, tables and appliances, clean the refrigerator, bag and carry out trash and recycling, run station linens/towels through laundry.

Washing and detailing apparatus and equipment: soap, brush and rinse the engine/ladder after runs and on weekly wash day, including wheels, chrome, windows and cabinet doors, then wipe/chamois dry in the bay or on the apron.
Exterior grounds and apron upkeep at the station: mow and trim the lawn in season, clear leaves, and shovel/blow snow and ice off the apron, walkways and hydrant area in winter.

tasks.label: Maintain knowledge of fire laws and fire prevention techniques and tactics.

instances.label: A fire captain at a municipal station reads and reviews updated fire code adoptions, NFPA standards, state statutes, and departmental SOP/SOG revisions, keeping current on legal requirements for inspections and enforcement.

A battalion chief or company officer completes continuing-education coursework (online modules, National Fire Academy or state fire marshal courses, ICS/officer certification refreshers) to keep certifications and knowledge of prevention techniques current.

A supervisor participates in classroom and tabletop training sessions, drills, and post-incident critiques at the station or training facility, absorbing updated tactics for structure fires, wildland-urban interface, and hazmat.

A fire prevention/inspection supervisor tracks new construction materials, suppression system technologies, and emerging hazards (lithium-ion batteries, solar arrays, EVs) through trade journals, manufacturer bulletins, conferences, and peer networks.
A volunteer or small-department officer keeps up informally through state association meetings, mutual-aid discussions, and periodic code-update bulletins with limited formal training time.

tasks.label: Inspect stations, uniforms, equipment, or recreation areas to ensure compliance with safety standards, taking corrective action as necessary.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Shift-change apparatus and equipment readiness inspection on the station apparatus floor: the captain opens every compartment, verifies the tool/inventory list, checks SCBA cylinder pressures and mask seals, starts saws and the generator, checks fluid levels and tire/brake condition, then corrects deficiencies on the spot (swaps a bottle, replaces a missing tool, re-mounts equipment) or places an item/apparatus out of service and writes the repair request.

Daily station housekeeping and facility safety walkthrough of a fire station built for people: kitchen, bunkroom, bathrooms, apparatus bay, storage and compressor room. The officer looks for slip/trip hazards, oil on the bay floor, clutter blocking egress, improperly stored flammables or gear, damaged cords, and takes immediate corrective action by cleaning or clearing the hazard himself and by assigning crew members to correct the rest.

Inspection of crew uniforms and personal protective equipment: the officer checks each member's duty uniform for compliance and each set of structural turnout gear (coat, pants, hood, gloves, helmet, boots) for soiling, contamination, thermal or abrasion damage, missing reflective trim, and liner integrity; corrective action means pulling gear for advanced cleaning or repair, issuing a spare set, documenting the finding, and counseling the member.

Inspection of the station fitness/recreation area and dayroom: gym equipment condition (frayed cables, loose bolts, worn treadmill belts), weights and plates stowed on racks, clear walking paths, floor mats intact, TV/kitchen appliances in the dayroom; corrective action means tagging out or removing unsafe equipment, restowing loose weights, and submitting a repair request.

Scheduled documented life-safety walkthrough of the station (monthly/quarterly): confirm each portable fire extinguisher is present, charged (gauge in the green), tagged and unobstructed, exit paths and exit signage clear, emergency lighting and posted safety placards in place, no spills or debris in circulation areas; deficiencies are logged on the inspection form and forwarded for service rather than fixed by hand.

Scheduled function testing of specific safety-critical equipment at the station or fleet shop under the officer's supervision: annual hose service test, SCBA performance/flow bench test, ground ladder inspection. Items are laid out and connected to test equipment, pressurized or cycled to the NFPA test protocol, and items that fail are removed from service and marked/documented.

sources.transferJustification: Establishes the boundary for the 'taking corrective action' half of this task: mobile inspection robots collect data autonomously but manipulate objects only under teleoperation, so they cannot autonomously clear a hazard, swap equipment, or handle gear.

tasks.label: Inspect and test new and existing fire protection systems, fire detection systems, and fire safety equipment to ensure that they are operating properly.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Routine in-service company inspection of a small/medium commercial occupancy (retail store, restaurant, warehouse, office suite): walk the premises, verify extinguisher placement/charge/tags, check sprinkler head clearance and control-valve position, read riser and fire pump gauges, verify kitchen hood suppression tag and fusible links, test exit/emergency lighting and any local alarm, then write a deficiency notice citing code sections. Layout, clutter and occupant activity differ at every address.

Acceptance/witness testing of newly installed fire protection and detection systems in a building under construction or renovation: sprinkler hydrostatic and main-drain tests, standpipe test, device-by-device alarm acceptance test (each detector, pull station, waterflow and tamper switch), notification appliance and elevator recall verification, fire pump start test — performed on an active construction site with unfinished surfaces, trades working around, ladders and scaffolds.

Periodic (quarterly/annual) inspection and witness testing of fire alarm, sprinkler, standpipe and fire pump systems in a large institutional or high-rise building (school, hospital, office tower): panel placed on test, pull stations and detectors actuated, inspector's test and main drain valves opened, audibility/visibility of notification appliances checked floor by floor, valves and gauges inspected, results recorded and deficiencies reported.

Functional/flow testing of the department's self-contained breathing apparatus at the fire station or equipment shop: each SCBA mounted on a bench, facepiece integrity, regulator performance, pressure accuracy, low-air alarm and breathing resistance verified against NFPA criteria, pass/fail recorded, failed units tagged out.

Annual service testing of fire hose and servicing/testing of portable fire extinguishers at the station or department shop: hoses connected and pressurized to service test pressure, held and monitored for leaks or bursts, results logged; extinguishers weighed, pressure-checked and hydrostatically tested on schedule, then recharged and tagged.

Fire hydrant and water-supply testing in the district: locating hydrants on streets, parking lots and industrial yards, opening and flowing them, taking static/residual/pitot readings, checking for damaged caps, stems and drainage, flushing and recording flow data for pre-plans — outdoors, in traffic and all weather.

sources.system: Spot (with Orbit/Autowalk and AI visual inspection)

sources.claim: Boston Dynamics' Spot quadruped runs programmed autonomous inspection routes ('Autowalks') in Cargill's oilseed crush and refinery plant, performing visual safety checks that include verifying fire extinguishers are in place and gauges/temperatures are within range; it is a visual presence/condition check, not an actuation test of a fire protection system.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: industrial plant safety rounds. It covers only the visual 'is the extinguisher present and charged' fragment of a fire-safety inspection along a manually taught fixed route; it involves no actuation of alarms, valves or suppression systems and no code-compliance write-up.

sources.title: Cargill Deploys Boston Dynamics' Robot Dog at Amsterdam Facility | Food Engineering
sources.claim: The Cargill deployment runs at high volume without an operator driving the robot, confirming that the inspection missions execute autonomously in a structured industrial facility.

sources.claim: A computerized NFPA-compliant SCBA test bench performs the standardized functional test of a self-contained breathing apparatus once the unit is mounted on the machine, evaluating facepiece integrity, regulator performance, pressure accuracy and alarms and automatically capturing pass/fail results.

instances.label: Routine periodic fire code inspection of a small commercial occupancy (restaurant, retail store, small office): the supervisor walks the premises with a company officer or inspector, checks exits and egress paths, exit/emergency lighting, extinguisher tags and gauges, kitchen hood suppression, electrical panel clearance and extension cords, storage and sprinkler clearances, then discusses findings with the owner and issues a written notice of violation.

Inspection of a large institutional or industrial occupancy (school, hospital, hotel, warehouse, manufacturing plant): multi-floor walkthrough with facility staff, checking fire alarm and sprinkler system condition and service records, standpipes, fire doors, hazardous materials storage, means of egress, and occupant load, producing a report of deficiencies.

Inspection of multi-family residential or mixed-use property: apartment/condo common areas, stairwells, laundry and boiler rooms, sometimes complaint-driven entry into cluttered units; checking smoke alarms, blocked exits, illegal storage, and address/access issues, with occupants present.

Inspection at an active new-construction or renovation site, including acceptance testing of fire protection systems (sprinkler flow/hydrostatic tests, fire alarm functional test, fire pump test, verification of rated assemblies and hydrant access) coordinated with contractors before occupancy sign-off.

Supervisory participation and quality control: accompanying subordinate company officers or fire inspectors on their inspections, spot-checking their findings, coaching on code interpretation, handling disputed or escalated violations on site, and reviewing/approving inspection reports and re-inspections of previously cited properties.

tasks.label: Plan, direct, and supervise prescribed burn projects.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Pre-burn planning phase in the office: the supervisor writes or reviews the prescribed fire plan (objectives, prescription parameters, complexity analysis, contingency and smoke management sections), obtains agency administrator approval and burn permits, orders resources, and coordinates notifications with cooperators, air-quality regulators, and neighbors. Output is approved paperwork and a resource order.

Day-of execution on an agency prescribed burn of tens to hundreds of acres on public forest or grassland: the burn boss checks spot weather against prescription, completes and signs the Go/No-Go checklist, briefs the crew, orders and evaluates a test fire, then directs ignition and holding crews by radio, adjusting firing pattern and pace as fire behavior and wind shift. Crews, not the supervisor, carry drip torches and hold line.

Municipal, county, or state fire department supervisor overseeing small hazard-reduction or landowner-assist burns near the wildland-urban interface: coordinating with the landowner and permitting authority, positioning engines and personnel, notifying dispatch and neighbors, and directing the burn by radio and face-to-face instruction, including calling a shutdown if conditions deteriorate.

Directing the post-ignition phase: assigning crews to mop-up, securing the perimeter, setting patrol and staffing levels for the holdover period, releasing resources, and deciding when the burn is declared out.

Post-burn documentation and review: conducting the after-action review, completing burn accomplishment and smoke-monitoring records, evaluating trainees' task books, and reporting results to the prescribed fire manager or agency administrator.

tasks.label: Investigate disturbances on the premises, such as security alarms, altercations, and suspicious activity.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: After-hours intrusion/door alarm inside a controlled facility (corporate building, school, warehouse, data center). Supervisor is dispatched or self-dispatches to the alarm point, sweeps the area and adjacent corridors, checks the door/window/access point, determines the cause (usually a false trip: cleaning crew, HVAC, badge tailgate), clears or escalates, and logs the event.

Outdoor perimeter or camera alarm at a large fenced site at night and in weather (distribution center, industrial plant, utility yard, employee parking lots). Supervisor drives/walks the fence line, gates, trailers and lots, identifies the cause (animal, wind, vehicle, trespasser), calls officers or police if real, clears and documents.

Suspicious person, loiterer, or unattended vehicle in an occupied, people-facing facility (mall, big-box retail, hospital lobby, campus building). Supervisor approaches and observes, questions the person, checks credentials/receipts/badges, judges intent, issues a trespass warning or escorts the person out, and writes an incident report.

Active altercation or disorderly/violent individual — a fight in a bar, stadium, school hallway, or hospital ED. Supervisor responds fast, separates and de-escalates the parties, may physically restrain or detain, takes statements from participants and witnesses, coordinates guards, police and EMS, and files a report.

Physical anomaly found or reported during a shift: a propped or forced door, unattended package or bag, smell of smoke, water leak, tripped equipment/panel, or an odd noise in a corridor. Supervisor goes to the location, inspects the object or area, decides whether to escalate or secure, and logs the finding.

Contract night patrol of an unstructured site — an active construction site, a vacant or partly gutted building, a remote lot or a residential development — where the layout changes week to week, footing is rough, lighting is poor and there is no institution keeping the premises to a standard.

instances.label: Retail store or shopping mall: the security supervisor responds to a loss-prevention call, contacts a shoplifter or a previously trespassed individual on the sales floor, physically detains/handcuffs or escorts the person to an LP office or off the property, manages resistance and bystanders, and turns the person over to police with documentation.

Corporate office building or campus: supervisor confronts an unbadged intruder, a terminated employee, or a solicitor in a lobby/corridor, verifies identity, verbally directs them out, and physically escorts them through turnstiles/doors off the premises, restraining or holding them if they refuse.

Stadium, arena, casino, or nightclub: supervisor and team eject an intoxicated or rule-violating patron from a dense crowd, moving through seating aisles or a gaming floor, applying escort holds or restraint if the patron resists, and handing off to police at an exit.

Industrial yard, warehouse, distribution center, or utility site at night: supervisor responds to a perimeter alarm, locates a trespasser (scrapper, encampment occupant, fisherman) in an unlit outdoor area with uneven terrain, orders them off the property, escorts them to the gate, and detains or holds for police if uncooperative.

Apartment complex, parking garage, or transit station: supervisor evicts loiterers, unauthorized vehicle occupants, or persons sleeping in stairwells, sometimes at night and sometimes involving intoxicated or mentally ill individuals, removing them physically when verbal direction fails.

tasks.label: Screen individuals and belongings to prevent passage of prohibited materials using walkthrough detectors, wands, or bag searches.

instances.label: Fixed entry checkpoint at an institutional building (courthouse, government office, hospital, K-12 school): supervisor works/backs up the magnetometer and X-ray lane, directs visitors to divest and place bags on the belt, hand-wands those who alarm, opens and hand-searches bags, confiscates and logs prohibited items (knives, pepper spray), and turns people away or calls police.

Large-venue event entry screening (stadium, arena, concert hall, theme park): high-throughput gate lines, walkthrough weapons-detection portals or magnetometers plus bag-check tables, wanding and targeted pat-downs of alarms, rummaging through purses/backpacks/coolers, resolving disputes over prohibited items with patrons in crowded, noisy conditions.

Corporate/industrial facility screening: visitor and contractor screening at a lobby or plant gate, plus random employee exit bag/lunchbox/tool-bag checks at a warehouse, distribution center, casino back-of-house, or manufacturing plant; supervisor operates the detector, inspects containers, and documents finds.

Bar/nightclub/private-party door screening: supervisor at the door of a queue that extends onto the sidewalk, performing hand-wanding and pat-downs, opening purses and jackets, in low light, crowded and often with intoxicated or uncooperative patrons; no fixed lane or conveyor.

Mobile or ad-hoc screening at temporary/outdoor sites: festival or rally entry in a public park, a temporary event tent, or a construction-site gate; portable wands and folding tables set up on uneven ground, variable weather, layout and crowd flow different each time.

tasks.label: Inspect and adjust security equipment to ensure it is operational or to detect evidence of tampering.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Interior equipment round at a fixed site (office tower, hospital, campus, plant): the supervisor walks the building checking installed CCTV cameras (housing intact, lens clean, aim correct, no obstruction or tamper), card readers, door contacts and mag locks, duress/panic buttons and intercoms; badges at readers, presses test buttons and confirms signal at the console, re-aims or wipes a camera, resets a tripped device, and tags faults for the technician.

Shift-change check of portable/issued security equipment at the guard office: two-way radios (power, channel, radio check, battery), body-worn cameras and docks, flashlights, handheld metal-detector wands, keys and key cabinets; swap batteries, correct settings, remove and tag defective units, log results.

Daily verification of screening equipment at a checkpoint (airport, courthouse, stadium, federal building): run the prescribed operational/calibration test on the walk-through metal detector and X-ray unit with test pieces, verify handheld wand and trace-detection function, inspect tamper seals and cabling on the machines, adjust sensitivity or settings to the standard, and record the check.

Off-hours perimeter integrity round at a fenced industrial/logistics/utility site: drive or walk the fence line and yard verifying that fencing, gates, exterior doors and windows are secure and undamaged, spotting cut fabric, forced hardware or other visible tampering, and reporting anomalies to the console.

Exterior security-device operational check at the same fenced site: exterior PTZ/fixed cameras, fence-mounted sensors, gate operators, call boxes, alarm enclosures and lighting; test each device with the console, clean or re-aim a camera, reseat/reset a device, tighten a loose mount, check enclosure seals for tampering, in rain, heat or darkness.

Contract-guard supervisor's mobile rounds across several client sites in a shift (construction site trailers with temporary cameras, vacant property, small retail strip, apartment complex): each site has a different, often improvised equipment set; check that cameras, alarm panels, temporary lighting and locks work and show no tampering, make small adjustments, and file a site report.

tasks.label: Rescue survivors from burning buildings, accident sites, and water hazards.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Primary search and rescue inside a burning single-family home or apartment: crawling in zero-visibility, high-heat smoke while on SCBA, sweeping rooms, finding an unconscious or disoriented occupant (possibly a child or bariatric adult), and dragging/carrying them down stairs or out a window to the exterior for EMS handoff, under collapse and flashover risk.

Rescue at a motor-vehicle crash: stabilizing a wrecked car on a roadway or ditch, managing fuel/EV battery hazards, cutting doors/roof with hydraulic tools, holding manual C-spine, and removing an entrapped, injured occupant onto a backboard/stretcher in traffic, weather, and darkness.

Removing occupants from a smoke-filled multi-family or commercial building: leading or physically assisting ambulatory, panicked, elderly or mobility-impaired people down stairways, and ladder/aerial rescues of people at windows or balconies, with irregular floor plans, crowding and debris.

Open/moving water rescue: swift-water flood, river current, ice, surf, capsized boat or submerged vehicle — reaching a struggling or unconscious victim, controlling them in current or cold water, and getting them to shore/boat for care.

Water rescue in calm, monitored water at a controlled aquatic facility: a submerged or struggling swimmer in a public swimming pool or lifeguarded swim lake, with the victim's position observable from fixed camera coverage or bystander report, retrieved and brought to the pool edge/shore.

Technical rescue: confined-space, trench collapse, high-angle rope, elevator or machinery entrapment — packaging a trapped, injured worker in a harness/litter after shoring or disentanglement and hauling them out to grade.

sources.title: Colossus - ROBOTS: Your Guide to the World of Robotics
sources.claim: Colossus, the best-known fire-service ground robot (Notre-Dame, structure and industrial fires), performs support work including dragging/carrying loads and casualty evacuation only under continuous remote piloting by a firefighter; no autonomous victim search-and-removal capability is claimed.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-assisted interior fire attack and casualty evacuation in burning structures. It is the closest fielded system to interior rescue, and its strictly teleoperated control shows the state of the art does not autonomously locate and remove victims from fire buildings.

sources.title: From Whales to Silver Foxes to Refugees: EMILY Robot is A Lifesaver | Office of Naval Research
sources.claim: EMILY, the most widely fielded water-rescue robot, is a remote-controlled motorized buoy driven by a human operator from shore; it delivers flotation to victims rather than autonomously completing a rescue.
sources.transferJustification: Direct task match (rescue of survivors from water hazards); cited to establish that fielded water-rescue robots are human-piloted, not autonomous.

sources.system: Autonomous underwater rescue robot (based on DEDAVE AUV)
sources.developer: Fraunhofer Institute for Optronics, System Technologies and Image Exploitation IOSB-AST, Ilmenau, with Wasserrettungsdienst Halle e.V.
sources.title: An autonomous underwater robot saves people from drowning — Fraunhofer-Gesellschaft
sources.claim: Fraunhofer IOSB-AST built an autonomous underwater rescue robot that, cued by fixed pool ceiling cameras (or drones over a swim lake), dives to the victim's coordinates, grips and secures the body, surfaces and carries it to shore; open-water test retrieved an 80 kg dummy from 3 m depth and delivered it 40 m to waiting rescuers in about two minutes.
sources.transferJustification: Direct task match for retrieving a submerged victim from calm, camera-monitored water; the setting is an instrumented pool or supervised swim lake, not moving water.

sources.system: Quadrupedal emergency transport robot / emergency rescue robot
sources.developer: CSSC Haishen Company with DEEP Robotics
sources.title: World's 1st emergency rescue robot, transport robot unveiled in China, operate from -20 C to 55 C - People's Daily Online
sources.claim: A quadrupedal emergency transport robot unveiled in Beijing carried an injured person on ... evacuation during a staged public demonstration; the reports do not establish that victim location, loading, or route selection were done without human control.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: carrying an injured person out of a hazard area, the removal step of firefighter rescue. Cited because it is the strongest recent claim of robotic victim carriage, yet autonomy is unestablished and the demonstration was staged.

sources.title: The Army is testing medevac drones that lift injured soldiers from battlefields
sources.claim: US Army casualty-evacuation drone trials in a NATO exercise flew a test dummy that soldiers loaded onto the aircraft; the robot performs transport only, with humans doing the locating, extrication and loading of the casualty.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: casualty evacuation from an incident scene. It shows even the most advanced casualty-movement robotics still require humans for the search, extrication and packaging steps that dominate firefighter rescue.

tasks.label: Administer first aid and cardiopulmonary resuscitation to injured persons or provide emergency medical care such as basic or advanced life support.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Medical call at a private residence: engine/ambulance crew enters a cluttered home, finds an unresponsive or ill patient on a floor, bed or bathroom, assesses airway/breathing/circulation and vitals, performs CPR and AED/defibrillation or gives oxygen, obtains IV access and administers medications, then packages and moves the patient for transport, with family present.

Trauma care at a roadway crash or other outdoor public scene: patient in or near a wrecked vehicle or on a sidewalk, in traffic/weather; crew controls bleeding with pressure dressings and tourniquets, maintains manual c-spine precautions, splints fractures, performs rapid trauma assessment and monitors vitals during and after extrication.

EMS response inside an institutional facility (nursing home, assisted living, school, office building, arena): staff meet the crew, patient is in a bed, wheelchair or hallway; crew takes report, assesses, treats (oxygen, glucose, cardiac monitoring, CPR if arrest), and lifts/transfers the patient to a stretcher.

Patient care at a working fire or rescue incident: treating civilians for smoke inhalation and burns and monitoring/rehabbing firefighters at the scene in full PPE, outdoors amid hose lines, apparatus, heat and debris; vitals, oxygen, cooling, cardiac monitoring.

Multi-patient or mass-casualty incident (bus crash, shooting, structure collapse): rapid triage of several patients, tourniquets and airway positioning, tagging and prioritizing, repeated reassessment while more units arrive.

sources.title: 81,468 chest compressions, applied perfectly | City of Covington, KY
sources.claim: Mechanical chest-compression devices such as the Stryker LUCAS 3 are widely deployed by US fire departments and deliver machine-controlled compressions, but a human crew must assess the patient, position the backplate and piston on the chest, and perform all other assessment, airway, defibrillation and drug care.
sources.transferJustification: Mechanical CPR is a sub-step of this task, not the whole instance; the device is a passive tool that must be carried, placed and aligned on the patient by firefighters, who retain assessment, airway, defibrillation and medication duties, so it does not substantiate autonomous completion at any tier.

sources.title: Performance, Safety, and Patient Experience of an Autonomous Robotic Phlebotomy Device: A Multicenter Trial (Clinical Chemistry)
sources.claim: An autonomous robotic phlebotomy device performs needle insertion without an operator in hospital outpatient departments, but only on a cooperative seated patient who places an arm into the machine's fixture, with a professional supervising up to three devices.
sources.transferJustification: Related task is venous access, one sub-step of advanced life support. Transfer fails: the device is a stationary fixture requiring a conscious, cooperative patient to insert an arm in a hospital phlebotomy room, and it performs no patient assessment, CPR, airway, hemorrhage control or patient movement.

sources.title: Sensor-guided robots could boost lifesaving combat casualty care | DARPA
sources.claim: Autonomous robotic treatment of severe bleeding is still a research goal: DARPA launched the MASH program in 2025 to develop robots that locate and stop torso hemorrhage with limited human help, indicating no fielded system does this today.
sources.transferJustification: Directly relevant to emergency hemorrhage care; cited as a statement of program intent only, which cannot support a positive capability judgment.

sources.system: Triage Challenge systems (Coordinated Robotics, DART, RoboScout)
sources.developer: DARPA / competing university and industry teams
sources.title: DART and MSAI triumph at DARPA Triage Challenge | DARPA
sources.claim: In DARPA's 2025 Triage Challenge, autonomous air and ground robots located casualties and assessed vital signs and injuries on staged mass-casualty courses, but the robots only detected and assessed patients — they did not administer any treatment.
sources.transferJustification: Related task is field casualty assessment/triage, the assessment half of this task. It does not transfer to completion: these systems deliver no first aid, CPR, airway management or medication, and operate as competition demonstrations rather than accepted patient care.

sources.title: Robot performs first realistic surgery without human help | Johns Hopkins Hub
sources.claim: The most advanced autonomous medical manipulation demonstrated to date is soft-tissue surgery on anesthetized animals in a highly controlled laboratory setting, not care of an injured person found in place.
sources.transferJustification: Related task is autonomous manipulation of human-like tissue. Transfer fails: the patient is anesthetized, immobilized and surgically exposed in a lab, with no requirement to approach, assess, resuscitate or move a spontaneously positioned emergency patient.

tasks.label: Dress with equipment such as fire-resistant clothing and breathing apparatus.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Alarm sounds at the station: firefighter runs to the apparatus-bay gear rack and dons the full structural ensemble — bunker boots/pants, coat, hood, gloves, helmet with chinstrap — inside roughly one minute, then straps into the seat-mounted SCBA harness in the moving apparatus en route.

At the incident curbside/fireground: donning or re-donning SCBA facepiece, hood and gloves off the rig, seating and sealing the mask, opening the cylinder valve, running the seal/air check and PASS activation, on uneven ground, at night, in smoke and cold or rain, under time pressure.

Field change into mission-specific protective gear at the scene: wildland brush coat/pants, shelter and line gear; or technical/water rescue PPE (harness, helmet, PFD, dry or ice-rescue suit) donned on a roadside, riverbank or wildland staging area.

Hazmat response: donning a Level A/B encapsulating chemical suit over SCBA in the cold zone of an industrial or roadside incident, with buddy assistance, taping seams, boot and glove ring attachment, and a checklist-verified integrity check before entry.
EMS/medical response at the station or in the ambulance module: donning exam gloves, eye protection, N95 respirator and gown before patient contact, and swapping/doffing between patients.
Station routine: donning drills and timed skills evaluations, SCBA fit testing, and putting on PPE for daily equipment checks, apparatus washdown or training-tower evolutions.

sources.system: Baxter robot-assisted dressing system (Zhang & Demiris, Imperial College London)
sources.developer: Imperial College London Personal Robotics Lab
sources.title: Learning Grasping Points for Garment Manipulation in Robot-Assisted Dressing (IEEE/IROS)
sources.claim: State-of-the-art robot-assisted dressing: a Baxter robot autonomously picks up a hospital gown from a rail and dresses a seated user's upper body in a laboratory setup — one loose garment, cooperative user, no fasteners, straps or respirators.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: robot-assisted dressing of a person. It is the closest robotic capability to donning protective clothing, but it covers only a single loose sleeved garment on a cooperative seated user in a lab, with no boots, helmet, straps, buckles, gloves or breathing apparatus, and at speeds far slower than the one-minute firefighting standard, so it does not carry over to donning a structural firefighting ensemble and SCBA.

sources.title: Self-Wearing Adaptive Garments via Soft Robotic Unfurling (arXiv:2507.07221)
sources.claim: A bespoke soft-robotic garment (SWAG) with pneumatic unfurling tubes dresses a wearer autonomously in about ten seconds in laboratory demonstrations; it is a purpose-built garment, not standard protective clothing, and does not handle helmets, boots or breathing apparatus.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous dressing of a human body. The garment itself is the actuator, so it applies only to specially fabricated soft garments; certified fire-resistant turnout gear, SCBA harness, facepiece seal and helmet cannot be replaced by or actuated as an unfurling tube garment, so the capability does not transfer.

sources.title: PPE Drills: Donning Quickly and Properly - Firefighter Training
sources.claim: Firefighter donning is held to a one-minute performance standard covering boots, pants, coat, gloves, hood ..., with a separate timed standard for SCBA, facepiece and going on air — the quality/speed bar any substitute must meet.
sources.transferJustification: Not a robotic system; cited only to establish the accepted-output bar (completeness and one-minute speed) for the task.

sources.developer: Howe & Howe Technologies (Textron), operated by Los Angeles Fire Department
sources.title: LAFD Unveils New RS3 Firefighting Robot
sources.claim: Robots that do operate on the fireground, such as the LAFD's Thermite RS3, are remote-controlled tracked nozzle vehicles that are inherently heat-resistant; they neither wear nor don protective clothing or breathing apparatus.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: fire attack by a fireground robot. Cited to show that deployed fireground robotics is teleoperated vehicle work and provides no demonstration of donning protective clothing or breathing apparatus.

tasks.label: Move toward the source of a fire, using knowledge of types of fires, construction design, building materials, and physical layout of properties.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Single-family or small residential structure fire: crew masks up, forces the door, advances a charged 1¾-inch hoseline through zero-visibility smoke and heat, reads smoke/fire behavior and the dwelling's layout to find the seat of the fire (kitchen, bedroom, basement), and positions to attack while avoiding collapse and flashover.

Vehicle, dumpster, rubbish or small outdoor fire on a public street or parking lot: engine company approaches from uphill/upwind, sizes up hazards (fuel tank, struts, hybrid battery, wires), pulls a line, and moves in on the burning object to knock it down.

Apartment building, hotel or high-rise fire: crew climbs stairwells, uses the standpipe, tracks apartment numbering and door layout, advances a stretched line down a smoke-charged public corridor to the fire apartment door, and controls the door before pushing in.

Commercial or light-industrial building fire (store, restaurant, warehouse, plant): heavy fire load and unfamiliar interior layout; crew advances through racks/partitions toward the fire's seat, or works a defensive approach with master streams when truss roofs or contents make entry unsafe.

Wildland/vegetation or wildland-urban-interface fire: crew hikes or drives a brush engine over unimproved terrain, reads fuel type, slope and wind, moves along the fire's flank toward the head, and applies water or cuts line at the fire's edge with escape routes identified.

Large flammable-liquid or industrial process fire at a fixed facility (tank farm, refinery, chemical plant, fuel depot): crew works from a pre-planned facility layout, advances hoselines/monitors as close as radiant heat allows, and cools/extinguishes from a defensive position.

sources.system: MHI Firefighting Robot System (Water Cannon Robot + Hose Extension Robot)
sources.title: FIREFIGHTING ROBOT SYSTEM : Product | Mitsubishi Heavy Industries
sources.claim: MHI's Water Cannon Robot travels autonomously to a designated position on ... and discharges water/foam at 4,000 L/min while withstanding 20 kW/m² radiant heat; the paired Hose Extension Robot autonomously lays up to 300 m of supply hose.
sources.transferJustification: Directly the task: the machine moves itself toward the fire source and takes up an attack position, the firefighter's advance-to-the-fire step.

sources.system: Firefighting robot system for petroleum complexes (flying/ground recon robots, water cannon robot, hose-laying robot)
sources.developer: Mitsubishi Heavy Industries / Japan Fire and Disaster Management Agency National Research Institute of Fire and Disaster
sources.title: A firefighting robot system that can be applied to large-scale fires in petroleum complexes | The Japan Society of Mechanical Engineers
sources.claim: The MHI/FDMA firefighting robot system has been fielded with a Japanese municipal fire department for petroleum-complex fires; the command system plans routes and discharge positions for operator approval, and the robots then move, lay hose and discharge water without human intervention near the burning facility.

sources.title: MHI Develops Autonomous "Water Cannon Robot" and "Hose Extension Robot" for Use in Firefighting
sources.claim: MHI publicly demonstrated the autonomous hose-connected robot pair maneuvering close to a fire scene with 4,000 L/min discharge, aimed at petrochemical plant fires humans cannot approach.

sources.system: Team NimbRo autonomous firefighting UAV "Splasher" and UGV
sources.title: Autonomous Fire Fighting with a UAV-UGV Team at MBZIRC 2020 (arXiv)
sources.claim: At the MBZIRC 2020 competition arena, autonomous UAV and UGV systems had to detect, approach and ... simulated fires both outside and inside a purpose-built building, using LiDAR localization and thermal tracking; Team NimbRo's ground robot drove through a door and inside the structure to the heat source, though competition runs suffered hardware failures.
sources.transferJustification: Same task: detect a fire source, navigate to it (including inside a building) and apply water; the arena fires are standardized props presented at fixed stations.

sources.developer: Howe & Howe / Textron Systems (operated by Los Angeles Fire Department)
sources.title: LAFD Debuts the RS3: First Robotic Firefighting Vehicle in the United States / Fire Departments Adopt Robotic Technologies for Their Operations
sources.claim: The only robotic firefighting vehicle in regular US structural fire service use is remotely operated by a firefighter with a controller and cameras, and is used mainly for defensive operations at commercial structure fires (39 assignments in its first years with LAFD).

sources.system: Sikorsky MATRIX Black Hawk with Rain Wildfire Mission Autonomy
sources.title: Sikorsky & Rain demonstrate autonomous flight capability to combat wildfires - Vertical Mag
sources.claim: Sikorsky and Rain demonstrated an optionally piloted Black Hawk that autonomously takes off, identifies a small fire's location and size, and drops water on it, tested on propane and live brush piles in California terrain; this is aerial suppression support, not ground crew advance.
sources.transferJustification: Related task (aerial initial attack): the aircraft moves itself to the fire source, but it does not deliver the ground crew's accepted output of a secured, lined and mopped-up fire edge.

sources.title: CAL FIRE and Overland AI Lead First Evaluation of Autonomous Ground Vehicles for Wildfire Response
sources.claim: CAL FIRE and Overland AI evaluated fully autonomous off-road ULTRA ground vehicles in wildfire operations at Camp Pendleton, but the autonomous missions were resupply, logistics and camera-based situational awareness rather than advancing on the fire to suppress it.

tasks.label: Drive and operate fire fighting vehicles and equipment.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: Emergency ('code 3') response driving of an engine/pumper from the station to an incident over public streets: lights and siren, clearing intersections against red lights, negotiating traffic that yields unpredictably, then spotting the rig at a hydrant or in front of the building so hose lines and other apparatus can work.

Working the pump panel at a structure fire: making the hydrant or drafting supply connection, engaging the pump, charging 1.75-in and 2.5-in attack lines, setting and adjusting discharge pressures as lines are added, shut down, and gated, on a smoky, congested fireground.

Aerial ladder / tower ladder operation: spotting the truck, setting outriggers on uneven street surfaces, raising and extending the aerial to a roof or upper-floor window for access, and running an elevated master stream onto the fire.

Station work: daily/weekly apparatus and equipment checks (fluid levels, pump test, generator, saws and other power tools started and run, SCBA and hose inventory, lights and warning devices) plus low-speed maneuvering and backing the rig into the apparatus bay and on the drill ground.

Aircraft rescue and firefighting at an airport: responding across the movement area to a standby or crash site under ATC control, then applying foam/water from the roof turret, bumper turret, or high-reach extendable turret onto burning fuel and the fuselage.

Wildland/brush engine work: driving unimproved dirt roads and off-road terrain to a vegetation fire, and pump-and-roll operation, driving slowly along a flank while flowing water from the bumper line or booster reel.

sources.developer: Howe & Howe Technologies (Textron Systems), operated by Los Angeles Fire Department
sources.title: LAFD Debuts the RS3: First Robotic Firefighting Vehicle in the United States
sources.claim: The LAFD's Thermite RS3 firefighting robot, in service since 2020, is a tracked firefighting vehicle that flows large water volumes but is driven and aimed by a human operator with a hand controller and video feed - i.e., teleoperated, not autonomous.
sources.transferJustification: Same task family (driving and operating a firefighting vehicle at incidents); cited to show the state of fielded fire-service robots is teleoperation, which cannot support a positive judgment.

sources.developer: Hyundai Motor Group / Hyundai Rotem with Korea National Fire Agency
sources.title: Hyundai Motor Group Donates Unmanned Firefighting Robots to Korea National Fire Agency for Safeguarding Firefighters
sources.claim: Hyundai Motor Group's Unmanned Firefighting Robot, donated to Korea's National Fire Agency and used at live fires in 2026, is driven and fought from a remote operator station; on-board autonomy is limited to collision-avoidance driver assistance.
sources.transferJustification: Same task (driving a firefighting vehicle and operating its water cannon at real fires); shows the most advanced fielded mobile firefighting vehicle remains human-driven, so mobile fire attack is not autonomous at E2/E3.

sources.title: Unifire's Force 50 Fire Monitors Attain RINA Compliance to New SOLAS & FSS Code for Ro-Ro Passenger Ship Weather Deck Fire Protection
sources.claim: Unifire's FlameRanger is a commercially available autonomous robotic fire suppression system: fixed, plumbed robotic monitors (Force 50) coupled to IR3 flame detectors that detect, locate, aim at and suppress a fire without human intervention; certified for ship weather decks and marketed for hangars, waste facilities and building facades.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: operating a fire monitor/pumped water stream on a real fire. When the water supply and nozzle are fixtured as a purpose-built installation presents them, this covers the water-delivery core of pump-panel and master-stream operation with comparable flows and targets.

sources.system: Autonomous fire monitor system (Unifire FlameRanger tested in LASH FIRE WP10)
sources.developer: LASH FIRE consortium (EU H2020) with Unifire AB
sources.title: WP10 | lashfire.eu
sources.claim: The EU LASH FIRE research project tested autonomous fire monitor systems against real vehicle-deck fires and found they detected, located and accurately targeted the fire within seconds with no human involvement, achieving fire control.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: applying a pumped water stream to a developing fuel/vehicle fire - the same suppression function a pump operator and elevated master stream deliver, verified by third-party fire testing rather than vendor claims.

sources.title: Unifire Force 50 Robotic Nozzle (Remote Control Fire Monitor) - Unifire AB
sources.claim: FlameRanger autonomous monitor installations are supplied for elevated facade protection and for aircraft hangars, waste and recycling facilities and battery storage - fixed installations that autonomously put water or foam on fires in those zones.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: elevated stream application onto facades/upper floors and foam application onto aircraft/fuel fires in hangars - the suppression outputs of aerial master-stream and ARFF turret work, delivered from a purpose-built fixed mounting.

sources.title: Cat Minestar Command for Hauling Manages the Autonomous Ecosystem to Increase Haulage Efficiency, Enhance Safety
sources.claim: Caterpillar's Cat MineStar Command for hauling runs hundreds of driverless 100+ ton haul trucks at dozens of mine sites, navigating shared haul roads among light vehicles and equipment and spotting precisely at loading and dumping points; over 8.6 billion tonnes hauled autonomously with no reported injuries.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: driving a very heavy vehicle at speed to an assigned point inside an institution-controlled site and spotting it precisely. Comparable vehicle mass and maneuvering precision to positioning a fire apparatus at a designated location on controlled premises.

sources.title: Aurora Begins Commercial Driverless Trucking in Texas, Ushering in a New Era of Freight
sources.claim: Aurora operates Class 8 driverless trucks in commercial freight service on Texas public highways, showing heavy-truck autonomy in normal traffic - but as routine, traffic-law-abiding driving, not emergency response.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous heavy-vehicle driving. Shows normal-speed highway driving is solved for Class 8 vehicles, while nothing in the record covers emergency-mode driving (siren, red-light traversal, opposing lanes) or fireground spotting.

sources.title: Waymo launching driverless robotaxis in 5 more cities
sources.claim: Waymo runs driverless robotaxis at scale on urban public roads (100+ million fully autonomous miles, 250,000+ paid rides per week), operating as ordinary traffic that yields to emergency vehicles rather than performing emergency response.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous driving on unstructured public streets. Establishes the ceiling of demonstrated street autonomy (law-abiding light vehicles), which does not extend to code-3 apparatus response.

sources.title: The World's First Autonomous Piling System for Utility-Scale Solar - Built Robotics
sources.claim: Built Robotics' RPD 35 is a fully ... heavy hydraulic boom machine (converted excavator) that surveys, distributes, positions and drives solar foundation piles unaided on construction sites at up to 300 piles per ..., deployed commercially with contractor Blattner.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: autonomous control of a large hydraulic boom to place a heavy end-effector at surveyed coordinates. Comparable boom kinematics and placement precision to positioning an aerial device tip at a designated point once the machine is set up.

tasks.label: Respond to fire alarms and other calls for assistance, such as automobile and industrial accidents.

automationEvidence.assessmentType: Published AI-assisted research assessment; not an independently observed task trial

instances.label: EMS/medical aid call (the largest share of run volume): tones drop, crew dons gear and rides the engine or ambulance emergency-mode through city streets to a private residence, business, or roadway; forces or negotiates entry, reaches the patient (often on a floor, in a bathroom, or up stairs), assesses, provides BLS care (airway, O2, CPR/AED, bleeding control), moves the patient to the stretcher, and assists transport.

Automatic fire alarm / alarm activation at a commercial, institutional, or multifamily building: apparatus responds through traffic, crew performs 360 size-up, contacts building staff, walks the building with TIC and irons, locates the cause (burnt food, steam, water-flow, detector fault, contractor dust), mitigates or confirms nothing found, resets the FACP, and returns to service.

Motor vehicle crash on a street or highway: respond emergency-mode, block traffic with the apparatus, stabilize the vehicle, control fuel/battery/airbag hazards, gain access to occupants, provide patient care and, if needed, extricate with hydraulic tools, then clean up fluids and debris.

Reported structure fire in a house or commercial occupancy: turnout in full PPE and SCBA, drive to an unfamiliar address, establish water supply, force entry, stretch and advance a hoseline into a smoke-filled interior, search for occupants, ventilate, overhaul and salvage.

Public-service / miscellaneous calls: odor of smoke or gas investigation, CO alarm, water leak or flooded basement, downed power line, elevator entrapment, lock-in, animal or person assist, arriving at varied private and public sites with unknown conditions.

On-site industrial or airport brigade response inside institution-controlled premises: an alarm or incipient fire in a refinery unit, waste/recycling plant, hangar, or terminal building; the on-site crew responds within the fenced facility, applies water/foam to the fire, confirms extinguishment, and hands the area back to operations.

sources.system: Unifire FlameRanger (robotic nozzle / automatic fire monitor)
sources.title: UNIFIRE's FlameRanger—The World's Most Advanced Autonomous Robotic Fire Suppression System
sources.claim: Unifire's FlameRanger is a commercially sold fixed robotic monitor system that autonomously detects a flame and aims and discharges water/foam onto it within seconds, installed in waste-to-energy, recycling and other large indoor/outdoor spaces; it covers only pre-engineered, plumbed coverage zones.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: automatic fire detection and suppression at a fixed installation. It covers only the 'alarm-to-water-on-the-fire' portion of a response, in a setting engineered around the machine (fixed monitor, plumbed supply, mapped line-of-sight zone); it does not travel, investigate, search, or handle patients.

sources.title: Waste & Recycling – Unifire
sources.claim: Unifire markets FlameRanger/HeatRanger for waste and recycling facilities as suppressing fires fully automatically after an alarm event, with no human in the loop.
sources.transferJustification: Same related task as above: fixed automatic suppression inside an institution-controlled industrial facility, supporting only the fire-knockdown element of an on-site brigade response.

sources.title: LAFD Unveils New RS3 Firefighting Robot
sources.claim: The Thermite RS3, the robotic firefighting vehicle in service with LAFD since 2020 and bought by other US departments, is remotely operated by a firefighter with a controller; it is carried to fires by crews and cannot respond or operate on its own.

sources.title: Colossus firefighting robot - Shark Robotics
sources.claim: Shark Robotics' Colossus, the best-known fire-service ground robot in Europe and the US (used at Notre-Dame), operates under continuous remote control by firefighters at structural fires, tunnels and industrial plants.

sources.system: Firefighting Robot System (Water Cannon Robot + Hose Extension Robot)
sources.developer: Mitsubishi Heavy Industries / Japan Fire and Disaster Management Agency
sources.title: Japan's First Firefighting Robot Deployed at Oil Refinery Firefighters | Firehouse
sources.claim: Japan's national Firefighting Robot System (MHI) — a water-cannon robot plus hose-extension robot — is deployed at the Ichihara City Fire Department for petrochemical complex fires; the robots drive themselves into position and lay hose, but are carried to the scene on human-driven transport vehicles and directed from a manned command unit.
sources.transferJustification: Related task: applying master-stream water at a petrochemical fire. It substantiates autonomous positioning and hose laying inside an industrial complex but not the call response itself (turnout, driving, size-up, search), which crews still perform.

sources.title: Fire Rover Remote Firefighting in Waste Management | Fike
sources.claim: Fire Rover, the widely installed AI-thermal fire detection and suppression product for waste, recycling and industrial sites, always routes detections to a live remote human operator who verifies the threat and activates the suppression spray.

sources.system: Skydio X10 DFR (Orlando Police Department network)
sources.title: Orlando Police Launch 11-Drone Skydio DFR Network
